nodes.title: INTRODUCTION
nodes.heading: INTRODUCTION
nodes.start_phrase:
The following is Management’s discussion and analysis of the 
financial condition and results of operations (“MD&A”) of 
JPMorgan Chase & Co. (“JPMorgan Chase” or the “Firm”) for 
the second quarter of 2022 .
nodes.summary:
- Presents the MD&A for JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s Q2 2022 Form 10-Q, to be read with the 2021 Form 10-K; references a glossary and LOB metrics (pp. 182–190).
- Includes forward-looking statements with cautionary notes; directs readers to the Form 10-Q (p. 87) and 2021 Form 10-K risk factors (pp. 9–33); no obligation to update such statements.
- Provides a firm overview: a Delaware-incorporated (1968) U.S.-based global financial services firm with $3.8 trillion in assets and $286.1 billion in stockholders’ equity as of June 30, 2022; leading in investment banking, consumer/small business banking, commercial banking, transaction processing, and asset management; operates under J.P. Morgan and Chase brands serving U.S. consumers and global corporate, institutional, and government clients.
- Identifies principal subsidiaries: JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. (U.S. branches in 48 states and Washington, D.C. as of June 30, 2022) and J.P. Morgan Securities LLC (U.S. broker-dealer); key non-U.S. operating subsidiaries are J.P. Morgan Securities plc (U.K.) and J.P. Morgan SE (Germany), both subsidiaries of JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
- Outlines management reporting segments: Consumer & Community Banking (CCB), Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB), Commercial Banking (CB), Asset & Wealth Management (AWM), plus a Corporate segment; references notes in the Form 10-Q and 2021 Form 10-K for segment details.
- States availability of SEC filings (Forms 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K) on the firm’s website and the SEC’s website; notes that important information is posted on the firm’s and Investor Relations websites and that website information is not incorporated by reference into the Form 10-Q.

nodes.title: EXECUTIVE OVERVIEW
nodes.heading: EXECUTIVE OVERVIEW
nodes.start_phrase:
This executive overview of the MD&A highlights selected information and does not contain all of the information that is important to 
readers of this Form 10-Q.
nodes.summary:
- Document scope: Executive Overview of JPMorgan Chase’s MD&A in the Q2 2022 Form 10-Q, intended to be read with the full 10-Q and the 2021 Form 10-K; comparisons are vs. Q2 2021 unless noted.

- Headline results: Net income $8.6B (down 28%); diluted EPS $2.76 (down 27%); ROE 13%, ROTCE 17%.

- Revenue: Total net revenue up 1% to $30.7B.
  - Net interest income (NII) up 19% to $15.1B; NII excluding Markets up 26% to $13.7B, driven by higher rates and balance sheet growth.
  - Noninterest revenue down 12% to $15.6B, reflecting:
    - Lower Investment Banking fees.
    - A loss in Credit Adjustments & Other versus a prior-year gain, and net losses on equity investments in CIB.
    - Lower Card income in CCB.
    - $337MM of markdowns on held-for-sale positions, primarily unfunded commitments, in the bridge financing portfolio in CIB and CB.
    - Partially offset by higher CIB Markets revenue.
  - On a managed basis: Markets revenue $7.8B (up 15%); total net revenue $31.6B (up 1%); NIR excluding Markets down 26%; NII excluding Markets up 26%.

- Expenses: Noninterest expense up 6% to $18.7B, driven by continued investments (technology, marketing) and higher structural expenses (primarily compensation), partially offset by lower revenue-related compensation.

- Credit: Provision for credit losses of $1.1B, including a net $428MM addition to the allowance for credit losses, primarily due to loan growth and a modest deterioration in the macroeconomic outlook.

- Profitability before credit: Pre-provision profit $12.0B (down 7%).

- Capital and book value: CET1 ratio 12.2%, Tier 1 14.1%, Total capital 15.7%; book value per share $86.38 (up 2%); tangible book value per share $69.53 (up 1%). Capital metrics reflect Federal Reserve COVID-19 relief, including CECL capital transition provisions.

- Year-to-date context (six months ended June 30, 2022 vs. 2021): Total net revenue down 2% to $61.4B; net income $16.9B (down 35%); diluted EPS $5.39 (down 35%).

nodes.title: Firmwide overview
nodes.heading: Firmwide overview
nodes.start_phrase:
For the second quarter of 2022 , JPMorgan Chase reported 
net income of $ 8.6 billion, down 28%, earnings per share 
of $2.76, an ROE of 13% and ROTCE of 17%.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Executive overview of JPMorgan Chase’s MD&A in the Q2 2022 Form 10‑Q, highlighting firmwide performance and key drivers versus Q2 2021 (and year-to-date), with references to non-GAAP measures and capital framework relief.
- Earnings and profitability: Net income $8.6B (−28%); EPS $2.76 (−27%); ROE 13%; ROTCE 17%; pre-provision profit down 7%.
- Revenue mix: Total net revenue $30.7B (+1%). Net interest income $15.1B (+19%); NII excluding Markets $13.7B (+26%) on higher rates and balance sheet growth. Noninterest revenue $15.6B (−12%) on lower Investment Banking fees, losses in Credit Adjustments & Other versus prior-year gain, net losses on equity investments, lower Card income, and $337M markdowns on held-for-sale bridge financing positions; partially offset by higher CIB Markets revenue (Markets +15%).
- Expenses: Noninterest expense $18.7B (+6%) from continued investments (technology, marketing) and higher structural compensation, partly offset by lower revenue-related compensation.
- Credit costs and quality: Provision for credit losses $1.1B (vs. $2.3B benefit prior year), including a $428M allowance build (loan growth and modest macro deterioration) and $657M net charge-offs (down, driven by Card). Total allowance for credit losses $20.0B; allowance-to-loans coverage 1.69% (vs. 2.02%). Nonperforming assets $7.8B (down $2.0B YoY) on improved consumer credit and wholesale portfolio activity.
- Balance sheet trends: Average loans $1.1T (+7%) across businesses. Average deposits $2.5T (+9%) reflecting prior-year government actions and CCB account growth; deposits declined during Q2 2022 due to migration of non-operating balances to higher-yielding alternatives (CB) and increased consumer spending (CCB).
- Capital and liquidity: CET1 capital $207B; CET1 ratios 12.2% (Standardized) and 12.9% (Advanced); Tier 1 14.1%; Total capital 15.7%; SLR 5.3%. Tangible book value per share $69.53 (+1%); book value per share $86.38 (+2%). Notes inclusion of CECL capital transition relief.
- Non-GAAP measures: Calls out pre-provision profit, ROTCE, TCE, TBVPS, NII/NIR excluding Markets, and managed-basis revenue, with references to reconciliation pages.
- Comparison basis: Metrics and commentary primarily compare Q2 2022 to Q2 2021 unless otherwise specified.

- Commercial Banking (CB): ROE 15%; Gross Investment Banking revenue $788M, down 32%; average loans up 7% YoY and 4% QoQ; average deposits up 4%.
- Asset & Wealth Management (AWM): ROE 23%; AUM $2.7T, down 8%; average loans up 11% YoY and 1% QoQ; average deposits up 22%.

Credit provided and capital raised in 1H22 totaled $1.4T, including: $138B to consumers; $16B to U.S. small businesses; $553B to corporations; $609B capital raised for corporate clients and non-U.S. government entities; and $36B for nonprofits and U.S. government entities (includes states, municipalities, hospitals, and universities).

nodes.title: Business Developments
nodes.heading: Business Developments
nodes.start_phrase:
The duration and potential outcomes of the war in Ukraine 
remain uncertain.
nodes.summary:
- Addresses business impacts of the war in Ukraine: uncertainty of duration/outcomes; actions taken to close positions and reduce exposures; assisting clients in fulfilling or terminating pre-existing obligations and managing Russia-related risks.
- States that exposure to Russia and Russia-associated clients/counterparties is not material to financial condition or results, but notes potential adverse secondary effects from market volatility, inflation, and government sanctions.
- Highlights ongoing monitoring of operational risks tied to the war, including sanctions compliance and heightened cyberattack risk.
- Provides internal definitions of “Russia” and “Russia-associated” based on the firm’s country risk framework and sanctions context.
- References related sections for deeper detail: Wholesale Credit Portfolio, Allowance for Credit Losses, Market Risk Management, Country Risk Management, and Operational Risk Management.
- Covers the IBOR transition: continued industry progress away from LIBOR to IOSCO-compliant, transaction-based benchmarks; cessation of principal USD LIBOR tenors scheduled for June 30, 2023.
- Notes ongoing client outreach for USD LIBOR-linked loans and continued monitoring of client, market, regulatory, and legislative developments, with a reference to prior 10-K disclosures.

nodes.title: War in Ukraine
nodes.heading: War in Ukraine
nodes.start_phrase:
The duration and potential outcomes of the war in Ukraine 
remain uncertain.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of business developments focused on two areas: impacts of the war in Ukraine and the industry transition away from IBORs, particularly USD LIBOR.
- War in Ukraine:
  - The firm has closed positions and reduced exposures related to the conflict, helping clients manage or exit pre-existing obligations and Russia-related risks.
  - Exposure to Russia and Russia-associated clients/counterparties is not material to the firm’s financial condition or results.
  - Secondary effects—market volatility, inflationary pressures, and sanctions—could adversely affect businesses.
  - Ongoing monitoring of operational risks, including sanctions compliance and heightened cyber risk.
  - Defines “Russia” and “Russia-associated” based on internal country risk criteria and sanctions associations.
  - Points to other sections (credit, market, country, and operational risk) for detailed information.
- IBOR transition:
  - Continued progress transitioning from LIBOR and other IBORs to transaction-based benchmark rates in line with IOSCO standards.
  - Publication of key USD LIBOR tenors scheduled to cease on June 30, 2023.
  - Ongoing client outreach on USD LIBOR-linked loans and monitoring of market, regulatory, and legislative developments.
  - References prior disclosures for additional background.

nodes.title: Interbank Offered Rate (“IBOR”) transition
nodes.heading: Interbank Offered Rate (“IBOR”) transition
nodes.start_phrase:
JPMorgan Chase and other market participants continue to 
make progress with respect to the transition from the use of 
the London Interbank Offered Rate (“LIBOR”) and other 
IBORs to comply with the International Organization of 
Securities Commission's standards for transaction-based 
benchmark rates.
nodes.summary:
- War in Ukraine: The firm has closed positions and reduced exposures tied to the conflict, assisting clients with fulfilling or terminating obligations and managing Russia-related risks. Direct exposure to Russia and Russia-associated clients/counterparties is not material to financial condition or results, but secondary effects—market volatility, inflation, and sanctions—could adversely impact businesses. The firm is actively managing operational risks, including sanctions compliance and elevated cyber threats. Definitions of “Russia” and “Russia-associated” are provided, and readers are directed to related risk management sections for more detail.

- IBOR transition: JPMorgan Chase continues progressing on the transition from LIBOR/IBORs to transaction-based benchmark rates aligned with IOSCO standards. Publication of key USD LIBOR tenors is scheduled to cease on June 30, 2023. The firm is conducting client outreach on USD LIBOR-linked loans and monitoring client, market, regulatory, and legislative developments, with further reference to its 2021 Form 10-K.

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED RESULTS OF OPERATIONS
nodes.heading: CONSOLIDATED RESULTS OF OPERATIONS
nodes.start_phrase:
This section provides a comparative discussion of JPMorgan Chase’s Consolidated Results of Operations on a reported basis for the 
three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021 , unless otherwise specified.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Comparative discussion of JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated results for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 vs. 2021, with segment-specific drivers referenced to respective sections and notes.
- Total revenue mix:
  - Q2 2022: Total net revenue $30.7B (+1%); Net interest income (NII) $15.1B (+19%); Noninterest revenue $15.6B (−12%).
  - 1H 2022: Total net revenue $61.4B (−2%); NII $29.0B (+13%); Noninterest revenue $32.4B (−13%).
  - Operating lease income: $945M in Q2 2022 vs. $1.3B prior year; $2.0B YTD vs. $2.6B prior year.
- Key revenue line items (Q2 2022 vs. Q2 2021; 1H 2022 vs. 1H 2021):
  - Investment banking fees: $1.6B (−54%); $3.6B (−44%).
  - Principal transactions: $5.0B (+22%); $10.1B (−5%).
  - Lending- and deposit-related fees: $1.9B (+6%); $3.7B (+8%).
  - Asset management, administration and commissions: $5.2B (+1%); $10.6B (+4%).
  - Investment securities losses: $(153)M (flat); $(547)M (wider vs. $(141)M).
  - Mortgage fees and related income: $378M (−31%); $838M (−33%).
  - Card income: $1.1B (−31%); $2.1B (−30%).
  - Other income: $540M (−55%); $2.0B (−12%).
- Drivers and segment commentary:
  - Investment banking fees (CIB): Declined due to volatile markets reducing debt/equity issuance and lower advisory from fewer announced deals.
  - Principal transactions (CIB): Increased on strong Fixed Income Markets (macro, particularly Currencies & Emerging Markets) and Equity derivatives; partially offset by a $218M loss in Credit Adjustments & Other (vs. $233M gain prior year) and $337M of markdowns on held-for-sale bridge financing positions in CIB and CB; Corporate saw net gains on certain legacy private equity investments vs. prior-year losses. CIB Markets performance assessed on total revenue basis due to offsets with NII.
  - Lending- and deposit-related fees (CCB): Increased on higher deposit-related fees.
  - Asset management revenues (AWM): Relatively flat; removal of most money market fund fee waivers increased fees, offset by lower market levels and performance fees.
  - Investment securities losses (Corporate/Treasury and CIO): Losses in both periods from repositioning of investment securities portfolios; relatively flat quarter-over-quarter.
  - Mortgage fees: Lower production revenue from reduced margins and volumes, largely offset by higher net MSR revenue (improved MSR risk management from changes in prepayment expectations) and higher servicing revenue on increased third-party loans serviced.
- Cross-references: Segment details for CIB, CB, CCB, AWM, and Corporate; critical accounting estimates; relevant notes (e.g., Note 5, Note 9).

- Headline results: Total net revenue was $30.7B in Q2 2022 (+1% YoY) and $61.4B YTD 2022 (-2% YoY). Mix shift toward higher net interest income (NII) offset by lower noninterest revenue.
- Investment banking fees: Declined sharply in CIB (Q2 -54%, YTD -44%) due to lower debt/equity underwriting amid volatile markets and fewer announced deals reducing advisory fees.
- Principal transactions: Q2 increased, led by strong Fixed Income Markets (macro, especially Currencies & EM) and Equity Markets (derivatives), but partially offset by:
  - Q2: $218MM loss in Credit Adjustments & Other (vs. $233MM gain prior year) and $337MM markdowns on held-for-sale bridge financing positions (CIB and CB); Corporate saw net gains on legacy private equity vs. prior-year losses.
  - YTD: Down overall due to a $742MM loss in Credit Adjustments & Other (funding spread widening, and losses tied to commodities and Russia-related exposures), the $337MM bridge markdowns, and Corporate private equity losses vs. prior-year gains; partially offset by stronger Markets (Fixed Income macro and Equity prime brokerage/derivatives).
  - Note: CIB Markets performance assessed on total revenue; principal transactions may offset with NII.
- Lending- and deposit-related fees: Increased (Q2 and YTD), driven by higher deposit-related fees in CCB and higher cash management fees in CIB and CB (YTD).
- Asset management, administration and commissions: Q2 roughly flat; YTD up on higher AWM fees due to removal of most money market fund fee waivers and strong cumulative net inflows (plus net inflows in CCB), partially offset by lower market levels and performance fees.
- Investment securities: Losses in both periods from Treasury and CIO portfolio repositioning; relatively flat Q2 but higher net losses YTD on sales of U.S. Treasuries and agency MBS.
- Mortgage fees and related income: Down Q2 and YTD on lower production margins and volume; largely offset by higher servicing revenue, including improved MSR risk management results from changes in prepayment expectations and higher operating revenue on a larger third‑party servicing book.
- Card income: Decreased Q2 and YTD due to higher amortization from new account originations; Q2 also impacted by lower net interchange from a renegotiated co-brand partner contract in late 2021.
- Other income: Decreased Q2 and YTD, reflecting lower auto operating lease income (volume decline) and net losses on equity investments (CIB and several in AWM) vs. prior-year gains; partially offset by gains on an equity-method investment received in partial loan satisfaction (CB), higher gains on certain Corporate investments, and an insurance settlement in Q1 2022; YTD also benefited from absence of prior-year weather-related write-downs on certain renewable energy investments (CIB).
- Net interest income: Increased Q2 and YTD on higher rates and balance sheet growth; partially offset by lower Markets NII and lower PPP loan NII.
  - Average interest-earning assets: $3.4T (Q2 up $209B; YTD up $242B).
  - Yields: Q2 asset yield 2.22% (+43 bps), net FTE yield 1.80% (+18 bps); net yield excluding Markets 2.26% (+36 bps). YTD asset yield 2.04% (+21 bps), net FTE yield 1.74% (+9 bps); net yield excluding Markets 2.11% (+19 bps).
- Cross-references: Segment details (CCB, CIB, CB, AWM, Corporate) and Notes provide additional breakdowns; non-GAAP reconciliation for net yield excluding Markets referenced.

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED BALANCE SHEETS AND CASH FLOWS ANALYSIS
nodes.heading: CONSOLIDATED BALANCE SHEETS AND CASH FLOWS ANALYSIS
nodes.start_phrase: The following is a discussion of the significant changes between J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2, and D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 1.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Analysis of consolidated balance sheet changes between June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021, highlighting key asset movements and drivers; references to related notes and sections for more detail.
- Overall size: Total assets up 3% to $3.84 trillion.
- Liquidity:
  - Cash and due from banks and deposits with banks declined (deposits with banks down 10%) due to Markets activities and loan growth; deposits reflect placements with central banks (e.g., Federal Reserve).
  - Federal funds sold and securities purchased under resale agreements rose 23% on higher collateral requirements, greater demand to cover short positions, and netting effects tied to client-driven market-making.
- Trading and market-related:
  - Trading assets up 7%, driven by higher FX and commodity derivative receivables from market moves and higher debt instruments, partly offset by lower equities; increased deployment in Treasury and CIO.
- Investment securities:
  - $73.2 billion transferred from available-for-sale (AFS) to held-to-maturity (HTM).
  - AFS down 28% due to paydowns and AOCI unrealized losses, partly offset by net purchases.
  - HTM up 21% on purchases, partly offset by paydowns.
- Lending:
  - Gross loans up 2% (net loans up 2% to $1.09 trillion), reflecting:
    - Higher CB loans from greater revolver utilization and originations.
    - Higher retained residential real estate loans in AWM and Home Lending (originations net of paydowns).
    - Higher Card balances on stronger consumer spending.
    - Higher wholesale loans in CIB.
    - Offsets: lower Home Lending mortgage warehouse balances (sales outpaced originations amid higher rates) and CBB decline from PPP loan forgiveness.
- Credit quality:
  - Allowance for loan losses up 8% with a net $1.4 billion build ($1.1 billion wholesale, $314 million consumer), reflecting increased weighting of adverse scenarios (inflation, monetary policy shifts, geopolitical risks including the war in Ukraine), modest macro forecast deterioration, loan growth in Card and CB, and Russia-related downgrades in CIB and AWM.
- Other notable movements: Accrued interest and accounts receivable up 42%; goodwill/MSRs/other intangibles up 5%; other assets up 10%; securities borrowed down 2%; premises and equipment slightly lower.

nodes.title: Consolidated balance sheets analysis
nodes.heading: Consolidated balance sheets analysis
nodes.start_phrase: The following is a discussion of the significant changes between J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2, and D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 1.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Analysis of significant changes in consolidated balance sheets (assets, liabilities, and equity) between December 31, 2021 and June 30, 2022, plus drivers behind those changes.
- Total size: Total assets up 3% to $3.84T; total liabilities up 3% to $3.56T; stockholders’ equity down 3% to $286B.

Assets
- Cash and deposits: Cash and due from banks slightly up; deposits with banks down 10% due to Markets activities and loan growth; central bank placements noted.
- Securities financing: Federal funds sold and securities purchased under resale agreements up 23%; securities borrowed down 2%; increases driven by Markets activity, higher collateral needs, demand to cover shorts, and netting effects.
- Trading assets: Up 7% on higher FX and commodity derivative receivables and higher debt instruments, partly offset by lower equities; additional deployment in Treasury and CIO.
- Investment securities: Portfolio reshaping with $73.2B transferred from AFS to HTM; AFS down 28% (paydowns, unrealized losses in AOCI, partly offset by net purchases); HTM up 21% (purchases partly offset by paydowns); total investment securities roughly flat.
- Loans: Up 2% driven by higher revolver use and originations in Commercial Banking, higher retained residential real estate in AWM and Home Lending, higher Card balances from consumer spending, and higher wholesale loans in CIB; partially offset by lower mortgage warehouse loans and PPP forgiveness in CBB.
- Allowance for loan losses: Up 8% (net addition of $1.4B) due to heavier weighting of adverse scenarios tied to inflation, monetary policy shifts, geopolitical risks (including war in Ukraine), modest macro deterioration, loan growth (Card, CB), and Russia-related downgrades (CIB, AWM).
- Accrued interest and receivables: Up 42% from higher client receivables tied to Markets (including prime brokerage).
- Goodwill, MSRs, and intangibles: Up 5% on MSR valuation increases (rate-driven) and acquisitions (Frosch Travel Group in CCB; Volkswagen Payments S.A. in CIB).
- Other assets: Up 10% from higher cash collateral placed with counterparties and increased securities financing in Markets.

Liabilities and equity
- Deposits: Flat overall; growth from new CCB accounts and higher balances in Securities Services and Payments offset by declines in CB (migration to higher-yielding alternatives) and seasonality in AWM and CB.
- Securities financing liabilities: Federal funds purchased and securities loaned/sold under repos up 15% on higher secured financing of trading assets and netting in Markets, partly offset by lower secured financing of AFS in Treasury and CIO.
- Short-term borrowings: Up 9% due to higher commercial paper issuance for short-term liquidity management.
- Trading liabilities: Up 16% on higher short positions in debt instruments driven by Fixed Income Markets activity.
- Accounts payable and other liabilities: Up 19% due to higher client payables (including prime brokerage).
- Beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs: Slightly down 1%.
- Long-term debt: Down 4% from fair value hedge accounting adjustments (higher rates) and lower fair value of structured notes in CIB, largely offset by net issuances in Treasury and CIO and CIB.
- Stockholders’ equity: Down 3% driven by net unrealized losses in AOCI from higher rates impacting the AFS portfolio and cash flow hedges.

Key themes and drivers
- Market volatility and client-driven market-making influenced trading assets/liabilities and securities financing.
- Rising interest rates impacted AFS valuations (AOCI), hedge accounting adjustments, MSR valuations, and funding mix.
- Strategic reclassification from AFS to HTM to manage OCI volatility.
- Loan growth across consumer and wholesale with corresponding increase in credit reserves amid a more adverse macro outlook and geopolitical risks.

nodes.title: EXPLANATION AND RECONCILIATION OF THE FIRM’S USE OF NON-GAAP FINANCIAL MEASURES
nodes.heading: EXPLANATION AND RECONCILIATION OF THE FIRM’S USE OF NON-GAAP FINANCIAL MEASURES
nodes.start_phrase:
The Firm prepares its Consolidated Financial Statements in 
accordance with U.S. GAAP and this presentation is referred 
to as “reported” basis; these financial statements appear on 
page 88-92 .
nodes.summary:
- Purpose: Explains how the firm supplements U.S. GAAP (“reported”) results with non-GAAP (“managed”) measures and provides reconciliations between them.
- Key non-GAAP metrics used:
  - Firmwide managed-basis results (including FTE adjustments to make tax-advantaged income comparable to taxable, and the overhead ratio).
  - Pre-provision profit (total net revenue less total noninterest expense).
  - Net interest income (NII), net yield, and noninterest revenue excluding Markets.
  - Tangible common equity (TCE), return on TCE (ROTCE), and tangible book value per share (TBVPS).
  - Adjusted expense (excluding Firmwide legal expense).
  - Allowance for loan losses to period-end loans retained (excluding trade finance and conduits).
- Reconciliation highlights (Q2 and first half 2022 vs 2021):
  - FTE adjustments increase total net revenue and pre-provision profit on a managed basis; overhead ratio improves on managed vs reported.
  - Provision for credit losses turned to a build in 2022 versus releases in 2021, reducing income before tax year-over-year.
  - Income tax expense is higher on a managed basis due to FTE; net income is unchanged by FTE adjustments.
- NII, yield, and noninterest revenue excluding Markets:
  - Managed NII rose year-over-year (Q2 up 19%; 1H up 13%), with higher net yields on average interest-earning assets.
  - Excluding Markets, NII grew faster (Q2 up 26%; 1H up 18%) and net yields were notably higher than total firm yields.
  - Noninterest revenue excluding Markets declined materially (Q2 down 26%; 1H down 21%), while total Markets net revenue increased (Q2 up 15%; 1H up 4%).
- TCE reconciliation:
  - TCE is derived by deducting goodwill and other intangibles and adding certain deferred tax liabilities to common stockholders’ equity.
  - Reported figures include period-end TCE around $204B at June 30, 2022; TBVPS of $69.53; ROTCE in 2022 below 2021 levels (e.g., Q2 2022 ~17% vs Q2 2021 ~23%).
- Footnotes/context:
  - FTE adjustments are recognized predominantly in CIB, CB, and Corporate; interest includes hedge effects.
  - References are provided to the firm’s 2021 Form 10-K for broader discussion and to another section for Markets details.

nodes.title: BUSINESS SEGMENT RESULTS
nodes.heading: BUSINESS SEGMENT RESULTS
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm is managed on an LOB basis.
nodes.summary:
- The firm reports results by line of business (LOB), with four major segments—Consumer & Community Banking, Corporate & Investment Bank, Commercial Banking, and Asset & Wealth Management—plus a Corporate segment.
- Segments are defined by products/services or customer type and align with how the Operating Committee evaluates performance; results are presented on a managed (non-GAAP) basis.
- Segment reporting aims to reflect each LOB as a stand-alone business, allocating shared income and expenses; methodologies and classifications are periodically reassessed and refined.
- The firm annually assesses and allocates capital (equity) to each LOB and uses various business metrics to evaluate performance.
- Revenue sharing is used when multiple LOBs collaborate, with primary revenue recognized in the product-owning segment and allocations to participating segments.
- Funds transfer pricing allocates interest income/expense to LOBs and transfers primary interest rate and liquidity risks to Treasury and CIO; assumptions are periodically updated, which can affect net interest income allocations.
- Certain foreign exchange risks are transferred from LOBs and Other Corporate to Treasury and CIO, which centrally manage and report FX impacts.
- Capital allocation methodologies are periodically reviewed, potentially changing LOB equity; references are provided to additional disclosures on non-GAAP measures and detailed segment reporting methodologies.

nodes.title: Description of business segment reporting methodology
nodes.heading: Description of business segment reporting methodology
nodes.start_phrase:
Results of the business segments are intended to present 
each segment as if it were a stand-alone business.
nodes.summary:
- The firm reports results by lines of business (LOB), with four reportable segments—Consumer & Community Banking, Corporate & Investment Bank, Commercial Banking, and Asset & Wealth Management—plus a Corporate segment.
- Segments are defined by products/services and customer types and align with how the Operating Committee evaluates performance; results are presented on a managed (non-GAAP) basis (see pages 18–19 for the definition and reconciliation).
- Segment reporting is designed to reflect each LOB as a stand-alone business, including allocations of certain income and expense items; assumptions, methodologies, and classifications are reviewed and refined periodically.
- Capital is assigned to each LOB as equity and reassessed at least annually; methodologies may change over time (see Line of business equity on page 47 and page 93 of the 2021 Form 10-K).
- Revenue sharing: when multiple segments collaborate on client transactions, revenue is recognized in the segment responsible for the product/service and allocated to participating segments per agreed sharing arrangements.
- Funds transfer pricing (FTP): allocates interest income/expense to LOBs and Other Corporate and transfers primary interest-rate and liquidity risks to Treasury and CIO; FTP reflects risk characteristics of assets, liabilities, and off-balance sheet items and is updated periodically, which can change net interest income allocations.
- Foreign exchange risk: certain FX exposures from LOBs and Other Corporate are transferred to Treasury and CIO, which centrally manage and report FX impacts.
- Additional detail on business segment reporting methodology is provided in the 2021 Form 10-K (pages 61–62).

  - Noninterest revenue declined 12% in Q2 and 11% in 1H; net interest income slightly lower in both periods.
- Credit costs: Provision for credit losses turned to a build (Q2: $59M vs a release of $79M; 1H: $504M vs a release of $410M), pressuring earnings.

Noninterest revenue fell 5% to $1.8 billion with the same drivers and offsets as the quarter. Noninterest expense increased 17% to $2.3 billion on higher structural and volume-/revenue-related costs. nodes.title: CAPITAL RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: CAPITAL RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase:
Capital risk is the risk the Firm has an insufficient level or 
composition of capital to support the Firm’s business 
activities and associated risks during normal economic 
environments and under stressed conditions.
nodes.summary:
- Defines capital risk as the possibility that the Firm lacks sufficient capital level or composition to support activities and risks in normal and stressed conditions; points to the 2021 Form 10-K, Note 21 of the Form 10-Q, and Pillar 3 disclosures for more detail.
- Basel III overview: capital adequacy is based on risk-weighted assets calculated under two approaches—Standardized and Advanced—with the Firm assessed against the more binding of the two; currently, the Firm’s Basel III Standardized risk-based ratios are more binding than its Advanced ratios.
- Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR): required for Advanced Approaches firms; currently more binding for the Firm than its Basel III Standardized risk-based ratios.
- CECL regulatory capital transition: the two-year delay ended 12/31/2021; beginning 1/1/2022, the $2.9 billion CECL capital benefit is being phased out at 25% per year over three years; as of 6/30/2022, $2.2 billion remains in CET1; 25% of other CECL transition effects were also phased out from Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, and total leverage exposure.
- Adoption of SA-CCR (effective 1/1/2022): replaced the Current Exposure Method for derivatives exposure under both Standardized and Advanced RWA (where internal models aren’t used) and for SLR leverage exposure; increased Standardized RWA by about $40 billion (based on 12/31/2021 positions), reducing the CET1 ratio by ~30 bps and modestly lowering total leverage exposure; Advanced RWA also increased, but less.
- Risk-based capital regulatory requirements: Firm targets a 12.5% Basel III Standardized CET1 ratio by end of Q4 2022, reflecting current rules and an expected increase in the Stress Capital Buffer (SCB).

nodes.title: Basel III Overview
nodes.heading: Basel III Overview
nodes.start_phrase:
The capital rules under Basel III establish minimum capital 
ratios and overall capital adequacy standards for large and 
internationally active U.S. Bank Holding Companies 
(“BHCs ”) and banks, including the Firm and its insured 
depository institution (“IDI”) subsidiaries, including 
JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
nodes.summary:
- Defines capital risk as the sufficiency and composition of capital to support business activities in normal and stressed conditions, with references to the firm’s 10-K, 10-Q Note 21, and Pillar 3 disclosures for more detail.
- Basel III overview:
  - Capital adequacy based on risk-weighted assets (RWA) under two methods: Standardized and Advanced.
  - The firm’s Standardized risk-based ratios are currently more binding than its Advanced ratios.
  - Advanced Approaches firms must also meet the Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR); the firm’s SLR is currently more binding than its Basel III Standardized risk-based ratios.
- Key regulatory developments:
  - CECL capital transition: Two-year delay expired 12/31/21; starting 1/1/22, the $2.9B CECL capital benefit is being phased out 25% per year over three years; $2.2B remained in CET1 as of 6/30/22. A 25% phase-out also applies to related Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, and total leverage exposure items.
  - Adoption of SA-CCR (effective 1/1/22) replacing the Current Exposure Method for derivatives exposure under both Standardized and Advanced RWAs (where models aren’t used) and for SLR. Impact: ~+$40B to Standardized RWA (as of 12/31/21 exposure), ~30 bps decrease in CET1 ratio, modest decrease in total leverage exposure; Advanced RWA also increased but less.
- Capital requirements outlook: Target Basel III Standardized CET1 ratio of 12.5% by end of Q4 2022, reflecting expected increase in the Stress Capital Buffer.

Also details a 25% phase-out of other CECL-related capital transition amounts from Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, and total leverage exposure.

A 25% phaseout also applied to related Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, and total leverage exposure.

nodes.title: LIQUIDITY RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: LIQUIDITY RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase:
Liquidity risk is the risk that the Firm will be unable to meet 
its contractual and contingent financial obligations as they 
arise or that it does not have the appropriate amount, 
composition and tenor of funding and liquidity to support 
its assets and liabilities.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and definition: Describes the Firm’s approach to liquidity risk management, defining liquidity risk and pointing to JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K (pp. 97–104) and U.S. LCR Disclosure reports for fuller discussion.

- LCR and HQLA framework:
  - Minimum LCR requirement of 100% for both JPMorgan Chase & Co. and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
  - Excess HQLA at the Bank that is not transferable to non-bank affiliates is excluded from the Firm’s reported HQLA.
  - Footnotes clarify HQLA components: eligible cash (central bank deposits) and eligible securities (mainly U.S. Treasuries, GSE/agency MBS, sovereigns), and where such securities may appear on the balance sheet.

- Reported LCR metrics (average, three months ended):
  - JPMorgan Chase & Co.:
    - Total HQLA: $741,953m (Jun-22), $722,515m (Mar-22), $716,556m (Jun-21)
    - Net cash outflows: $676,234m (Jun-22), $658,998m (Mar-22), $647,757m (Jun-21)
    - LCR: 110% (Jun-22), 110% (Mar-22), 111% (Jun-21)
    - Net excess eligible HQLA: $65,719m (Jun-22), $63,517m (Mar-22), $68,799m (Jun-21)
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.:
    - LCR: 169% (Jun-22), 181% (Mar-22), 171% (Jun-21)
    - Net excess eligible HQLA: $487,867m (Jun-22), $560,987m (Mar-22), $489,311m (Jun-21)

- Drivers and variability:
  - Bank’s average LCR declined in Q2 2022 vs. Q1 2022 due to lower HQLA, largely from reduced cash as loans grew and a decline in market value of HQLA-eligible investment securities in Treasury and CIO (with a reference to Note 9 on unrealized gains/losses).
  - LCR for both the Firm and the Bank fluctuates with changes in eligible HQLA and estimated net cash outflows from ongoing business activity.

- Other liquidity sources:
  - Unencumbered marketable securities (including excess eligible HQLA at the Bank not transferable to non-bank affiliates): ~$826bn at Jun 30, 2022 vs. ~$914bn at Dec 31, 2021; decline mainly from lower excess eligible HQLA at the Bank.
  - Additional contingent capacity via collateral pledged to FHLBs and the Federal Reserve discount window of approximately $308bn at both Jun 30, 2022 and Dec 31, 2021; the Firm does not view the discount window/other central banks as a primary liquidity source.

- NSFR:
  - Both the Firm and the Bank were compliant with the 100% minimum NSFR as of Jun 30, 2022.
  - Public disclosure of quarterly average NSFR will occur semiannually beginning in 2023.

nodes.title: LCR and HQLA
nodes.heading: LCR and HQLA
nodes.start_phrase:
The LCR rule requires that the Firm and JPMorgan Chase 
Bank, N.A. maintain an amount of eligible HQLA that is 
sufficient to meet their respective estimated total net cash 
outflows over a prospective 30 calendar-day period of 
significant stress.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: JPMorgan Chase’s liquidity risk management framework, definitions, regulatory metrics, and available liquidity sources.
- Liquidity risk defined as the risk of not meeting obligations or lacking appropriate funding mix and tenor; references to 2021 Form 10-K (pp. 97–104) and U.S. LCR Disclosure reports.
- LCR and HQLA:
  - Minimum LCR requirement of 100% for both the Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
  - Excess HQLA held at the Bank that is not transferable to non-bank affiliates is excluded from Firm-level eligible HQLA.
  - Average LCR metrics (three months ended):
    - JPMorgan Chase & Co.:
      - LCR: 110% (Jun 30, 2022), 110% (Mar 31, 2022), 111% (Jun 30, 2021)
      - Total HQLA: $741,953m; $722,515m; $716,556m
      - Eligible cash: $634,480m; $680,003m; $673,724m
      - Eligible securities: $107,473m; $42,512m; $42,832m
      - Net cash outflows: $676,234m; $658,998m; $647,757m
      - Net excess eligible HQLA: $65,719m; $63,517m; $68,799m
    - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.:
      - LCR: 169%; 181%; 171%
      - Net excess eligible HQLA: $487,867m; $560,987m; $489,311m
  - Notes: Eligible cash primarily central bank deposits; eligible securities include U.S. Treasuries, U.S. GSE/agency MBS, and sovereign bonds (net of LCR haircuts); eligible HQLA may be recorded across several balance sheet lines.
  - Bank’s average LCR fell in Q2 2022 vs. Q1 2022 due to lower HQLA from loan-driven cash reductions and declines in market values of HQLA-eligible securities in Treasury and CIO; references Note 9 for unrealized gains/losses. LCR fluctuates with changes in HQLA and net cash outflows from ongoing business activity.
- Other liquidity sources:
  - Unencumbered marketable securities (including excess eligible HQLA at the Bank not transferable to non-bank affiliates): fair value ~$826B (Jun 30, 2022) vs. ~$914B (Dec 31, 2021), primarily lower due to reduced excess eligible HQLA at the Bank; realizable liquidity depends on market conditions.
  - Available borrowing capacity at FHLBs and Federal Reserve discount window of approximately $308B at both Jun 30, 2022 and Dec 31, 2021, based on pledged collateral; excludes HQLA and currently pledged securities; discount window capacity is not viewed as a primary liquidity source.
- NSFR:
  - Requirement to maintain available stable funding ≥ required stable funding over a one-year horizon; 100% minimum.
  - As of Jun 30, 2022, both the Firm and the Bank were compliant; public disclosure of quarterly average NSFR will begin semiannually in 2023.

nodes.title: Other liquidity sources
nodes.heading: Other liquidity sources
nodes.start_phrase:
In addition to the assets reported in the Firm’s eligible 
HQLA discussed above, the Firm had unencumbered 
marketable securities, such as equity and debt securities, 
that the Firm believes would be available to raise liquidity.
nodes.summary:
- Defines liquidity risk and points to JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K (pp. 97–104) and U.S. LCR Disclosure reports for further detail.
- Explains LCR and HQLA framework:
  - Both the Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. must maintain a minimum 100% LCR, holding eligible HQLA sufficient to cover 30 days of stressed net cash outflows.
  - Excess eligible HQLA at the Bank that is not transferable to non-bank affiliates is excluded from the Firm’s reported eligible HQLA.
  - References additional detail on HQLA and net cash outflows on page 98 of the 2021 Form 10-K.
- Reports average LCR metrics for the three months ended June 30, 2022, March 31, 2022, and June 30, 2021:
  - JPMorgan Chase & Co.: LCR ~110% across periods; Q2 2022 HQLA $742B (eligible cash $634B; eligible securities $107B), net cash outflows $676B, net excess eligible HQLA $66B.
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.: LCR 169% in Q2 2022 (down from 181% in Q1 2022; 171% in Q2 2021); net excess eligible HQLA $488B in Q2 2022.
  - Notes on composition: eligible cash is primarily central bank deposits; eligible securities mainly U.S. Treasuries, GSE/agency MBS, and sovereigns; HQLA securities may appear across multiple balance sheet line items.
- Highlights drivers and variability:
  - The Bank’s average LCR decreased in Q2 2022 versus Q1 2022 due to reduced cash from loan growth and declines in market values of HQLA-eligible investment securities in Treasury and CIO.
  - LCRs fluctuate with changes in eligible HQLA and estimated net cash outflows from ongoing business activity.
- Other liquidity sources:
  - Unencumbered marketable securities that could be used to raise liquidity totaled about $826B at June 30, 2022 (down from $914B at December 31, 2021), largely due to lower excess eligible HQLA at the Bank.
  - Additional borrowing capacity at FHLBs and the Federal Reserve discount window was approximately $308B at both June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021, based on pledged collateral; the discount window is not viewed as a primary liquidity source.
- NSFR:
  - Describes requirement to maintain sufficient “available” stable funding relative to “required” stable funding over a one-year horizon.
  - Confirms the Firm and the Bank met the 100% minimum NSFR as of June 30, 2022.
  - Notes semiannual public disclosure of quarterly average NSFR will begin in 2023.

nodes.title: NSFR
nodes.heading: NSFR
nodes.start_phrase:
The net stable funding ratio (“NSFR”) rule requires that the 
Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. maintain an amount of 
“available” stable funding that is sufficient to meet their 
“required” amounts of stable funding over a one-year 
horizon.
nodes.summary:
- Defines liquidity risk and points to JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K (pp. 97–104) and U.S. LCR Disclosure reports for more detail.
- Explains LCR and HQLA requirements: firms must hold sufficient eligible HQLA to cover 30-day stressed net cash outflows; excess HQLA at JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. that is not transferable to non‑bank affiliates is excluded from the Firm’s HQLA; minimum LCR is 100%.
- Presents average LCR metrics for JPMorgan Chase & Co. and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. for the three months ended June 30, 2022, March 31, 2022, and June 30, 2021:
  - JPMorgan Chase & Co.: Total HQLA $742B (6/30/22), net cash outflows $676B, LCR 110%, net excess eligible HQLA $66B; comparable figures for prior periods provided.
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.: LCR 169% (6/30/22), 181% (3/31/22), 171% (6/30/21); net excess eligible HQLA $488B (6/30/22), $561B (3/31/22), $489B (6/30/21).
  - Notes HQLA composition (central bank cash; U.S. Treasuries, agency MBS, sovereigns) and reporting locations.
- Attributes the Bank’s LCR decline in 2Q22 versus 1Q22 to reduced cash from loan growth and lower market values of HQLA‑eligible investment securities in Treasury and CIO; references Note 9 on unrealized gains/losses.
- Acknowledges normal period‑to‑period LCR fluctuations due to changes in eligible HQLA and estimated net cash outflows.
- Details other liquidity sources:
  - Unencumbered marketable securities with fair value of ~$826B (6/30/22) vs. ~$914B (12/31/21), with the decline mainly from lower excess eligible HQLA at the Bank.
  - Available borrowing capacity at FHLBs and the Federal Reserve discount window of ~ $308B at both 6/30/22 and 12/31/21, based on pledged collateral; not considered a primary liquidity source and excludes HQLA and certain pledged unencumbered securities.
- Summarizes NSFR: both the Firm and the Bank were compliant with the 100% minimum NSFR as of 6/30/22; public semiannual disclosure of quarterly average NSFR to begin in 2023.

nodes.title: Funding
nodes.heading: Funding
nodes.start_phrase:
Management believes that the Firm’s unsecured and 
secured funding capacity is sufficient to meet its on- and 
off-balance sheet obligations, which includes both short- 
and long-term cash requirements.
nodes.summary:
- Topic: Firm’s funding sources and deposit trends.
- Funding strategy: Management asserts sufficient unsecured and secured funding capacity to meet on- and off-balance sheet obligations. The Firm uses diversified funding: stable deposits, secured and unsecured capital markets funding, and stockholders’ equity.
- Entity-specific funding:
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.: Primarily funded by deposits; can access short- and long-term secured borrowings, issue unsecured long-term debt, or borrow from the Intermediate Holding Company (IHC).
  - Non-bank subsidiaries: Funded mainly via long-term unsecured borrowings and short-term secured borrowings (including securities lending and repurchase agreements).
- Liquidity deployment: Excess funding is invested by Treasury and CIO in investment securities or placed in cash/short-term liquid assets based on interest rate and liquidity risk.
- Deposits as stable funding: Consumer deposits and wholesale operating deposits are highlighted as stable due to operating relationships.
- Deposit levels (by LOB and total):
  - Total Firm deposits at period-end: $2,471.5B (Jun 30, 2022) vs $2,462.3B (Dec 31, 2021).
  - Average deposits:
    - Three months ended Jun 30: $2,532.3B (2022) vs $2,323.8B (2021).
    - Six months ended Jun 30: $2,524.0B (2022) vs $2,274.5B (2021).
  - LOB period-end (Jun 30, 2022 vs Dec 31, 2021): CCB $1,178.8B vs $1,148.1B; CIB $738.8B vs $707.8B; CB $283.3B vs $324.0B; AWM $257.4B vs $282.1B; Corporate $13.2B vs $0.4B.
- Balance sheet ratios:
  - Deposits as % of total liabilities: 70% (Jun 30, 2022) vs 71% (Dec 31, 2021).
  - Loans: $1,104.2B (Jun 30, 2022) vs $1,077.7B (Dec 31, 2021).
  - Loans-to-deposits ratio: 45% (Jun 30, 2022) vs 44% (Dec 31, 2021).
- Trends and drivers:
  - Average deposits increased year-over-year for both the three- and six-month periods ended Jun 30, 2022, largely reflecting residual effects of prior-year government actions.
  - CCB growth supported by new and existing consumer and small business accounts.
  - In 2Q22, deposits declined in certain areas: CB due to migration of non-operating deposits into higher-yielding alternatives; CCB due to increased consumer spending.
  - Corporate deposit increases tied to international consumer growth initiatives.
- References: Note 22 for off-balance sheet obligations; further deposit/liability trends in Consolidated Balance Sheets Analysis and Business Segment Results sections.

nodes.title: Deposits
nodes.heading: Deposits

The table below summarizes, b y LOB and Corporate, the period-end deposit balances as of J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2, and D e c e m b e r 3 1 ,

nodes.summary:
- Focus: JPMorgan Chase’s funding strategy, sources, and trends as of June 30, 2022, with comparisons to December 31, 2021 and prior-year periods.
- Funding capacity: Management asserts sufficient unsecured and secured capacity to meet on- and off-balance sheet obligations.
- Diversified funding mix:
  - Primary reliance on stable deposits at JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
  - Additional bank funding via secured borrowings, unsecured long-term debt, and borrowings from the Intermediate Holding Company (IHC).
  - Non-bank subsidiaries funded mainly by long-term unsecured and short-term secured borrowings (repos and securities lending).
  - Excess funding invested by Treasury and CIO in investment securities and other liquid assets.
- Deposits:
  - Total deposits of approximately $2.47T at June 30, 2022; deposits represent ~70% of total liabilities.
  - Loans of ~$1.10T; loans-to-deposits ratio ~45%.
  - Average deposits viewed as more representative than period-end; YoY average deposits increased due to residual effects of prior-year government actions and growth in Consumer & Community Banking.
  - Q2 2022 saw some decline: migration of non-operating deposits to higher-yielding alternatives in Commercial Banking and continued consumer spending in CCB; Corporate increases tied to international consumer growth initiatives.
- Non-deposit funding (as of June 30, 2022 and averages):
  - Short-term unsecured: commercial paper (up due to net issuance for liquidity management), other borrowed funds, federal funds purchased.
  - Short-term secured: repos and securities lending (predominantly high-quality collateral), conduit obligations, and other borrowed funds; repo balances higher vs year-end on increased secured financing of trading assets and netting effects, partly offset by lower AFS securities financing.
  - Long-term unsecured: senior notes, subordinated debt, structured notes (including TLAC-eligible).
  - Long-term secured: credit card securitizations, FHLB advances, and secured structured notes.
  - Capital: preferred stock and common stockholders’ equity.
- Variability drivers: Secured financing balances fluctuate with client activity, the Firm’s financing needs, and liability mix management.
- References: Notes and sections cited for off-balance sheet obligations, capital, and detailed balance sheet analyses.

nodes.title: Short-term funding

- Scope: Summarizes the firm’s non-deposit funding mix as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021, plus average balances for the three- and six-month periods ended June 30, 2022 and 2021, with cross-references to other 10-Q and 10-K sections.
- Short-term unsecured funding: Comprised mainly of commercial paper, other borrowed funds, and federal funds purchased. Commercial paper outstanding and average balances increased versus year-end 2021 and prior-year periods, driven by higher net issuance for short-term liquidity management.
- Short-term secured funding: Dominated by securities sold under agreements to repurchase and securities loaned, plus other borrowed funds and obligations of firm-administered multi-seller conduits. Repos rose at June 30, 2022 versus December 31, 2021 due to higher secured financing of trading assets and netting effects from client-driven market-making, partially offset by lower secured financing of AFS investment securities in Treasury and CIO.
- Collateral quality: Short-term secured funding is backed predominantly by high-quality collateral, including government-issued debt and U.S. GSE and agency MBS.
- Balance dynamics: Secured funding balances fluctuate with client investment/financing activity, the firm’s financing demand, liability-mix management between secured and unsecured funding, and market/portfolio factors.
- Long-term unsecured funding: Includes senior notes, subordinated debt, and structured notes (some TLAC-eligible). Totals modestly declined from year-end 2021 to June 30, 2022.
- Long-term secured funding: Includes credit card securitizations, FHLB advances, and other long-term secured funding (including secured long-term structured notes).
- Equity: Presents preferred stock and common stockholders’ equity balances, with references to detailed capital risk management and stockholders’ equity disclosures.
- Consolidation/VIE notes: Obligations of multi-seller conduits and credit card securitizations are included in beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs. Structured notes include certain TLAC-eligible parent company long-term debt.
- Key quantitative highlights at June 30, 2022 vs. December 31, 2021:
  - Total short-term unsecured funding: $33.7B vs. $26.9B (increase, led by commercial paper: $21.7B vs. $15.1B).
  - Total short-term secured funding: $254.4B vs. $227.3B (increase, mainly repos).
  - Total long-term unsecured funding: $273.4B vs. $286.0B (slight decrease).
  - Total long-term secured funding: $16.6B vs. $17.4B (slight decrease).
  - Preferred stock: $32.8B; Common stockholders’ equity: $253.3B (point-in-time figures shown alongside averages).

nodes.title: Long-term funding and issuance
nodes.heading: Long-term funding and issuance
nodes.start_phrase: Long-term funding provides an additional source of stable funding and liquidity for the Firm.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: The section explains the Firm’s long-term funding strategy, sources, issuance activity, and maturities/redemptions for both unsecured and secured funding, with comparisons for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021.

- Strategy and objectives:
  - Long-term funding is used to provide stable funding and liquidity.
  - The plan is driven by expected client activity, liquidity needs, and regulatory requirements, including TLAC.
  - Objectives include diversification, maximizing market access, and optimizing funding costs, with evaluation across markets, tenors, and currencies.

- Funding structure:
  - The significant majority of long-term unsecured funding is issued by the Parent Company, which advances substantially all net proceeds to the IHC; the IHC does not issue external debt.
  - Some structured notes issued by the Parent Company are TLAC-eligible.

- Long-term unsecured funding activity (Q2 and H1 2022 vs. 2021):
  - Parent Company:
    - Issuance: $13.9bn in Q2 2022 ($24.2bn in Q2 2021); $25.9bn in H1 2022 ($37.8bn in H1 2021).
    - Maturities/redemptions: $5.4bn in Q2 2022 ($5.8bn in Q2 2021); $10.1bn in H1 2022 ($10.5bn in H1 2021).
    - Mix includes senior notes (U.S. and non-U.S.) and structured notes.
  - Subsidiaries:
    - Issuance is entirely structured notes: $11.2bn in Q2 2022 ($7.3bn in Q2 2021); $19.7bn in H1 2022 ($17.8bn in H1 2021).
    - Maturities/redemptions: $7.4bn in Q2 2022 ($9.7bn in Q2 2021); $15.1bn in H1 2022 ($18.2bn in H1 2021).

- Long-term secured funding:
  - Sources include securitization of consumer credit card loans, FHLB advances, and other secured long-term structured notes.
  - 2022 activity was modest:
    - Q2 2022: $82m issuance; $35m maturities/redemptions.
    - H1 2022: $284m issuance; $748m maturities/redemptions (including $650m of credit card securitization maturities).
  - Client-driven securitizations by wholesale businesses are excluded as they are not a source of Firm funding.

- Cross-references: Points to Liquidity Risk Management and 2021 Form 10-K notes for more detail on the IHC, long-term debt, and client-driven securitizations.

nodes.title: Credit ratings
nodes.heading: Credit ratings
nodes.start_phrase:
The cost and availability of financing are influenced by 
credit ratings.
nodes.summary:
- Explains that credit ratings materially affect the Firm’s cost and availability of funding; downgrades could limit access to liquidity, increase funding costs, trigger additional collateral or funding requirements, and reduce the pool of willing investors and counterparties.
- Notes that the impact of downgrades varies by contractual and behavioral factors and is incorporated into the Firm’s liquidity risk management and stress testing; the Firm believes it holds sufficient liquidity to withstand reduced funding capacity from potential downgrades.
- Indicates that downgrades may also adversely affect funding needs for VIEs and other third‑party commitments; directs readers to Note 4 for details on liquidity risk and credit‑related contingent features tied to VIEs, derivatives, and collateral agreements.
- Provides the long‑ and short‑term issuer ratings and outlooks as of June 30, 2022 from Moody’s, S&P, and Fitch for the Parent and principal bank and non‑bank subsidiaries (including JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.; J.P. Morgan Securities LLC; J.P. Morgan Securities plc; and J.P. Morgan SE). Highlights include:
  - JPMorgan Chase & Co.: Moody’s A2/P‑1 (positive long‑term, stable short‑term outlooks), S&P A‑/A‑2 (Positive), Fitch AA‑/F1+ (Stable).
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.: Moody’s Aa2/P‑1 (Stable), S&P A+/A‑1 (Positive), Fitch AA/F1+ (Stable).
  - J.P. Morgan Securities LLC: Moody’s Aa3/P‑1 (Stable), S&P A+/A‑1 (Positive), Fitch AA/F1+ (Stable).
- Notes that in January 2022, the three major agencies affirmed J.P. Morgan SE’s ratings, aligned with those of its predecessor entities.
- Refers to the 2021 Form 10‑K (page 104) for a discussion of factors that could affect the credit ratings of the Parent Company and key subsidiaries.

nodes.title: CREDIT AND INVESTMENT RISK MANAGEMENT

Credit and investment risk is the risk associated with the

nodes.title: CREDIT PORTFOLIO
nodes.heading: 9.5.1 CREDIT PORTFOLIO
nodes.start_phrase: Credit risk is the risk associated with the default or change in credit profile of a client, counterparty or customer.
nodes.summary:
- Defines credit risk as the risk of default or a change in a counterparty’s credit profile.
- Scope of reported totals: includes loans retained (held-for-investment), loans held-for-sale, and certain loans at fair value; excludes loans accounted for at fair value and classified as trading assets (see Notes 2 and 3). Additional references: Notes 11, 22, 4 (loans, lending-related commitments, derivative receivables), Note 9 (investment securities credit risk), Note 10 (securities financing credit risk), Consumer Credit Portfolio (pp. 57–61), Wholesale Credit Portfolio (pp. 62–70).
- Total loans and nonperforming:
  - Loans retained: $1,052,390m (Jun 30, 2022) vs $1,010,206m (Dec 31, 2021); nonperforming $6,269m vs $6,932m.
  - Loans held-for-sale: $4,709m vs $8,688m; nonperforming $80m vs $48m.
  - Loans at fair value: $47,056m vs $58,820m; nonperforming $813m vs $815m.
  - Total loans: $1,104,155m vs $1,077,714m; nonperforming $7,162m vs $7,795m.
- Other credit-related assets and nonperforming:
  - Derivative receivables: $81,317m vs $57,081m; nonperforming $447m vs $316m.
  - Receivables from customers: $58,349m vs $59,645m; no nonperforming reported.
  - Total credit-related assets: $1,243,821m vs $1,194,440m; nonperforming $7,609m vs $8,111m.
- Assets acquired in loan satisfactions (nonperforming only): Real estate owned $211m vs $213m; Other $25m vs $22m; Total $236m vs $235m.
- Lending-related commitments: $1,302,005m vs $1,262,313m; nonperforming $397m vs $764m.
- Total credit portfolio: $2,545,826m vs $2,456,753m; total nonperforming $8,242m vs $9,110m.
- Credit risk management tools:
  - Credit derivatives and credit-related notes used in portfolio management: net notional $(16,939)m (Jun 30, 2022) vs $(20,739)m (Dec 31, 2021); prior period revised to conform to current presentation.
  - Liquid securities and other cash collateral held against derivatives: $19,801m vs $10,102m.
- Key footnotes:
  - Customer receivables are held-for-investment margin loans in CIB, CCB, and AWM, reported in accrued interest and accounts receivable.
  - Net notional represents protection purchased and sold via credit derivatives/notes.
  - Nonperforming assets exclude U.S. government–insured mortgage loans 90+ days past due ($453m vs $623m) and REO ($8m vs $5m); credit card loans generally exempt from nonaccrual.
  - Nonaccrual loans exclude PPP loans 90+ days past due guaranteed by the SBA ($119m vs $633m).
- Net charge-offs and loss metrics:
  - Three months ended Jun 30: net charge-offs $657m (2022) vs $734m (2021); average retained loans $1,035,933m vs $954,155m; net charge-off rate 0.25% vs 0.31%.
  - Six months ended Jun 30: net charge-offs $1,239m (2022) vs $1,791m (2021); average retained loans $1,020,180m vs $953,118m; net charge-off rate 0.24% vs 0.38%.
- Overall themes: portfolio size increased; nonperforming balances declined; lending-related commitments rose; derivative receivables increased with higher collateral held; charge-off rates improved year over year.

nodes.title: CONSUMER CREDIT PORTFOLIO

Includes references to related accounting policies and lending-commitment disclosures elsewhere in the filings.

- Asset quality:
  - Nonaccrual loans (consumer excluding credit card): $4.672B, down from $5.350B.

nodes.title: Consumer, excluding credit card
nodes.heading: 9.5.2.1 Consumer, excluding credit card
nodes.start_phrase:
Loans decreased from D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 1 driven by 
residential real estate loans at fair value and auto and other 
loans, largely offset by higher retained residential real 
estate loans.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Consumer lending portfolio excluding credit cards, with emphasis on residential real estate.
- Overall trend: Total loans declined since Dec 31, 2021, driven by decreases in residential real estate loans measured at fair value and in auto/other loans, partly offset by higher retained residential mortgage balances.
- Residential real estate composition: Predominantly prime first-lien mortgages and home equity lines of credit (HELOCs).
- Retained mortgages: Balances increased net of paydowns; nonaccrual retained loans fell due to improved credit performance. Net recoveries were lower in Q2 2022 versus prior year on reduced prepayments from higher rates; first-half net recoveries were roughly flat year over year.
- Loans at fair value: Decreased as Home Lending warehouse loan sales outpaced originations amid higher rates and lower loan purchase activity in CIB; nonaccrual fair value loans also declined, driven by CIB.
- HELOCs: $16.9B outstanding at June 30, 2022, including $5.5B recast/modified and $5.5B interest-only balloon HELOCs maturing mostly after 2030; risk managed by closing/reducing undrawn lines when borrower credit deteriorates.
- Interest-only mortgages: $34.4B at June 30, 2022 (up from $30.0B), typically higher-balance AWM borrowers; Q2 2022 showed net charge-offs due to a loan sale; 1H 2022 showed net recoveries; credit performance comparable to the broader prime portfolio.
- Government-insured/guaranteed mortgages: $1.158B at June 30, 2022 (down from $1.447B), with current $584M, 30–89 days past due $121M, and 90+ days past due $453M; allowance incorporates exposure to potential unrecoverable claim payments.
- Modified residential mortgages: Retained modified loans to borrowers in financial difficulty (including TDRs and certain modified PCD loans) totaled $12.185B (down from $13.251B); nonaccrual retained modified loans were $3.543B (down from $3.938B). Includes $2.8B (vs. $2.7B) of nonaccrual TDRs less than 90 days past due.
- Additional references: Note 11 for geographic and LTV details; prior Form 10-K for TDR nonaccrual treatment.

Loans in COVID-19 payment deferral programs that are performing under modified terms are generally not treated as delinquent.

nodes.title: WHOLESALE CREDIT PORTFOLIO
nodes.heading: 9.5.3 WHOLESALE CREDIT PORTFOLIO
nodes.start_phrase:
In its wholesale businesses, the Firm is exposed to credit 
risk primarily through its underwriting, lending, market-
making, and hedging activities with and for clients and 
counterparties, as well as through various operating 
services (such as cash management and clearing activities), 
securities financing activities and cash placed with banks.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and sources of risk: The wholesale credit portfolio reflects credit risk from underwriting, lending, market-making, hedging, operating services (cash management, clearing), securities financing, and cash placed with banks. The firm retains a portion of originated/acquired loans and distributes a significant share via syndication to manage concentrations and credit risk. Active management includes ongoing reviews of client credit quality, transaction structure (including collateral), and industry/product/client concentrations.

- Portfolio coverage: Includes exposures in CIB, CB, AWM, and Corporate, plus risk-rated exposures in CCB (business banking and auto dealer), which use the wholesale methodology to determine the allowance for credit losses.

- 1H22 credit performance: Credit continued to perform well with historically low charge-offs. Nonperforming exposure declined due to lower lending-related commitments (predominantly in CIB), partially offset by higher nonperforming derivatives. Nonperforming loans were relatively flat; activity included paydowns on Russia and Russia-associated clients downgraded in 1Q22.

- Balance trends as of June 30, 2022 (vs. Dec 31, 2021):
  - Retained loans increased by $23.9 billion, driven by CB and CIB, partly offset by AWM.
  - Total loans: $621.4 billion ($584.3b retained; $4.0b held-for-sale; $33.2b at fair value).

nodes.title: Wholesale credit exposure – maturity and ratings profile
nodes.heading: 9.5.3.1 Wholesale credit exposure – maturity and ratings profile

The following tables present the maturity and internal risk ratings profiles of the wholesale credit portfolio as of J u n e 3 0 , 
2022 , and D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 1.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Presents JPMorgan Chase’s wholesale credit exposure by maturity and internal risk ratings as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021.
- Investment-grade definition: Internal ratings qualitatively equivalent to BBB-/Baa3 or higher; collateral and structural support are considered in assigning internal ratings. Cross-reference to 2021 Form 10-K Note 12.
- Components covered:
  - Loans retained (by maturity buckets: ≤1 year, 1–5 years, >5 years; and by ratings: investment-grade vs non-investment-grade).
  - Derivative receivables net of liquid securities and cash collateral (by maturity and ratings).
  - Lending-related commitments (by maturity and ratings).
  - Subtotal of the above, plus loans held-for-sale/at fair value and receivables from customers, to arrive at total exposure net of derivative collateral.
  - Credit derivatives and credit-related notes used in credit portfolio management (not qualifying for hedge accounting), shown by maturity and ratings of the reference entities; notional amounts presented on a net basis.
- Key figures and trends:
  - Total wholesale credit exposure (net of derivative collateral) increased to $1.23 trillion at 6/30/22 from $1.19 trillion at 12/31/21.
  - Loans retained rose to $584.3 billion (72% investment-grade) from $560.4 billion (73% IG).
  - Derivative receivables net of collateral increased to $61.5 billion (72% IG) from $47.0 billion (68% IG).
  - Lending-related commitments were broadly flat at ~$487.5 billion (68% IG both periods).
  - Subtotal of primary exposures increased to $1.133 trillion, with the investment-grade share modestly lower (70% vs 71% prior).
  - Loans held-for-sale/at fair value declined to $37.2 billion (from $39.8 billion); receivables from customers edged down to $58.3 billion (from $59.6 billion).
- Maturity profile: Exposure is concentrated in the 1–5 year bucket, with meaningful amounts also due within 1 year; smaller portion extends beyond 5 years in both periods.
- Credit portfolio management:
  - Net purchased credit protection via credit derivatives and credit-related notes decreased to $15.4 billion notional (from $18.7 billion).
  - Majority of reference entities are investment-grade (83% at 6/30/22 vs 80% at 12/31/21); counterparties for purchased protection are predominantly investment-grade.
- Methodology/footnotes:
  - Maturities are based on remaining contractual maturity; derivative receivables can become payable before stated maturity due to cash flows/market changes.
  - Loans held-for-sale primarily include syndicated loans and transfers from the retained portfolio.
  - Prior-period amounts revised to conform to current presentation.

nodes.title: Lending-related commitments
nodes.heading: 9.5.3.4 Lending-related commitments
nodes.start_phrase:
The Firm uses lending-related financial instruments, such as 
commitments (including revolving credit facilities) and 
guarantees, to address the financing needs of its clients.
nodes.summary: The excerpt explains the firm’s credit exposure management across lending commitments, customer receivables, and derivatives. It notes that contractual amounts of commitments and guarantees represent maximum potential credit risk but are not indicative of expected future exposure because they are often refinanced, extended, canceled, or expire undrawn. Customer receivables primarily consist of collateralized margin loans to brokerage clients in CIB, CCB, and AWM, for which allowances are generally unnecessary; risk is managed through margin requirements, monitoring, and calls, and balances are reported in accrued interest and accounts receivable. For derivatives, the firm both serves clients and hedges its own risks, with credit risk dependent on whether trades are OTC (counterparty risk) or exchange-traded/cleared (CCP risk); it mitigates risk via enforceable netting and collateral agreements, with about 87%–88% of OTC derivatives under collateral agreements (excluding FX spot and daily-settled cleared trades). Derivative receivables at fair value rose to $81.3 billion at June 30, 2022 from $57.1 billion at December 31, 2021, driven by FX and commodity market movements; reported amounts reflect netting and cash collateral. The firm also holds liquid securities and other collateral (including non-HQLA) considered in assessing current credit risk, subject to enforceable netting and limited to net receivable exposure. Additional collateral posted at trade initiation, for non-daily call frequencies, or pending return does not offset reported balances but is available to secure potential future exposures. References are made to related notes for further detail.

nodes.title: Receivables from customers
nodes.heading: 9.5.3.5 Receivables from customers
nodes.start_phrase:
Receivables from customers reflect held-for-investment 
margin loans to brokerage clients in CIB, CCB and AWM that 
are collateralized by assets maintained in the clients’ 
brokerage accounts (e.g., cash on deposit, and liquid and 
readily marketable debt or equity securities).
nodes.summary:
- The Firm employs lending-related financial instruments—such as commitments (including revolving credit facilities) and guarantees—to meet client financing needs. While contractual amounts represent the maximum potential credit risk if drawn or if guarantees are called and clients default, most commitments historically refinance, extend, cancel, or expire undrawn; thus, contractual totals are not indicative of expected future exposure or funding needs (see Note 22).

- Receivables from customers consist of held-for-investment margin loans to brokerage clients in CIB, CCB, and AWM, secured by clients’ brokerage account assets (cash and liquid, marketable securities). Given the collateralization, no allowance for credit losses is generally recorded. The Firm manages risk via margin requirements and ongoing monitoring, requiring additional collateral or position reductions as needed. These receivables are reported within accrued interest and accounts receivable on the Consolidated balance sheets.

- Derivative activities support client risk management (credit, interest rate, FX, equity, commodity) and the Firm’s own market and credit risk management. Credit exposure depends on counterparty type and settlement mechanism: OTC derivatives expose the Firm to counterparty credit risk; ETD and OTC-cleared derivatives can introduce exposure to CCPs. The Firm mitigates exposures through legally enforceable master netting arrangements and collateral agreements.

- Approximately 87% and 88% of OTC derivative transactions (excluding FX spot and centrally cleared trades) were subject to collateral agreements at June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021, respectively (see Note 4).

- Derivative receivables at fair value were $81.3 billion at June 30, 2022 and $57.1 billion at December 31, 2021, with the increase driven by market movements in FX and commodities. Reported receivables reflect the effect of enforceable netting and related cash collateral.

- The Firm also holds liquid securities and cash collateral consistent with HQLA under the LCR rule, as well as other collateral that does not qualify as HQLA. Management considers these additional collateral amounts—subject to enforceable netting and limited to each counterparty’s net receivable—in assessing current credit risk.

- Additional collateral (e.g., cash, G7 government securities, other liquid agency/guaranteed securities, corporate debt and equity) is held for initial margins, non-daily margining, and amounts agreed to be returned but unsettled at the reporting date. While not reducing reported receivable balances, this collateral is available to secure potential future exposure (see Note 4).

nodes.title: Derivative contracts
nodes.heading: 9.5.3.6 Derivative contracts
nodes.start_phrase:
Derivatives enable clients and counterparties to manage 
risk including credit risk and risks arising from fluctuations 
in interest rates, foreign exchange and equities and 
commodities prices.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Discusses the Firm’s credit exposure management across lending-related commitments, margin loan receivables, derivatives, collateral practices, counterparty credit quality, and credit portfolio management (CPM) activities.
- Lending-related commitments and guarantees: Represent maximum potential credit risk if drawn or triggered, but are often refinanced, extended, canceled, or expire without draw or default; therefore, contractual amounts overstate expected future exposure and funding needs. Reference to Note 22.
- Receivables from customers (margin loans): Held-for-investment margin loans to brokerage clients in CIB, CCB, and AWM; collateralized by cash and liquid, marketable securities in client accounts; generally no allowance for credit losses due to collateralization. The Firm enforces margin requirements, monitors positions, and can require additional collateral or position reduction. Reported within accrued interest and accounts receivable.
- Derivatives purpose and risk: Used to help clients hedge risks and for the Firm’s market-making and own risk management (including managing counterparty credit risk and the Firm’s credit/market risks). Credit risk depends on counterparty type and settlement mechanism: OTC exposes the Firm to counterparty risk; ETD and OTC-cleared also expose the Firm to CCP risk.
- Risk mitigation: Broad use of legally enforceable master netting and collateral agreements. Approximately 87% (June 30, 2022) and 88% (December 31, 2021) of OTC derivatives (excluding FX spot and centrally cleared trades) are under collateral agreements. Refer to Note 4 for collateral and derivative details.
- Derivative receivables and collateral:
  - Fair value of derivative receivables (net of legally enforceable netting and cash collateral): $81.3B at June 30, 2022 vs. $57.1B at December 31, 2021, driven by FX and commodities market movements.
  - After liquid securities and other cash collateral: $61.5B (2022) vs. $47.0B (2021).
  - After all collateral (including other eligible collateral): $59.8B (2022) vs. $45.4B (2021).
  - The Firm also holds additional collateral (cash, G7 government securities, other liquid government/agency and guaranteed securities, corporate debt/equity) related to initiation, non-daily call frequency, and unsettled returns—available as security but not netted in the presented balances.
  - “Liquid securities” align with HQLA under the LCR rule; management’s view of current credit risk also considers other, non-HQLA collateral under enforceable netting, capped at net receivables per counterparty.
- Counterparty credit quality (exposure net of collateral):
  - June 30, 2022: Investment-grade 72% ($43.1B), Noninvestment-grade 28% ($16.7B).
  - December 31, 2021: Investment-grade 67% ($30.3B), Noninvestment-grade 33% ($15.2B).
- Credit portfolio management (CPM):
  - The Firm uses credit derivatives and credit-related notes both as a market-maker and as an end-user to manage credit risk on loans, lending-related commitments, and derivative receivables in wholesale businesses.
  - Net notional protection used in CPM: $15.4B at June 30, 2022 vs. $18.7B at December 31, 2021.
    - For loans and lending-related commitments: $4.6B (2022) vs. $4.1B (2021).
    - For derivative receivables: $10.8B (2022) vs. $14.6B (2021; revised).
  - Amounts are presented net by reference entity or index. References to Note 4 of the Form 10-Q and Note 5 of the 2021 Form 10-K for further CPM and credit derivatives details.

  - Noninvestment-grade: $16,685m (28%) in 2022 vs $15,157m (33%) in 2021.

- Describes credit portfolio management activities:

  - Obtains credit protection on certain retained wholesale loans via credit-related notes.
