  - References provided to related notes in the current 10-Q and the 2021 10-K for further detail.

nodes.title: ALLOWANCE FOR CREDIT LOSSES
nodes.heading: 9.5.4 ALLOWANCE FOR CREDIT LOSSES
nodes.start_phrase:
The Firm’s allowance for credit losses represents 
management's estimate of expected credit losses over the 
remaining expected life of the Firm's financial assets 
measured at amortized cost and certain off-balance sheet 
lending-related commitments.
nodes.summary:
- Explains the Firm’s allowance for credit losses as management’s estimate of expected lifetime losses on financial assets at amortized cost and certain off-balance-sheet lending commitments.
- Details the three components and where they appear on the Consolidated balance sheets: allowance for loan losses (retained loan portfolios), allowance for lending-related commitments (in accounts payable and other liabilities), and allowance for credit losses on investment securities (within investment securities).
- Reports the allowance at June 30, 2022 of $20.0 billion, up $1.3 billion from December 31, 2021, driven by a $1.0 billion increase in wholesale and $311 million in consumer.
- Attributes the increase to heavier weighting of adverse macro scenarios amid higher inflation, monetary policy changes, and geopolitical risks (including the war in Ukraine), modest deterioration in the macro forecast, loan growth in Card and Commercial Banking in Q2 2022, and Russia-related client downgrades in CIB and AWM in Q1 2022.
- Describes the estimation methodology using a weighted average of five internally developed macroeconomic scenarios; adverse scenarios imply U.S. unemployment above 4% through 4Q23 and a U.S. real GDP level 1.1% lower by 4Q23 versus the central case.
- Provides central case macro assumptions:
  - As of June 30, 2022: U.S. unemployment 3.6%, 3.6%, 3.7% for 4Q22, 2Q23, 4Q23; YoY U.S. real GDP growth 1.3%, 1.7%, 1.2%.
  - As of December 31, 2021: U.S. unemployment 4.2%, 4.0%, 3.9% for 2Q22, 4Q22, 2Q23; YoY U.S. real GDP growth 3.1%, 2.8%, 2.1%.
- Notes that future changes in forecasts will be reflected in the provision for credit losses.
- References other sections/notes for detailed policies, portfolio information, and critical accounting estimates (2021 Form 10-K Notes 13 and 10; Consumer and Wholesale Credit Portfolio pages; Note 11; Critical Accounting Estimates pages).

nodes.title: Allowance for credit losses and related information
nodes.heading: 9.5.4.1 Allowance for credit losses and related information
nodes.start_phrase:
(a)Includes collateral dependent loans, including those considered TDRs and those for which foreclosure is deemed probable, modified PCD loans, and non-
collateral dependent loans that have been modified or are reasonably expected to be modified in a TDR.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Six months ended June 30, 2022 vs. 2021 allowance for credit losses, disaggregated by Consumer (excluding credit card), Credit card, and Wholesale, plus firmwide totals.
- Allowance for loan losses rollforward: Beginning balances, gross charge-offs, gross recoveries, net charge-offs/(recoveries), provision for loan losses, other, and ending balances for each segment and total.
- Allowance for lending-related commitments rollforward: Beginning balances, provision, other, and ending balances by segment and total.
- Impairment methodology split: Asset-specific vs. portfolio-based components for both loan loss allowance and lending-related commitments.
- Investment securities allowance: Firmwide totals presented (no segment detail).
- Total allowance for credit losses: Aggregation of loan losses, lending-related commitments, and investment securities allowances.
- Loan exposure context: Memo of retained loans (end-of-period and average) by segment and total.
- Credit quality/coverage ratios:
  - Allowance for loan losses to retained loans (by segment and total).
  - Allowance for loan losses to retained nonaccrual loans (and excluding credit card).
  - Net charge-off/(recovery) rates by segment and total.
- Key period-over-period themes highlighted by the data:
  - Total allowance for loan losses decreased year over year (driven largely by lower credit card reserves), while wholesale and consumer ex-credit card were relatively stable to slightly higher.
  - Allowance for lending-related commitments declined year over year (primarily in wholesale).
  - Net charge-offs fell overall, led by improved credit card performance; consumer ex-credit card moved from a small net recovery to a small net charge-off; wholesale remained low.
  - 2022 reflected a reserve build (positive provision) versus significant reserve releases in 2021.
  - Retained loans grew meaningfully across segments, especially in wholesale and credit card.
  - Allowance-to-loans ratio declined overall, notably in credit card; coverage of nonaccrual loans increased.
- Footnotes clarify:
  - What constitutes asset-specific allowances (including collateral-dependent loans, TDRs/PCD, and nonaccrual wholesale).
  - Policy generally exempting credit card loans from nonaccrual status.

nodes.title: Allocation of allowance for loan losses
nodes.heading: 9.5.4.2 Allocation of allowance for loan losses
nodes.start_phrase: The table below presents a breakdown of the allowance for loan losses by loan class.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose: Presents the allocation of the allowance for loan losses by loan class and each class’s share of total retained loans; references Note 11 for loan class definitions.
- Periods covered: June 30, 2022 vs. December 31, 2021; amounts in millions (ratios shown as percent of retained loans to total retained loans).
- Total allowance: Increased to $17,750 from $16,386.
- Consumer segment (total allowance up to $12,329 from $12,015; share of retained loans 44% vs. 45%):

nodes.title: INVESTMENT PORTFOLIO RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: 9.5.5 INVESTMENT PORTFOLIO RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase:
Investment portfolio risk is the risk associated with the loss 
of principal or a reduction in expected returns on 
investments arising from the investment securities portfolio 
or from principal investments.
nodes.summary:
- Defines investment portfolio risk as potential loss of principal or reduced expected returns from the Firm’s investment securities portfolio and principal investments; investments are generally long-term with no expectation of short-term realized gains.
- Investment securities risk: primarily default risk on principal and interest; mitigated by a predominantly high-quality portfolio held by Treasury and CIO for balance sheet and asset-liability management. As of June 30, 2022, portfolio was $661.9 billion net of allowance for credit losses with an average AA+ rating. Cross-references provided for liquidity and market risk details.
- Principal investment risk: relates to privately held ownership interests and junior capital, including tax-oriented investments and strategic investments that support business objectives; excludes investments consolidated on the Firm’s balance sheet. Managed within the lines of business and Corporate, aligning with strategies such as supporting underserved communities and minority-owned businesses.
- Principal investment carrying values: total $33.3 billion at June 30, 2022 vs. $30.5 billion at December 31, 2021, comprising $23.7 billion in tax-oriented investments (primarily alternative energy and affordable housing) and $9.6 billion in private equity, various debt and equity instruments, and real assets; includes a 40% stake in C6 Bank.
- Notes governance and oversight framework referenced in JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K (page 132).

nodes.title: Investment securities risk
nodes.heading: 9.5.5.1 Investment securities risk
nodes.start_phrase:
Investment securities risk includes the exposure associated 
with a default in the payment of principal and interest.
nodes.summary:
- Defines investment portfolio risk as potential loss of principal or reduced expected returns from investment securities and principal investments; notes investments are generally long-term with no expectation of short-term realized gains.
- Investment securities portfolio: held primarily by Treasury and CIO for balance sheet and asset-liability management; key risk is default of principal and interest; risk mitigated by high quality of holdings.
- As of June 30, 2022, Treasury and CIO investment securities portfolio was $661.9 billion (net of allowance for credit losses) with an average AA+ credit rating (based on external ratings where available, otherwise internal ratings).
- Principal investments: typically privately held ownership or junior capital, including tax-oriented investments and strategic investments; managed within LOBs and Corporate; exclude consolidated investments; aligned with firm strategies, including support for underserved communities and minority-owned businesses.
- Carrying values of principal investment portfolios:
  - June 30, 2022 total: $33.3 billion vs. December 31, 2021 total: $30.5 billion.
  - Tax-oriented investments (alternative energy, affordable housing): $23.7B vs. $23.2B.
  - Private equity, various debt/equity instruments, real assets: $9.6B vs. $7.3B (includes 40% stake in C6 Bank).
- Cross-references provided to detailed discussions on investment securities portfolio, liquidity risk, market risk, and governance/oversight in other sections and the 2021 Form 10-K.

nodes.title: Principal investment risk
nodes.heading: 9.5.5.2 Principal investment risk
nodes.start_phrase:
Principal investments are typically privately-held financial 
instruments representing ownership interests or other 
forms of junior capital .
nodes.summary:
- Defines investment portfolio risk as potential loss of principal or reduced returns from the investment securities portfolio or principal investments; investments are generally long-term with no expectation of short-term realized gains.
- Describes the investment securities portfolio as predominantly held by Treasury and CIO for balance sheet and asset-liability management purposes.
- Investment securities risk focuses on default risk of principal and interest; mitigated by high-quality holdings. As of June 30, 2022, the Treasury and CIO portfolio was $661.9 billion (net of allowance for credit losses) with an average AA+ credit rating (external where available, otherwise internal).
- Principal investments are typically privately held ownership or junior capital instruments, including tax-oriented investments (alternative energy, affordable housing), private equity, various debt and equity instruments, and real assets; they are managed within the lines of business and Corporate, generally excluded if consolidated, and support strategic goals including underserved communities and minority-owned businesses.
- Portfolio balances: as of June 30, 2022 versus December 31, 2021:
  - Tax-oriented investments: $23.7B vs. $23.2B
  - Private equity/debt/equity/real assets: $9.6B vs. $7.3B (includes a 40% stake in C6 Bank)
  - Total carrying value: $33.3B vs. $30.5B
- Provides cross-references for detailed discussions: Corporate segment results (investment securities and internal ratings), Liquidity Risk Management, Market Risk Management, and governance/oversight in the 2021 Form 10-K.

nodes.title: MARKET RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: 9.6 MARKET RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase:
Market risk is the risk associated with the effect of changes 
in market factors such as interest and foreign exchange 
rates, equity and commodity prices, credit spreads or 
implied volatilities, on the value of assets and liabilities held 
for both the short and long term.
nodes.summary:
- Defines market risk as potential losses from changes in interest rates, foreign exchange rates, equity and commodity prices, credit spreads, and implied volatilities affecting assets and liabilities.
- References the firm’s Market Risk Management framework (organization, measurement, monitoring, control, and business activities) in the 2021 Form 10-K.
- Highlights inherent imprecision and limitations of market risk models, especially under sudden or severe market shifts, and points to the firm’s model risk management discussion.
- Notes ongoing review and calibration of market risk measures by Market Risk Management.
- Describes Value-at-Risk (VaR) as the primary statistical measure, with a single framework underpinning both Risk Management VaR and Regulatory VaR.
- Details Risk Management VaR: one-day holding period, expected tail-loss methodology approximating a 95% confidence level, aligned with daily risk management decisions.
- Details Regulatory VaR: a separately calculated daily aggregated measure per regulatory rules used to determine Basel III regulatory capital requirements.
- Explains that VaR models are periodically evaluated and enhanced due to portfolio, market, and modeling changes, which may affect historical comparability; references model reviews and approvals.
- Directs to further resources: Form 10-K page 135 for VaR limitations and differences between VaR types; Basel III Pillar 3 disclosures for Regulatory VaR, stressed VaR, and backtesting; and pages 138–140 for nonstatistical market risk measures.

nodes.title: Value-at-risk
nodes.heading: 9.6.1 Value-at-risk
nodes.start_phrase:
JPMorgan Chase utilizes value-at-risk (“VaR”), a statistical 
risk measure , to estimate the potential loss from adverse 
market moves in the current market environment.
nodes.summary:
- Defines market risk as the potential impact of changes in interest rates, foreign exchange rates, equity and commodity prices, credit spreads, and implied volatilities on asset/liability values across time horizons.
- Points to JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for detailed discussion of the Market Risk Management organization, measurement, monitoring and control, and main market risk–generating activities.
- Emphasizes model limitations and uncertainty, especially under sudden or severe market shifts; refers to Estimations and Model Risk Management in the 10-K for model risk governance.
- Describes the Firm’s single value-at-risk (VaR) framework:
  - Risk Management VaR: one-day holding period, expected tail-loss methodology approximating a 95% confidence level, aligned with day-to-day risk management.
  - Regulatory VaR: separately calculated per Basel III for regulatory capital; further details available in Pillar 3 disclosures.
  - Notes periodic model evaluation/enhancements that can affect historical comparability; references to 10-K pages for inherent limitations and differences between Risk Management VaR and Regulatory VaR.
  - Mentions other, nonstatistical market risk measures described in the 10-K.
- Presents Risk Management VaR results (95% confidence) with averages, mins, and maxes for Q2 2022, Q1 2022, and Q2 2021 across:
  - CIB trading by risk type (Fixed income, Foreign exchange, Equities, Commodities and other) with diversification benefits.
  - Credit Portfolio VaR.
  - CIB VaR (including diversification with Credit Portfolio).
  - CCB VaR.
  - Corporate and other LOB VaR.
  - Total Firm VaR with diversification benefits across units.
- Highlights key total VaR figures and drivers:
  - Average total VaR: $54m (Q2’22), $63m (Q1’22), $43m (Q2’21).
  - Quarter-over-quarter: down $9m in Q2’22 vs. Q1’22, mainly from lower Credit Portfolio VaR as nickel-related counterparty exposure declined, partly offset by higher Fixed income volatility.
  - Year-over-year: up $11m in Q2’22 vs. Q2’21, driven by greater Fixed income volatility and elevated Credit Portfolio VaR linked to March 2022 nickel market dislocations.
- Notes specific footnotes and governance changes:
  - In Q1’22, the credit risk component of CVA for certain counterparties was removed from Credit Portfolio VaR (and related hedges removed), with exposure moved to other sensitivity-based measures.
  - Nickel price spikes and volatility drove elevated Credit Portfolio VaR in Q1’22; levels decreased in Q2’22 as exposure was reduced but remained elevated vs. prior year.
  - Corporate and other LOB VaR decreased due to lower market values of a legacy publicly traded private equity position.
  - Diversification benefits reflect non-additivity of VaR; min/max diversification not meaningful due to differing dates of component extremes.
- References a daily VaR chart showing a March 2022 spike, attributed to nickel-related counterparty exposure in the Credit portfolio.

nodes.title: VaR backtesting
nodes.heading: 9.6.2 VaR backtesting
nodes.start_phrase:
The Firm performs daily VaR model backtesting , which compares the daily Risk Management VaR results with the daily gains 
and losses that are utilized for VaR backtesting purposes.
nodes.summary:
- The firm conducts daily Value-at-Risk (VaR) backtesting by comparing daily Risk Management VaR to daily gains and losses used specifically for backtesting.
- The backtesting gains/losses exclude components of total net revenue—such as intraday new transactions, fees, commissions, certain valuation adjustments, and net interest income—so they do not reflect reported revenue and excluded items may offset backtesting results.
- The definition of backtesting gains/losses is consistent with Basel III requirements.
- A backtesting exception occurs when a day’s backtesting loss exceeds the prior day’s Risk Management VaR.
- Expected frequency of exceptions is about five in every 100 trading days; actual exceptions can differ if current market volatility diverges from the volatility in the 12-month historical window used for VaR.
- For the 12 months ended June 30, 2022: 148 of 261 days showed gains and 22 backtesting exceptions were observed. For the three months ended June 30, 2022: 37 of 65 days showed gains and 3 exceptions were observed.
- A chart displays the distribution of daily backtesting gains and losses over the trailing 12 months and three months ended June 30, 2022, with losses expressed as a percentage of daily VaR, grouped in 50-percentage-point intervals; exceptions appear in intervals above 100%.
- These results differ from those in the firm’s Basel III Pillar 3 disclosures, which are based on Regulatory VaR for covered positions rather than Risk Management VaR.

nodes.title: Earnings-at-risk
nodes.heading: 9.6.3 Earnings-at-risk
nodes.start_phrase:
The effect of interest rate exposure on the Firm’s reported 
net income is important as interest rate risk represents one 
of the Firm’s significant market risks.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: How JPMorgan Chase measures and manages interest rate risk to net income using an earnings-at-risk (EaR) framework, a key market risk for the Firm arising from both trading and traditional banking activities (loans, deposits, debt issuance, investment securities).
- Scope of positions and modeling: Simulations cover interest rate–sensitive assets and liabilities in U.S. dollars and non-U.S. currencies, including retained loans, deposits (and deposits with banks), investment securities, long-term debt, related interest rate hedges, and funds transfer pricing of other positions; LOB/Corporate inclusion referenced to 2021 Form 10-K, p.134.
- Methodology: EaR estimates the sensitivity of net interest income plus certain interest-sensitive fees over the next 12 months relative to a baseline that reflects market rates and deposit pricing assumptions. It is not a forecast of net interest income.
- Scenario design:
  - Parallel shifts: simultaneous equal changes in short- and long-term rates (±100 bps shown).
  - Steeper curve: short-term rates held constant, long-term rates increase.
  - Flatter curve: short-term rates rise while long-term rates are constant, or short-term rates constant while long-term rates fall.
- Key modeling assumptions:
  - Instantaneous rate shocks from baseline.
  - Forecasted balance sheet; modeled prepayment and reinvestment behavior; excludes management/client actions post-shock.
  - Mortgage prepayments depend on scenario rates vs contractual rates, seasoning, and historical factors.
  - Deposit forecasts include assumptions on Quantitative Easing reversal.
  - Deposit betas and repricing lags drive deposit rate sensitivity.
  - Models and scenarios are periodically enhanced for balance sheet mix, market conditions, and simulation improvements; related VaR/sensitivity measures are referenced (2021 10-K, p.134).
- U.S. dollar EaR results (impact on next-12-month net interest income; in billions):
  - June 30, 2022: Parallel +100 bps: (1.4); Parallel −100 bps: (1.0); Steeper (+100 bps long-term): 0.5; Steeper (−100 bps short-term): (0.4); Flatter (+100 bps short-term): (1.8); Flatter (−100 bps long-term): (0.6).
  - December 31, 2021: Parallel +100 bps: 5.0; Steeper (+100 bps long-term): 1.8; Flatter (+100 bps short-term): 3.2; other scenarios “NM” (not meaningful) given then-prevailing rate levels.
- Drivers of change (USD): Shifts from 12/31/2021 to 6/30/2022 reflect a higher-rate baseline and balance sheet changes. As of 6/30/2022, negative sensitivity to +100 bps parallel and short-term increases reflects liabilities repricing faster/more than assets; sensitivity to +100 bps long-term increases and −100 bps parallel rates primarily reflects greater asset repricing effects relative to liabilities.
- Non-U.S. dollar EaR results (in billions):
  - June 30, 2022: Parallel +100 bps: 0.9; Parallel −100 bps: (0.8); Steeper (−100 bps short-term): (0.8); Flatter (+100 bps short-term): 0.8.
  - December 31, 2021: Parallel +100 bps: 0.8; Flatter (+100 bps short-term): 0.8; other scenarios “NM.”
  - Steeper/flatter scenarios with long-term-only moves were not material at both dates.
- Notes: Certain 2021 scenarios were not meaningful due to rate levels; results are sensitivities around a baseline for the next 12 months and are not an outlook/forecast (see Outlook, p.8).

nodes.title: Other sensitivity-based measures
nodes.heading: 9.6.4 Other sensitivity-based measures
nodes.start_phrase:
The Firm quantifies the market risk of certain debt and equity and credit and funding-related exposures by assessing the 
potential impact on net revenue, other comprehensive income (“OCI”) and noninterest expense due to changes in relevant 
market variables.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Presentation of “other sensitivity-based measures” used to quantify market risk for certain debt, equity, credit, and funding-related exposures that are not captured in VaR or earnings-at-risk.
- Method: Sensitivity analysis showing potential impacts to net revenue, other comprehensive income (OCI), and noninterest expense from defined shocks in relevant market variables; hedging instruments are shown net of the positions hedged. Sensitivities are not predictive of future outcomes and may vary across maturities.
- Scope covered:
  - Debt and equity exposures:
    - Asset Management activities (seed capital, fund co-investments, deferred compensation and related hedges).
    - Other debt and equity (real estate-related fair value option loans, privately held equity, and other fair value investments).
  - Credit- and funding-related exposures:
    - Non-USD long-term debt (LTD) cross-currency basis risk on hedging derivatives.
    - FX revaluation on non-USD LTD hedging derivatives.
    - Derivatives funding spread risk via FVA.
    - CVA counterparty credit risk and associated hedges (moved here from Credit Portfolio VaR in 1Q22 due to elevated counterparty spread levels).
    - Fair value option (FVO) elected liabilities: DVA (funding spread risk) and interest rate sensitivity related to changes in the Firm’s own credit spread, plus related risk-management positions.
- Key quantitative indications (June 30, 2022 vs. December 31, 2021):
  - A 10% decline in market value of “Other debt and equity” would reduce net revenue by about $1.1B (vs. ~$1.0B prior), the largest sensitivity disclosed.
  - Asset Management activities show smaller downside to a 10% market decline (about $50M vs. $69M prior).
  - A 1 bp tightening of non-USD LTD cross-currency basis produces a modest OCI loss (about $14M vs. $16M prior).
  - A 10% currency depreciation on non-USD LTD hedges yields a small OCI impact (about -$5M vs. +$15M prior).
  - A 1 bp increase in funding spreads affects derivatives FVA slightly negatively in net revenue (about -$5M vs. -$7M prior).
  - A 10% credit spread widening for CVA shows a small net revenue loss (about -$1M; previously not shown).
  - A 1 bp increase in spreads on FVO liabilities (DVA) benefits OCI (about +$44M vs. +$41M prior); related interest rate sensitivities and hedges are near zero in 2022 (small offsets in 2021).
- Financial statement presentation:
  - Certain impacts recognized in net revenue (e.g., seed capital, other fair value investments, FVA, and related risk-management positions).
  - Certain impacts recognized in noninterest expense (e.g., deferred compensation and related hedges).
  - Certain impacts recognized in OCI (e.g., non-USD LTD hedges and DVA on FVO liabilities).
- Additional notes:
  - Excludes equity securities measured under the measurement alternative (no readily determinable fair values).
  - References the Firm’s 2021 Form 10-K (page 140) for business activities that give rise to market risk.

nodes.title: COUNTRY RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: 9.7 COUNTRY RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase:
The Firm, through its LOBs and Corporate, may be exposed 
to country risk resulting from financial, economic, political 
or other significant developments which adversely affect 
the value of the Firm’s exposures related to a particular 
country or set of countries.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: How the firm manages country risk arising from adverse financial, economic, political, or other developments that could impact exposures tied to specific countries.
- Governance: A dedicated Country Risk Management group monitors portfolios, assesses diversification, and aligns exposures with the firm’s strategy and country risk tolerance.
- Scope of exposure: Stems from lending, deposits, investing, and market‑making, both cross‑border and locally funded, and includes government and private‑sector counterparties.
- Country attribution: Exposures are assigned to the country where the largest share of a counterparty’s assets are located or revenues are derived, which may differ from legal domicile/incorporation.
- Measurement basis: Aggregates risk to an immediate default with zero recovery of attributed counterparties; excludes contingent/indirect activities (e.g., clearing services, secondary exposure to collateral on securities financing receivables).
- Assumptions and limitations: Certain products (e.g., non‑linear or index) and counterparties require assumptions; differing approaches could change reported exposure.
- Measurement framework:
  - Lending: total committed (funded and unfunded), net of allowance for credit losses and eligible cash/marketable securities collateral.
  - Deposits: cash balances placed with central and commercial banks.
  - Securities financing: receivable balance net of eligible collateral.
  - Debt and equity securities: fair value of all long and short positions.
  - Derivative receivables: fair value net of eligible collateral.
  - Credit derivatives: net notional protection bought/sold for the same reference entity, inclusive of derivative fair values, reflecting management practice.
- Reporting distinction: Internal country risk reporting differs from FFIEC regulatory reporting.
- Reference: Further discussion in JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10‑K, pages 141–142.

nodes.title: Sources and measurement
nodes.heading: 9.7.1 Sources and measurement
nodes.start_phrase:
The Firm is exposed to country risk through its lending and 
deposits, investing, and market-making activities, whether 
cross-border or locally funded.
nodes.summary:
- Describes JPMorgan Chase’s approach to managing country risk across lines of business and Corporate, with active monitoring of portfolios and diversification relative to strategy and risk tolerance.
- Notes exposure sources: lending, deposits, investing, and market-making, both cross-border and locally funded, involving government and private-sector entities.
- Explains country attribution methodology based on where the counterparty/issuer/obligor/guarantor has the largest proportion of assets or revenue, which may differ from legal domicile.
- Defines country exposure as the aggregate risk to immediate default with zero recovery for parties attributed to that country; excludes contingent or indirect exposures (e.g., clearing services, secondary exposure to collateral on securities financing).
- Acknowledges use of assumptions for complex, non-linear, or index products and cases where attribution to a single country is unsuitable; different methods could change reported exposure.
- Details measurement framework by product:
  - Lending: total committed (funded and unfunded) net of allowance for credit losses and eligible cash/marketable securities collateral.
  - Deposits: cash balances with central and commercial banks.
  - Securities financing: receivable balance net of eligible collateral.
  - Debt and equity securities: fair value of all long and short positions.
  - Derivative receivables: fair value net of eligible collateral.
  - Credit derivatives: net notional protection purchased or sold for the same reference entity, inclusive of derivative fair values, aligned with management practice.
- States that internal country risk reporting differs from FFIEC regulatory reporting.
- References additional detail in JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K, pages 141–142.

nodes.title: Risk Reporting
nodes.heading: 9.7.2 Risk Reporting
nodes.start_phrase:
The following table presents the Firm’s top 20 exposures by 
country (excluding the U.S.) as of J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2 and their 
comparative exposures as of D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 1.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Firm’s risk reporting on top 20 non-U.S. country exposures as of June 30, 2022, with comparisons to December 31, 2021, based on the Firm’s internal country risk management approach; not an assessment of credit conditions. Exposures can fluctuate with client activity and market flows.
- Key drivers of changes:
  - Germany exposure increased largely due to higher cash placements at the German central bank tied to balance sheet and liquidity management.
  - U.K. exposure decreased due to reduced central bank cash placements from liquidity management actions.
  - Australia exposure declined due to reduced cash at the Reserve Bank of Australia, driven by client market-making and lower client cash deposits following interest rate hikes.
  - Russia exposure was approximately $600 million as of June 30, 2022.
- Notable exposure levels and trends (total exposure, 6/30/22 vs. 12/31/21):
  - Germany up to $95.2b (from $61.7b); U.K. down to $75.2b (from $96.4b); Japan up to $49.1b (from $45.5b); Australia down to $19.3b (from $39.1b); France up to $18.9b (from $14.0b); Switzerland down to $17.1b (from $20.9b); China down to $17.0b (from $18.6b); Canada stable at $16.4b (from $16.9b); Brazil up to $16.3b (from $12.0b); Netherlands and Belgium both up to $10.0b (from $6.8b); India down to $9.3b (from $14.7b); Ireland up to $5.1b (from $2.7b). Other countries showed smaller changes.
- Exposure composition categories in the table:
  - Lending and deposits: loans and accrued interest, lending commitments (net of collateral and ACL), deposits with banks/central banks, acceptances, other monetary assets, and LCs net of risk participations; excludes intra-day/operational exposures (e.g., settlement/clearing).
  - Trading and investing: market-making inventory, investment securities, and counterparty exposure on derivatives and securities financing, net of eligible collateral and hedging; includes single-name and index exposures referencing entities in listed countries.
  - Other: predominantly physical commodity inventory.
- Coverage and methodology notes:
  - Table captures 88% (June 30, 2022) and 87% (December 31, 2021) of total firmwide non-U.S. exposure attributable to individual countries.
  - December 31, 2021 country rankings are shown aligned to June 30, 2022 rankings for comparability.

nodes.title: OPERATIONAL RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: 9.8 OPERATIONAL RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase:
Operational risk is the risk of an adverse outcome resulting 
from inadequate or failed internal processes or systems, 
human factors, or external events impacting the Firm’s 
processes or systems.
nodes.summary:
- Defines operational risk as losses from failed processes/systems, human factors, or external events; includes compliance, conduct, legal, estimation and model risk.
- Notes operational risk is inherent and can arise from fraud, business disruptions, cyberattacks, employee misconduct, regulatory non-compliance, and third-party/vendor failures.
- States the Firm manages operational risk in line with its financial position, business profile, and regulatory/market environments; references JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K (pages 143–149) for more detail.
- Highlights increased operational and compliance risk from evolving Russia/Ukraine-related sanctions; describes added controls to avoid dealings with sanctioned parties and to block/restrict payments per regulations.
- Describes business and technology resiliency risks (pandemics, severe weather, power/telecom outages, third-party failures, cyberattacks, terrorism) and the Firmwide Business Resiliency Program to prepare for, adapt to, withstand, and recover from disruptions through governance, training, planning, testing, and risk management initiatives across staff, technology, facilities, and third parties.
- Addresses heightened cybersecurity risk potentially linked to sanctions retaliation; notes implementation of enhanced threat monitoring and other controls, while acknowledging that absolute security cannot be guaranteed.

nodes.title: Business and technology resiliency risk
nodes.heading: 9.8.1 Business and technology resiliency risk
nodes.start_phrase:
Disruptions can occur due to forces beyond the Firm’s 
control such as the spread of infectious diseases or 
pandemics, severe weather, power or telecommunications 
loss, failure of a third party to provide expected services, 
cyberattacks and terrorism.
nodes.summary:
- Defines operational risk as losses from failed processes/systems, human factors, or external events, encompassing compliance, conduct, legal, and model/estimation risks.
- Notes operational risk is inherent and can manifest via fraud, business disruptions (including extraordinary events), cyberattacks, employee misconduct, regulatory noncompliance, and third‑party/vendor failures.
- States the Firm’s Operational Risk Management aims to manage risk at appropriate levels given its financial position, business mix, markets, and regulatory environments; references further detail in JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10‑K (pp. 143–149).
- Highlights increased compliance and operational challenges from evolving Russia‑related sanctions tied to the war in Ukraine; describes additional controls to mitigate noncompliance and block/restrict prohibited dealings and payments.
- Describes business and technology resiliency risk and the Firmwide Business Resiliency Program designed to prepare for, withstand, and recover from disruptions (e.g., pandemics, severe weather, power/telecom loss, third‑party failures, cyberattacks, terrorism) through governance, training, planning, testing, and risk management initiatives.
- Addresses heightened cybersecurity risk, including potential retaliation for sanctions; notes enhanced threat monitoring and precautionary controls while acknowledging no assurance of absolute protection against cyberattacks.

nodes.title: Cybersecurity Risk
nodes.heading: 9.8.2 Cybersecurity Risk
nodes.start_phrase:
The Firm continues to face increased risk of cyber attacks 
due to potential retaliation for the sanctions imposed as a 
result of the war in Ukraine.
nodes.summary: The document outlines the firm’s operational risk framework, defining operational risk as losses from failed processes, systems, human factors, or external events, and encompassing compliance, conduct, legal, and model risk. It highlights key manifestations such as fraud, business disruptions, cyberattacks, regulatory non-compliance, and third-party failures. The firm aims to manage these risks in line with its financial position, business profile, and regulatory environments, referencing detailed practices in JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K (pp. 143–149). It notes elevated operational risk from evolving sanctions related to the war in Ukraine and describes added controls to ensure sanctions compliance and payment restrictions. The Business Resiliency Program is detailed as a governance, training, planning, and testing framework to prepare for and recover from disruptions like pandemics, severe weather, utility outages, third-party failures, cyberattacks, and terrorism. The document also addresses heightened cybersecurity risk, enhanced threat monitoring, and acknowledges that absolute protection cannot be guaranteed.

nodes.title: CRITICAL ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES USED BY THE FIRM
nodes.heading: 10 CRITICAL ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES USED BY THE FIRM
nodes.start_phrase:
JPMorgan Chase ’s accounting policies and use of estimates 
are integral to understanding its reported results.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of JPMorgan Chase’s critical accounting estimates, emphasizing the central role of management judgment in determining asset and liability carrying values, supported by policies, controls, independent review, and consistent application across periods.
- Primary focus on the allowance for credit losses, which covers:
  - Allowance for loan losses (scored and risk-rated portfolios),
  - Allowance for lending-related commitments, and
  - Allowance for credit losses on investment securities.
- Key judgment factors in estimating expected credit losses over the remaining asset life: development and weighting of macroeconomic forecasts, use of historical loss experience, assessment of risk characteristics and ratings, collateral valuation, and remaining expected life; with references to related 10-K and 10-Q notes.
- Central role of an eight-quarter macroeconomic forecast using hundreds of macroeconomic variables (MEVs), with fewer than 20 driving modeled losses; key MEVs differ by portfolio:
  - Consumer: U.S. unemployment, home price index (HPI), U.S. real GDP.
  - Wholesale: U.S. real GDP, U.S. unemployment, equity prices, corporate credit spreads, oil prices, commercial real estate prices, HPI.
- Acknowledgment that assumption changes can significantly affect allowances; impacts are interrelated, nonlinear, and vary by geography and product, making single-factor sensitivities difficult.
- Scenario analysis comparing central vs. relative adverse scenarios (two of five used), highlighting adverse assumptions:
  - Unemployment ~2.2% higher on average (peak ~3.7% in Q2 2023),
  - Real GDP ~2.9% lower by end of forecast (peak ~5.8% lower in Q2 2023),
  - National HPI peak difference of ~17.6% lower in Q1 2024.
- Caveats: the analysis is not a forecast of allowance changes; the recorded allowance already reflects weighting to adverse scenarios; MEV effects are interrelated and nonlinear, preventing simple extrapolation.

nodes.title: Allowance for credit losses
nodes.heading: 10.1 Allowance for credit losses
nodes.start_phrase:
The Firm’s allowance for credit losses represents 
management’s estimate of expected credit losses over the 
remaining expected life of the Firm’s financial assets 
measured at amortized cost and certain off-balance sheet 
lending-related commitments.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and governance: Describes JPMorgan Chase’s critical accounting estimates, emphasizing management judgment, robust policies, controls, independent review, consistent application over time, and controlled processes for methodology changes.
- Allowance for credit losses (ACL):
  - Coverage: Allowance for loan losses (scored and risk-rated portfolios), lending-related commitments, and credit losses on investment securities.
  - Methodology: Estimates expected credit losses over the remaining expected life; incorporates macroeconomic forecasts (eight-quarter horizon), historical loss experience, portfolio risk characteristics, risk ratings, collateral valuation, and remaining life.
  - Macroeconomic variables (MEVs): Hundreds considered; key drivers vary by portfolio/geography.
    - Consumer: U.S. unemployment, home price index (HPI), U.S. real GDP.
    - Wholesale: U.S. real GDP, U.S. unemployment, U.S. equity prices, corporate credit spreads, oil prices, commercial real estate prices, HPI.
  - Sensitivity and uncertainty: Results are highly sensitive to assumptions; impacts are interrelated and nonlinear; geographic/product differences and directional inconsistencies can offset.
  - Scenario analysis (central vs relative adverse as of June 30, 2022):
    - Adverse scenario assumptions: U.S. unemployment ~+2.2% on average (peak +3.7% in Q2 2023); U.S. real GDP ~2.9% lower by end of forecast (peak −5.8% in Q2 2023); national HPI peak −17.6% in Q1 2024.
    - Modeled loss impacts (excluding qualitative offsets): +$0.6B residential real estate loans and commitments; +$2.0B credit card loans; +$3.0B wholesale loans and commitments.
  - Caveats: Allowance already reflects weighting of adverse scenarios; scenario impacts aren’t linearly scalable; portfolio mix and borrower behavior changes matter; qualitative adjustments also affect the final ACL.
  - Conclusion: Estimates deemed reasonable and appropriately governed for the period ended June 30, 2022.
- Fair value measurements:
  - Scope: Assets and liabilities at fair value on a recurring basis (e.g., derivatives, structured notes, certain securities financing) and nonrecurring basis (e.g., certain loans measured via collateral fair value).
  - Level 3 transparency: Presents assets measured at fair value and the portion classified as Level 3.
  - Key figures at June 30, 2022 (in billions):
    - Total assets at fair value: $1,156.7; Level 3: $24.0.
    - Total Firm assets: $3,841.3.
    - Level 3 as % of total Firm assets: 0.6%; as % of total assets at fair value: 2.1%.
    - Selected line items (fair value/Level 3): Trading assets $465.5/$12.2 (incl. trading debt & equity $384.2/$3.3; derivative receivables $81.3/$8.9), AFS securities $222.1/$0.2, Loans $47.1/$2.0, MSRs $7.4/$7.4, Nonrecurring fair value assets $3.3/$1.7.
  - Note: Derivative receivables Level 3 disclosure is presented before netting; netting (incl. cash collateral) would reduce reported Level 3 balances but is not relevant to input transparency.

nodes.title: ACCOUNTING AND REPORTING DEVELOPMENTS
nodes.heading: 11 ACCOUNTING AND REPORTING DEVELOPMENTS
nodes.start_phrase:
•Provides optional expedients and exceptions to 
current accounting guidance when financial 
instruments, hedge accounting relationships, and 
other transactions are amended due to reference 
rate reform.
nodes.summary:
- The section outlines Accounting and Reporting Developments, focusing on FASB standards adopted since January 1, 2021 and those issued but not yet adopted.
- Adopted: Reference Rate Reform (issued March 2020; updated January 2021)
  - Provides optional expedients/exceptions for contracts, hedge relationships, and other transactions affected by reference rate reform.
  - Permits treating certain contract amendments as modifications rather than extinguishments; allows hedge term changes without automatic dedesignation; offers a one-time option to transfer securities out of held-to-maturity; and provides expedients for “discounting transition” on derivatives.
  - The firm elected certain expedients for contract modifications, hedge accounting, and discounting transition (applied retrospectively), beginning Q3 2020; no material impact on the Consolidated Financial Statements.
- Issued but not yet adopted:
  - Derivatives and Hedging: Fair Value Hedging – Portfolio Layer Method (issued March 2022; effective January 1, 2023; early adoption permitted)
    - Expands portfolio hedging to include more of a portfolio of prepayable assets and allows non-prepayable assets in the same portfolio.
    - Clarifies eligible derivatives, balance sheet presentation, and updates disclosure requirements for hedge accounting adjustments.
    - The firm is evaluating the impact and its adoption timing.
  - Financial Instruments – Credit Losses: Troubled Debt Restructurings and Vintage Disclosures (issued March 2022; effective January 1, 2023; early adoption permitted)
    - Eliminates TDR accounting and disclosure requirements and the discounted cash flow requirement for allowance measurement.
    - Requires disclosures on loan modifications for borrowers in financial difficulty (e.g., principal forgiveness, interest rate reductions, other-than-insignificant payment delays, term extensions) and charge-offs by origination year.
    - May be adopted prospectively or via modified retrospective method; the firm plans to adopt on January 1, 2023 and is evaluating the impact.

- Presents JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s unaudited Consolidated Statements of Income and Consolidated Statements of Comprehensive Income for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021 (in millions, except per share data).
- Income statement highlights:
  - Total net revenue was roughly flat year-over-year for Q2 (2022: $30.7B vs 2021: $30.5B) and slightly lower for the first half (2022: $61.4B vs 2021: $62.7B).
  - Net interest income increased (Q2: $15.1B vs $12.7B; 1H: $29.0B vs $25.6B) on higher interest income, partially offset by higher interest expense.
  - Noninterest revenue declined (Q2: $15.6B vs $17.7B; 1H: $32.4B vs $37.1B), with notable decreases in investment banking fees, card income, mortgage fees, and other income; principal transactions were higher; investment securities losses increased.
  - Provision for credit losses shifted from a net release in 2021 to a build in 2022 (Q2: +$1.1B vs -$2.3B; 1H: +$2.6B vs -$6.4B).
  - Noninterest expense rose (Q2: $18.7B vs $17.7B; 1H: $37.9B vs $36.4B), led by compensation, marketing, and professional services.
  - Net income declined (Q2: $8.6B vs $11.9B; 1H: $16.9B vs $26.2B); net income to common stockholders followed the same trend.
  - Diluted EPS fell (Q2: $2.76 vs $3.78; 1H: $5.39 vs $8.28); average diluted shares outstanding decreased year-over-year.
- Comprehensive income highlights:
  - Significant other comprehensive losses after tax in 2022 (Q2: -$4.8B; 1H: -$14.3B) versus gains or smaller losses in 2021, driven primarily by unrealized losses on investment securities and cash flow hedges; partially offset by gains from DVA on fair value option liabilities and modest positive pension/OPEB effects.
  - As a result, comprehensive income decreased sharply (Q2: $3.8B vs $13.5B; 1H: $2.6B vs $20.8B).
- Notes to the unaudited consolidated financial statements are referenced as integral to the statements.

- Key footnotes and clarifications:
  - GSE-related mortgage obligations included within certain categories and their amounts.
  - Physical commodities inventories accounted for at net realizable value, which approximates fair value; effect of fair value hedge accounting on carrying values.

- Unobservable input types highlighted: prices (when no quoted market prices), yields, prepayment speeds, default and loss assumptions, credit spreads and correlations, recovery rates, interest rate and spread volatilities, forward curves/prices (equity, commodities), and cross‑risk‑factor correlations (IR, FX, equity).
- Methodological notes:
  - Categories are aggregated by product type and may differ from balance sheet classification; not all listed inputs apply to every instrument.
  - Composition details:
    - RMBS/loans include U.S. GSE/agency, nonagency, and non‑trading loans.
    - CMBS/loans include nonagency, trading loans, and non‑trading loans.
    - Loans include both trading and non‑trading balances.
  - Structured notes within debt/borrowings/deposits contain embedded derivatives; fair value incorporates derivative features with inputs aligned to derivative receivables.
  - Equity securities without readily available quotes are valued using internal techniques (e.g., EBITDA multiples, comparable analysis); all other Level 3 items are individually and in aggregate insignificant.
  - Price input is shown assuming par value of $100; forward equity price is expressed as a percentage of current price.
  - Averages are weighted averages except derivative‑related inputs, which use arithmetic averages.

- Focus: Disclosure of JPMorgan Chase’s Level 3 fair value measurements (those using significant unobservable inputs), including how changes in unobservable inputs affect fair value and the role of external market factors; references Note 2 of the 2021 Form 10-K for broader methodology and input relationships.

- Scope of rollforward tables: Detailed reconciliations for assets and liabilities classified in Level 3 for:
  - Three months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021
  - Six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021
  These show beginning balances, total realized/unrealized gains/losses, transfers in/out of Level 3, purchases, sales, issuances, settlements, and ending balances, plus unrealized gains/losses on instruments still held.

- Categories covered:
  - Assets: trading assets (debt instruments such as various mortgage-backed securities, U.S. states/municipal obligations, non-U.S. government and corporate debt, loans, asset-backed securities), equity securities, physical commodities, other; net derivative receivables (interest rate, credit, FX, equity, commodity) presented on a net basis; available-for-sale securities; loans; mortgage servicing rights (MSRs); other assets.
  - Liabilities: deposits, short-term borrowings, trading liabilities, accounts payable and other liabilities, long-term debt, and beneficial interests of consolidated VIEs (where applicable).

- Important caveats:
  - Level 3 valuations can include observable components; reported gains/losses include effects from both observable and unobservable inputs.
  - Risk management hedges in Level 1/2 are excluded from the Level 3 tables, so table results do not reflect hedge impacts.

- Reporting locations/footnotes:
  - Most changes run through principal transactions revenue; certain mortgage-related items are in mortgage fees and related income.
  - AFS securities: realized gains/losses in investment securities gains/losses; unrealized in OCI, with amounts disclosed.
  - DVA on fair value option liabilities: realized effects not material; unrealized in OCI, with amounts disclosed.
  - Loan originations included in purchases; settlements include maturities, repayments, modifications, VIE deconsolidations, etc.

- Level 3 analysis and key period highlights:
  - Level 3 assets were $22.3 billion at June 30, 2022, up $329 million from March 31, 2022 and up $4.8 billion from December 31, 2021.
  - Primary six-month drivers to June 30, 2022: approximately $1.6 billion increase in gross derivative receivables (gains and purchases, partly offset by transfers) and a $1.9 billion increase in MSRs.

- Transfers between fair value hierarchy levels:
  - Transfers are driven by changes in input observability and/or significance and are assumed to occur at the start of the quarter.
  - Three months ended June 30, 2022: no significant Level 2 to Level 3 transfers; notable Level 3 to Level 2 transfer of interest rate derivative receivables due to increased observability.
  - Six months ended June 30, 2022: significant transfers into Level 3 included equity securities (driven by reduced market observability, including restricted access) and equity derivative payables; significant transfers out included interest rate derivative receivables and both equity derivative receivables/payables as observability improved.
  - 2021 comparable periods: no significant Level 2 to Level 3 transfers; notable transfers out of Level 3 included equity derivatives and trading loans as observability improved.

- Proportion of Level 3 to total fair value:
  - Level 3 assets were 2% of total firm assets at fair value at both June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021.
  - Level 3 liabilities were 8% and 10% of total firm liabilities at fair value at June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021, respectively.

nodes.title: Additional disclosures about the fair value of financial instruments that are not carried on the Consolidated balance sheets at fair value

Footnote explains fair value is typically derived from discounted cash flow models (considering loan terms, expected lifetime credit losses, interest rates, prepayments, and market spreads) or collateral values; differences from carrying value arise from rates, credit spreads, liquidity premiums, and other market factors. Footnotes note exclusion of the guarantee liability and offsetting asset recognized at inception and inclusion of the wholesale allowance for lending-related commitments.

nodes.title: Fair value option
nodes.heading: Note 3 – Fair value option
nodes.start_phrase: The fair value option provides an option to elect fair value for selected financial assets, fina ncial liabilities, unrecognized firm commitments, and written loan commitments.
nodes.summary:
- Explains the fair value option (FVO), which allows the Firm to elect fair value measurement for certain financial assets and liabilities, unrecognized firm commitments, and written loan commitments.
- States the rationale for electing FVO: to reduce income statement volatility arising from mixed measurement bases versus related risk management instruments measured at fair value, and to align accounting with instruments managed on a fair value basis.
- Lists the instruments for which FVO has been elected:
  - Loans purchased or originated for securitization warehousing, subject to bifurcation accounting, or otherwise managed on a fair value basis (including lending-related commitments).
  - Certain securities financing agreements.
  - Owned beneficial interests in securitized financial assets with embedded credit derivatives (otherwise separable as derivatives).
  - Structured notes and other hybrid instruments with embedded derivatives issued or transacted in client-driven activities.
  - Certain long-term beneficial interests issued by CIB’s consolidated securitization trusts when underlying assets are at fair value.
- Describes presentation of changes in fair value under FVO in the Consolidated statements of income for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021, noting:
  - The table includes only the elected instruments; related risk management instruments (also measured at fair value) are excluded.
  - Amounts are disaggregated between “Principal transactions” and “All other income,” and, for loans, split between instrument-specific credit risk and other changes in fair value.
- Highlights from the three months ended June 30 comparison:
  - Long-term debt showed a significant gain in 2022 (+5,419 million total) versus a loss in 2021 (−2,152 million).
  - Trading assets (debt and equity, excluding loans) declined in 2022 (−1,255 million) versus a gain in 2021 (+443 million).
  - Loans under FVO (non-trading): instrument-specific credit risk was −72 million in 2022 versus +181 million in 2021; other changes were −761 million in 2022 versus +927 million in 2021.
  - Deposits and short-term borrowings recorded gains in 2022 (+382 million and +471 million, respectively) versus losses in 2021 (−258 million and −489 million).
  - Securities financing assets saw losses in 2022 (federal funds sold/resale −145 million; securities borrowed −101 million) compared with smaller losses in 2021.
  - Other line items were comparatively small; beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs showed no change in both periods.

nodes.title: Changes in fair value under the fair value option election

nodes.summary:
- Scope and purpose: Explains the Firm’s use of the fair value option to measure selected financial assets and liabilities, unrecognized firm commitments, and written loan commitments. The primary reasons are to reduce income statement volatility arising from mixed measurement bases and to align accounting with instruments managed on a fair value basis.

- Instruments elected for fair value:
  - Loans tied to securitization warehousing, subject to bifurcation, or otherwise managed on a fair value basis (including lending-related commitments).
  - Certain securities financing agreements.
  - Owned beneficial interests in securitized assets that contain embedded credit derivatives (avoiding separate derivative accounting).
  - Structured notes and other hybrid instruments (primarily with embedded derivatives) issued or transacted in client-driven activities.
  - Certain long-term beneficial interests issued by CIB consolidated securitization trusts where underlying assets are at fair value.

- Results presented: A table of changes in fair value recognized in the Consolidated statements of income for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021, split between principal transactions and all other income, and by instrument category. Related risk management instruments (which are at fair value) are excluded from the table.

- Key performance highlights:
  - 2022 saw sizable gains in long-term debt measured at fair value (predominantly structured notes): approximately $5.4B in Q2 and $9.4B YTD, versus losses in 2021.
  - Trading assets (debt and equity, excluding loans) showed losses in 2022 versus gains in 2021.
  - Loans measured at fair value reflected negative “other changes in fair value” in 2022, while instrument-specific credit risk effects were mixed and smaller.
  - Deposits and short-term borrowings recorded gains in 2022 versus losses in 2021.
  - Federal funds sold/securities purchased under resale and securities borrowed showed losses in 2022.
  - Minimal activity for beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs.

- Presentation and accounting details:

nodes.title: Derivative instruments
nodes.heading: Note 4 – Derivative instruments
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase makes markets in derivatives for clients and also uses derivatives to hedge or manage its own risk exposures.
nodes.summary:
- Overview: JPMorgan Chase uses derivatives both to make markets for clients and to hedge or manage its own risk exposures. Disclosures are organized by accounting treatment and purpose, with a reference to the Firm’s 2021 Form 10-K (Note 5) for detailed policies.
- Hedge accounting vs. non-hedge: A limited number of derivatives are designated in qualifying hedge accounting relationships (fair value, cash flow, or net investment hedges). The remainder are not designated and include specified risk management positions and market-making/other activities.
- Qualifying hedge accounting uses:
  - Interest rate derivatives: hedge fixed-rate assets/liabilities (fair value hedges) and floating-rate assets/liabilities (cash flow hedges) in Corporate.
  - Foreign exchange derivatives: hedge FX-denominated assets/liabilities (fair value hedges), forecasted revenue/expense (cash flow hedges), and investments in non-USD functional currency entities (net investment hedges) in Corporate.
  - Commodity derivatives: hedge commodity inventory (fair value hedges) in CIB and AWM.
- Specified risk management (not designated as hedges):
  - Interest rate: manage risks of mortgage commitments, warehouse loans, and MSRs in CCB.
  - Credit: manage credit risk of wholesale lending exposures in CIB.
  - Interest rate and foreign exchange: manage risks of other specified assets/liabilities in Corporate.
- Market-making and other activities:
  - Various derivatives used for client market-making and related risk management in CIB.
  - Other derivatives used across CIB, AWM, and Corporate.
- Segments referenced: Corporate, CIB (Corporate & Investment Bank), AWM (Asset & Wealth Management), CCB (Consumer & Community Banking).
- Cross-references: The table links each use/designation to affected segments and specific 10-Q page references (primarily pages 119–123).

nodes.title: Impact of derivatives on the Consolidated balance sheets

- Scope and dates: Data as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021, shown by accounting designation (designated as hedges vs. not) and by contract type within trading assets and liabilities (interest rate, credit, foreign exchange, equity, commodity).

  - From 2021 to mid‑2022, gross balances increased notably, especially in foreign exchange and commodities.
- Netting and presentation:

nodes.title: Derivatives netting
nodes.heading: Derivatives netting
nodes.start_phrase: The following tables present, as of J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2, and D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 1, gross and net derivative receivables and payables by contract and settlement type.
nodes.summary:
- Topic: Disclosure of derivatives netting, collateral, and resulting exposures.
- Scope and dates: Presents, in millions, gross and net derivative receivables and payables by contract type and settlement type as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021.
- Netting methodology: Derivative positions and related cash collateral are netted on the Consolidated balance sheets only when governed by a master netting agreement supported by an appropriate legal opinion; otherwise they are shown separately and are not eligible for GAAP netting.
- Collateral treatment:
  - Cash collateral related to OTC and OTC-cleared derivatives is included in amounts netted on the balance sheets.
  - Additional collateral (liquid securities and other cash held at third‑party custodians) mitigates counterparty credit risk but is not eligible for net presentation; it is disclosed as “Collateral not nettable on the Consolidated balance sheets,” limited to the fair value exposure to each counterparty.
  - Excess collateral over exposure and collateral tied to agreements lacking appropriate legal opinions are excluded from the collateral totals shown.
  - “Liquid securities” align with high-quality liquid assets under the LCR rule.
- Product and settlement breakdown: Detailed tables for interest rate, credit, foreign exchange, equity, and commodity contracts, split into OTC, OTC‑cleared, and exchange‑traded categories, showing gross amounts, amounts netted, and resulting net receivables/payables.
- Legal opinion status: Totals distinguish between derivatives with appropriate legal opinions (eligible for GAAP netting) and those without (reported gross and not netted), for both receivables and payables.
- Consolidated totals: Provides total derivative receivables and payables recognized on the balance sheets, followed by “Collateral not nettable” and resulting net amounts after considering such collateral.
- Footnotes/highlights:
  - Exchange‑traded futures are settled daily.
  - Collateral disclosure relates only to OTC and OTC‑cleared derivatives.
  - For some counterparties, reported third‑party collateral is capped at the net derivative balance.
  - Discloses the cash collateral amounts included in netted positions at each date (for both net derivatives receivable and payable).

nodes.title: Liquidity risk and credit-related contingent features
nodes.heading: Liquidity risk and credit-related contingent features
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 5 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for a more detailed discussion of liquidity risk and credit-related contingent features related to the Firm’s derivative contracts.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Liquidity risk and credit-related contingent features associated with JPMorgan Chase’s OTC and OTC-cleared derivatives, including downgrade-triggered collateral and termination provisions; reference to Note 5 of the 2021 Form 10-K for broader context.
- Net derivative payables and collateral (in millions):
  - June 30, 2022: net derivative payables $16,037; collateral posted $14,926.
  - December 31, 2021: net derivative payables $20,114; collateral posted $19,402.
- Ratings downgrade impact on liquidity for JPMorgan Chase & Co. and subsidiaries (predominantly JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.):
  - Additional collateral required (in millions):
    - Single-notch: $273 (6/30/22) vs. $219 (12/31/21)
    - Two-notch: $1,552 (6/30/22) vs. $1,577 (12/31/21)
  - Termination payment amounts (fair values of payables; exclude collateral) (in millions):
    - Single-notch: $85 (6/30/22) vs. $98 (12/31/21)
    - Two-notch: $700 (6/30/22) vs. $787 (12/31/21)
- Mechanics/assumptions:
  - Downgrade triggers require collateral posting or contract termination when predefined rating thresholds are breached.
  - A downgrade by a single agency that does not fall below a corresponding rating from another major agency generally does not trigger additional collateral or termination, except in certain cases where additional initial margin may be required.
  - Liquidity impact is calculated assuming a downgrade below the lowest current rating referenced in each contract.
- Derivatives executed in contemplation of asset sales:
  - The Firm sometimes transfers financial assets while retaining economic exposure via a derivative with the same counterparty.
  - Generally accounted for as collateralized financings (see Note 10); in limited cases, accounted for as a sale plus a derivative under U.S. GAAP.
  - Amounts outstanding under such sales-with-derivative structures were not material at June 30, 2022, and December 31, 2021.

nodes.title: Fair value hedge gains and losses

- Focus: Impact of derivatives on the Consolidated statements of income, specifically fair value hedge accounting.
- Content of tables: Pre-tax gains/losses on derivatives and related hedged items by contract type (interest rate, foreign exchange, commodity) for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021.
- Presentation details:
  - Gains/losses on hedging derivatives are reported in the same income statement line as the hedged items.
  - Income statement impacts shown include: (1) derivative and hedged item effects, (2) the impact of excluded components via amortization and current-period fair value changes, and (3) related OCI impact for excluded components.
- Contract-type specifics:
  - Interest rate hedges: Benchmark rate risk (e.g., LIBOR, SOFR) of fixed-rate long-term debt and AFS securities; impacts recorded in net interest income. From Jan 1, 2022, presentation includes amortization of the inception hedge accounting adjustment; prior periods revised. Interest accruals on swaps and related hedged items are excluded.
  - Foreign exchange hedges: Spot FX risk of long-term debt and AFS securities; impacts recorded primarily in principal transactions revenue and net interest income.
  - Commodity hedges: Overall fair value hedges of physical commodities inventories; impacts recorded in principal transactions revenue.
- Excluded components policy: Certain elements (e.g., forward points, time value, cross-currency basis spreads) are excluded from effectiveness assessment and affect earnings either through amortization over the derivative’s life or through current-period fair value changes; changes in excluded amounts under the amortization approach are recorded in OCI and amortized to earnings.
- Prior-period revisions: Select 2021 amounts revised to conform to the current presentation.
- Balance sheet disclosures (June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021):
  - Carrying amounts of hedged AFS securities, long-term debt, and beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs, and the cumulative fair value hedge basis adjustments embedded in those carrying amounts, shown separately for active and discontinued hedging relationships.

  - Exclusions: Physical commodities inventories measured at fair value under hedge accounting (no incremental future net income impact), and items hedged solely for FX risk (basis adjustments do not reverse through earnings). Carrying amount for AFS is at amortized cost, net of allowance.

nodes.title: Gains and losses on derivatives used for specified risk management purposes

Gains and losses on derivatives used for specified risk 
management purposes

nodes.title: Credit derivatives
nodes.heading: Credit derivatives
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 5 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for a more detailed discussion of credit derivatives.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Extract from JPMorgan Chase’s financial notes covering credit derivatives exposure/details and components of noninterest revenue for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 (with prior-year comparisons) and positions as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021.
- Credit derivatives overview:
  - Notional amounts are not the Firm’s primary risk metric because they ignore credit event probability, recoveries, and hedges.
  - Summary of gross protection sold and purchased by product:
    - Credit default swaps and other credit derivatives (e.g., credit swap options, total return swaps), plus credit-related notes.
    - As of June 30, 2022: $526.1B protection sold; $551.6B protection purchased with identical underlyings; net protection purchased of $25.5B; $28.4B of other protection purchased (incl. $9.0B credit-related notes).
    - As of December 31, 2021: $499.6B protection sold; $537.8B purchased with identical underlyings; net protection purchased of $38.2B; $25.1B other protection purchased (incl. $9.4B credit-related notes).
  - Protection sold ratings/maturity profile (seller of protection only):
    - Breakout by investment-grade vs noninvestment-grade and by remaining maturity buckets (<1 year, 1–5 years, >5 years).
    - Fair value shown gross (pre-netting/collateral): June 30, 2022 net fair value liability of $5.1B vs net asset of $3.6B at December 31, 2021.
    - Ratings based on S&P/Moody’s; maturity based on contractual remaining term.
  - Clarifying footnotes: definition of “identical underlyings,” settlement values exclude reference obligation fair value at settlement, and “other protection purchased” represents positions without an offsetting identical sold position.
- Noninterest revenue (Note 5) components and trends:
  - Investment banking fees:
    - Breakdowns for underwriting (equity, debt) and advisory.
    - Notable year-over-year declines in underwriting in 2Q22 and 1H22; total IB fees fell to $1.59B in 2Q22 from $3.47B; to $3.59B in 1H22 from $6.44B.
  - Principal transactions:
    - Trading revenue by instrument type: interest rate, credit, foreign exchange, equity, commodity.
    - Stronger FX and equity trading in 2Q22; total principal transactions up to $4.99B in 2Q22 (from $4.08B); $10.10B in 1H22 (vs $10.58B).
    - Includes impacts of funding valuation adjustments (FVA), credit valuation adjustments (CVA), and markdowns on held‑for‑sale bridge financing exposures.
    - Note that trading revenue by instrument type is not indicative of any single line-of-business performance.
  - Lending- and deposit-related fees:

nodes.title: Contractual maturities and yields
