nodes.title: Securities financing activities
nodes.heading: Note 10 – Securities financing activities
nodes.start_phrase:
Refer to Note 11 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for 
a discussion of accounting policies relating to securities 
financing activities.
nodes.summary:
- Focus of the note: Securities financing activities, with cross-references to (i) 2021 Form 10-K Note 11 for accounting policies, (ii) Note 3 for fair value option elections on certain securities borrowing/lending, and (iii) Note 23 for assets pledged and collateral received.
- Netting and presentation under U.S. GAAP: Explains use of master netting agreements and when balances under securities financing agreements (repos/reverse repos, securities borrowed/loaned) are netted on the Consolidated balance sheets. Clarifies that exchanged securities/cash collateral reduce economic exposure but generally are not eligible for balance sheet netting; such amounts are shown as “Amounts not nettable on the Consolidated balance sheets” and reduce the “Net amounts” in the disclosure.
- Legal opinions and gross presentation: Where a legal opinion supporting the master netting agreement exists but other netting criteria are not met, related balances and collateral are shown as “Amounts not nettable.” Where a legal opinion has not been sought or obtained, related balances are presented gross within the “Net amounts” line of the table.
- Accounting for securities-for-securities lending when JPMorgan Chase is the lender: Securities received that can be pledged or sold are recognized at fair value in other assets, with a corresponding obligation to return them recorded in accounts payable and other liabilities.
- Quantitative disclosures (June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021): Tables summarize, by asset and liability category, gross amounts, amounts netted on the balance sheet, amounts presented on the balance sheet, amounts not nettable, and resulting net amounts for (i) securities purchased under resale agreements, (ii) securities borrowed, (iii) securities sold under repurchase agreements, and (iv) securities loaned and other. Footnotes identify: (a) fair value–accounted securities-for-securities lending balances; (b) constraints where collateral exchanged exceeds the related net asset/liability; and (c) the portion of positions lacking legal opinions on master netting agreements included in the “Net amounts.”
- Collateral composition: Breakout of the types of financial assets pledged in securities financing agreements by class (U.S. agency/GSE MBS, nonagency RMBS and CMBS, U.S. Treasury/agency/GSE, U.S. municipals, non-U.S. sovereigns, corporate debt, ABS, and equities), shown separately for repos and securities loaned at both dates.
- Maturity profile: Remaining contractual maturities for repos and securities loaned presented across overnight/continuous, up to 30 days, 30–90 days, and greater than 90 days as of both reporting dates.
- Transfers not qualifying for sale accounting: Discloses small amounts of financial assets transferred to third parties that failed sale accounting ($342 million at June 30, 2022; $440 million at December 31, 2021), recognized as collateralized financings, with the assets in trading assets and loans and the corresponding liabilities predominantly in short-term borrowings.

nodes.title: Transfers not qualifying for sale accounting
nodes.heading: Transfers not qualifying for sale accounting
nodes.start_phrase:
At J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2, and D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 1, the Firm held $342 million and $440 million , respectively, of financial assets for 
which the rights have been transferred to third parties; however, the transfers did not qualify as a sale in accordance with U.S. 
GAAP.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Excerpt details securities financing agreements (repos and securities lending), related collateral types and maturities, transfers that failed sale accounting, and loan accounting/portfolio composition with balances as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021.

- Securities financing agreements – collateral types and balances:
  - Presents gross liability balances by collateral type for:
    - Securities sold under repurchase agreements and securities loaned/other.
  - Key collateral categories: mortgage‑backed securities (U.S. GSEs/government agencies; residential and commercial nonagency), U.S. Treasury/GSEs/government agencies, obligations of U.S. states and municipalities, non‑U.S. government debt, corporate debt, asset‑backed securities, and equity securities.
  - Totals:
    - June 30, 2022: repos $511.7B; securities loaned/other $54.1B.
    - December 31, 2021: repos $532.9B; securities loaned/other $52.6B.
  - Mix highlights: repos predominantly backed by U.S. Treasury/GSE/government and non‑U.S. government debt; securities lending largely against equities.

- Contractual maturity profile:
  - Breaks down agreements into overnight/continuous, up to 30 days, 30–90 days, and greater than 90 days.
  - June 30, 2022:
    - Repos: $202.8B overnight/continuous; $183.9B up to 30 days; $40.6B 30–90 days; $84.4B >90 days (total $511.7B).
    - Securities loaned/other: $52.9B overnight/continuous; minimal term balances (total $54.1B).
  - December 31, 2021:
    - Repos: $195.0B overnight/continuous; $231.2B up to 30 days; $47.2B 30–90 days; $59.5B >90 days (total $532.9B).
    - Securities loaned/other: $50.0B overnight/continuous; small term components (total $52.6B).
  - Overall, activity is concentrated in overnight and short‑term tenors, with a higher >90‑day share in mid‑2022 versus year‑end 2021.

- Transfers not qualifying for sale accounting:
  - Assets with transferred rights that failed sale accounting under U.S. GAAP recognized as collateralized financings.
  - Balances held: $342M at June 30, 2022; $440M at December 31, 2021.
  - Recorded as trading assets and loans; related liabilities chiefly in short‑term borrowings.

- Loan accounting framework:
  - Categories: originated/purchased loans held‑for‑investment (retained), loans held‑for‑sale, and loans at fair value.
  - Cross‑references to other notes for policies and fair value elections.

- Loan portfolio segmentation and classes:
  - Segments: Consumer (excluding credit card), Credit card, and Wholesale.
  - Classes monitored:
    - Consumer ex‑credit card: residential real estate; auto and other.
    - Credit card: credit card loans.
    - Wholesale: secured by real estate; commercial and industrial; other (including financial institutions, municipalities, SPEs, nonprofits, personal investment/trust entities, and private banking clients).
  - Footnotes clarify scored loans across lines of business and wholesale methodology application.

- Loan balances by segment and measurement category:
  - June 30, 2022 (total $1,104.2B): Consumer ex‑credit card $317.2B; Credit card $165.5B; Wholesale $621.4B.
    - Retained: $1,052.4B; Held‑for‑sale: $4.7B; At fair value: $47.1B.
  - December 31, 2021 (total $1,077.7B): Consumer ex‑credit card $323.3B; Credit card $154.3B; Wholesale $600.1B.
    - Retained: $1,010.2B; Held‑for‑sale: $8.7B; At fair value: $58.8B.
  - Trends: total loans increased; Wholesale and Credit card grew; Consumer ex‑credit card declined modestly; held‑for‑sale decreased; loans at fair value declined overall.

- Presentation notes:
  - Accrued interest receivables excluded from loan totals: $3.2B (June 30, 2022) and $2.7B (December 31, 2021).
  - Accrued interest write‑offs: $8M for Q2 2022 and Q2 2021; $20M and $21M for the six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021.
  - Non‑fair‑value loans presented net of unamortized discounts/premiums and net deferred fees/costs; amounts not material at both dates.

nodes.title: Loans
nodes.heading: Note 11 – Loans
nodes.start_phrase: The accounting for a loan depends on management’s strategy for the loan.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 11 – Loans outlines JPMorgan Chase’s loan accounting framework, portfolio structure, and summarized period-end loan balances.
- Accounting framework: Loans are categorized as (1) originated or purchased and held-for-investment (“retained”), (2) held-for-sale, or (3) at fair value. Cross-references direct readers to detailed accounting policies (2021 Form 10-K Note 12), fair value option elections (this 10-Q Note 3), and loans at fair value classified as trading assets (this 10-Q Note 2).
- Portfolio segmentation: The loan portfolio is grouped into three segments used for the allowance for loan losses—Consumer (excluding credit card), Credit card, and Wholesale.
- Loan classes within segments:
  - Consumer, excluding credit card: Residential real estate; Auto and other (includes scored auto and business banking loans and overdrafts).
  - Credit card: Credit card loans.
  - Wholesale: Secured by real estate; Commercial and industrial; Other (includes loans to financial institutions, states/political subdivisions, SPEs, nonprofits, personal investment companies/trusts, and individuals, notably Global Private Bank clients). Wholesale classes align with bank regulatory agency classifications by collateral, purpose, and borrower; includes loans across CIB, CB, AWM, Corporate, and certain risk-rated CCB loans.
- Segment/class notes: Residential real estate includes scored mortgage and home equity loans in CCB and AWM, and scored mortgages in CIB and Corporate. Additional detail on SPEs is in 2021 Form 10-K Note 14.
- Loan balances by segment and accounting category:
  - June 30, 2022 (in millions): Consumer excl. credit card $317,212; Credit card $165,494; Wholesale $621,449; Total $1,104,155. Of this total: Retained $1,052,390; Held-for-sale $4,709; At fair value $47,056.
  - December 31, 2021 (in millions): Consumer excl. credit card $323,306; Credit card $154,296; Wholesale $600,112; Total $1,077,714. Of this total: Retained $1,010,206; Held-for-sale $8,688; At fair value $58,820.
  - Notable shifts: Total loans increased to $1.104T from $1.078T, driven by higher retained loans and wholesale/credit card growth; held-for-sale and fair value categories declined period-over-period.
- Presentation and accruals:
  - Accrued interest receivables excluded from loan totals: $3.2B at June 30, 2022 and $2.7B at December 31, 2021.
  - Accrued interest receivable write-offs: $8M in each of the three-month periods ended June 30, 2022 and 2021; $20M and $21M for the six-month periods ended June 30, 2022 and 2021, respectively.
  - Loans not at fair value are presented net of unamortized discounts/premiums and net deferred fees/costs (amounts not material).

nodes.title: Loan accounting framework
nodes.heading: Loan accounting framework
nodes.start_phrase: The accounting for a loan depends on management’s strategy for the loan.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines the loan accounting framework, which depends on management’s strategy, with three categories: originated or purchased loans held-for-investment (retained), loans held-for-sale, and loans at fair value.

Notes that wholesale classifications align with bank regulatory agencies and include certain risk-rated loans in CCB; references Note 14 of the 2021 Form 10-K for SPEs.

nodes.title: Loan portfolio
nodes.heading: Loan portfolio
nodes.start_phrase:
The Firm’s loan portfolio is divided in to three portfolio segments, which are the same segments used by the Firm to determine 
the allowance for loan losses: Consumer, excluding credit card; Credit card; and Wholesale.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 11 – Loans outlines JPMorgan Chase’s loan accounting framework, portfolio segmentation and classes, period-end loan balances by segment and measurement category, loan activity (purchases, sales, reclassifications), and gains/losses on loan sales and lending-related commitments. It references related accounting policy notes in the 2021 Form 10-K and current Form 10-Q.

- Accounting framework:
  - Loans are accounted for as (i) originated or purchased loans held-for-investment (retained), (ii) loans held-for-sale (HFS), or (iii) loans at fair value.
  - Cross-references: Note 12 (2021 Form 10-K) for detailed loan accounting policies; Note 3 (current 10-Q) for fair value option elections; Note 2 (current 10-Q) for loans at fair value classified as trading assets.

- Portfolio segmentation and classes used for allowance determination:
  - Segments: Consumer (excluding credit card), Credit card, and Wholesale.
  - Classes:
    - Consumer, excluding credit card: Residential real estate; Auto and other (includes scored auto, business banking loans, and overdrafts).
    - Credit card: Credit card loans.
    - Wholesale: Secured by real estate; Commercial and industrial; Other.
  - Clarifications:
    - Residential real estate includes scored mortgage and home equity loans in CCB and AWM, and scored mortgage loans in CIB and Corporate.
    - Wholesale segment includes loans across CIB, CB, AWM, Corporate, and certain risk-rated CCB loans; classes align with bank regulatory classifications.
    - “Other” includes loans to financial institutions, states/political subdivisions, SPEs, nonprofits, personal investment companies/trusts, and individuals (predominantly AWM Global Private Bank clients). Reference to Note 14 (2021 Form 10-K) for SPEs.

- Loan balances by segment and measurement:
  - June 30, 2022 total loans: $1,104.2 billion (Retained $1,052.4b; HFS $4.7b; At fair value $47.1b).
    - Consumer ex-CC: $317.2b; Credit card: $165.5b; Wholesale: $621.4b.
  - December 31, 2021 total loans: $1,077.7 billion (Retained $1,010.2b; HFS $8.7b; At fair value $58.8b).
    - Consumer ex-CC: $323.3b; Credit card: $154.3b; Wholesale: $600.1b.
  - Notes:
    - Accrued interest receivables excluded: $3.2b (6/30/22) and $2.7b (12/31/21); related write-offs were $8m for both Q2’22 and Q2’21, and $20m and $21m for 1H’22 and 1H’21.
    - Unamortized discounts/premiums and net deferred fees/costs were not material for non-FV loans.
    - Prior-period amounts revised to conform with current presentation.

- Loan activity (retained loans purchased, sold, and reclassified to HFS):
  - Q2 2022: Purchases $1.2b (Consumer ex-CC $0.97b; Wholesale $0.23b); Sales $12.1b (predominantly Wholesale); Reclassified to HFS $0.48b.
  - Q2 2021: Purchases $0.41b; Sales $8.75b; Reclassified to HFS $0.98b.
  - 1H 2022: Purchases $1.49b; Sales $21.84b; Reclassified to HFS $0.83b.
  - 1H 2021: Purchases $0.83b; Sales $14.66b; Reclassified to HFS $1.91b.
  - Footnotes:
    - Reclassifications to HFS are non-cash.
    - Purchases predominantly include voluntary repurchases of certain delinquent Ginnie Mae loans the Firm services.
    - Excludes correspondent channel purchases of retained loans: $6.0b (Q2’22) vs $5.0b (Q2’21); $9.2b (1H’22) vs $12.0b (1H’21).

- Gains and losses on sales:
  - Noninterest revenue impact from net gains/(losses) on sales of loans and lending-related commitments:
    - Q2 2022: $(352)m total, of which $(67)m related to loans.
    - 1H 2022: $(314)m total, of which $(32)m related to loans.
    - Q2 2021: $62m total, of which $47m related to loans.
    - 1H 2021: $194m total, of which $182m related to loans.
  - Note that loan sales may also drive write-downs, recoveries, or changes in the allowance recognized in the provision for credit losses.

nodes.title: Loan modifications

- Explains nature of concessions under the Firm’s and government (including U.S. GSE) programs: interest rate reductions; term or payment extensions; delays/deferrals of principal and/or interest; principal forgiveness; and “other” items such as converting variable to fixed rates and payment delays that meet the TDR definition.
- Activity metrics:
  - Trial modifications approved: 1,165 (Q2 2022) vs 1,165 (Q2 2021); 2,691 (H1 2022) vs 2,566 (H1 2021).
  - Permanent modifications: 1,289 (Q2 2022) vs 1,186 (Q2 2021); 2,831 (H1 2022) vs 2,900 (H1 2021).
- Mix of concessions among permanent modifications (percent of loans; totals exceed 100% as most loans receive multiple concessions; trial mod concessions generally align with permanent):
  - Q2 2022 vs Q2 2021: interest rate reduction 45% vs 78%; term/payment extension 54% vs 51%; principal/interest deferred 10% vs 18%; principal forgiveness 1% vs 0%; other 46% vs 34%.
  - H1 2022 vs H1 2021: interest rate reduction 56% vs 74%; term/payment extension 67% vs 45%; principal/interest deferred 12% vs 26%; principal forgiveness 1% vs 2%; other 36% vs 44%.
- Notes exclusions: Chapter 7 loans where the only concession is debt discharge and loans with short-term or otherwise insignificant non-concession modifications.

nodes.title: Financial effects of modifications and redefaults
nodes.heading: Financial effects of modifica tions and redefaults
nodes.start_phrase:
The following table provides information about the financial effects of the various concessions granted in modifications of 
residential real estate loans under the loss mitigation programs described above and about redefaults of certain loans 
modified in TDRs for the periods presented.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Financial effects of permanent loan modifications (TDRs) and subsequent redefaults for residential real estate loans under loss mitigation programs.
- Scope and exclusions: Presents only permanent modifications; excludes trial/temporary concessions, Chapter 7 cases with only debt discharge, and short-term or insignificant changes not deemed concessions.
- Periods covered: Three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021; amounts in millions and certain weighted-average metrics.
- Interest rate effects: Weighted-average rates on loans with interest rate reductions declined post-TDR (e.g., 2022 three-month period from 4.76% to 3.36; 2021 three-month from 4.39% to 2.85; similar declines for six-month periods).
- Term extensions: Weighted-average remaining contractual terms increased significantly post-TDR (e.g., 22 to 38 years for Q2 2022; comparable increases in other periods).
- Loss recognition and concessions:
  - Charge-offs on permanent modifications: $1 million in 2022 periods; none in 2021.
  - Principal deferred: $4 million (Q2 2022) vs $6 million (Q2 2021); $11 million (H1 2022) vs $18 million (H1 2021).
  - Principal forgiven: $0 in Q2; $1 million in H1 for both 2022 and 2021.
- Redefaults: Balances of loans redefaulting within one year of permanent modification increased (e.g., $27 million in Q2 2022 vs $21 million in Q2 2021; $70 million in H1 2022 vs $45 million in H1 2021).
- Redefault definition/notes: Payment default occurs when two contractual payments past due; balances reflect amounts at period-end when default occurred; redefaults often lead to foreclosure or similar liquidation; recent redefault experience may not indicate ultimate levels.
- Loan life: As of June 30, 2022, weighted-average estimated remaining life of TDR-modified residential real estate loans was six years, incorporating voluntary and involuntary prepayments.
- Foreclosure status: As of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021, $696 million and $619 million, respectively, of residential real estate loans (excluding U.S. government–insured) were in active or suspended foreclosure but not in REO.

nodes.title: Credit card loan portfolio

nodes.title: Loan modifications
nodes.heading: Loan modifications
nodes.start_phrase:
The Firm may offer loan modification programs granting 
concessions to credit card borrowers who are experiencing 
financial difficulty.
nodes.summary:

- If borrowers fail to comply with modified terms, loans continue to age and are ultimately charged off under the firm’s standard charge-off policy; in most cases, the borrower’s credit line is not reinstated.
- Financial effects and activity levels: new TDR enrollments were less than 1% of total retained credit card loans for all periods presented.
- Balances of new TDRs: $81 million (Q2 2022) vs $90 million (Q2 2021); $163 million (H1 2022) vs $233 million (H1 2021).

- Redeaults within one year of modification: $8 million (Q2 2022) vs $13 million (Q2 2021); $17 million (H1 2022) vs $32 million (H1 2021).
- Payment default for modified credit card loans is defined as missing two consecutive contractual payments; defaulted modified loans remain in the program and are charged off per standard policy.
- Footnotes clarify that new TDR balances represent outstanding balances prior to modification and that redefault amounts reflect balances at quarter-end of the default.

nodes.title: Wholesale loan portfolio

nodes.start_phrase: The following table provides information on the geographic distribution and delinquency for retained wholesale loans.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Additional disclosures on retained wholesale loans, especially those secured by real estate (multifamily and other commercial), including credit quality, geography, delinquency, nonaccrual details, and loan modifications/TDRs.
- Real estate–secured portfolio size: Total $123.4B at Jun 30, 2022 vs $118.8B at Dec 31, 2021 (multifamily $77.4B vs $73.8B; other commercial $46.1B vs $45.0B).
- Credit quality (real estate–secured):
  - Criticized loans: $3.87B vs $3.97B; 3.14% vs 3.34% of the portfolio.
  - By class: Multifamily criticized 2.22% vs 2.26%; Other commercial criticized 4.69% vs 5.11%.
  - Criticized nonaccrual: $328M vs $326M; 0.27% both periods (multifamily $75M vs $91M; other commercial $253M vs $235M).
- Geographic distribution (retained wholesale loans):
  - Total loans: $584.3B vs $560.4B; U.S. $458.0B vs $437.9B; non-U.S. $126.3B vs $122.4B.
  - Secured by real estate: U.S. $120.3B vs $115.7B; non-U.S. $3.1B vs $3.1B (total $123.4B vs $118.8B).
  - Commercial & industrial (C&I): U.S. $119.3B vs $106.4B; non-U.S. $40.1B vs $39.2B (total $159.5B vs $145.7B).
  - Other: U.S. $218.3B vs $215.8B; non-U.S. $83.0B vs $80.1B (total $301.3B vs $295.8B).
- Delinquency (retained wholesale loans):
  - Current/<30 days: $578.4B vs $555.0B.
  - 30–89 days: $3.30B vs $3.11B.
  - 90+ days and still accruing (well-collateralized): $480M vs $206M.
  - Criticized nonaccrual: $2.083B vs $2.054B (real estate $328M/$326M; C&I $986M/$969M; other $769M/$759M).
  - Note: Nonaccrual totals exclude PPP loans 90+ days past due guaranteed by SBA ($33M at Jun 30, 2022; $127M at Dec 31, 2021), predominantly in C&I.
- Nonaccrual loans detail (retained wholesale):
  - Total: $2.083B vs $2.054B.
  - With allowance: $1.425B vs $1.144B; Without allowance: $658M vs $910M.
  - By category (with/without allowance):
    - Real estate: $247M/$81M vs $254M/$72M.
    - C&I: $656M/$330M vs $604M/$365M.
    - Other: $522M/$247M vs $286M/$473M.
  - Rationale for no allowance: discounted cash flows or collateral value ≥ amortized cost (often after partial charge-offs or interest receipts).
  - Cash-basis interest income on nonaccrual loans was immaterial for the three and six months ended Jun 30, 2022 and 2021.
- Loan modifications/TDRs:
  - New TDRs: $60M (Q2 2022) vs $224M (Q2 2021); $479M (6M 2022) vs $652M (6M 2021).
  - Common concessions: maturity extensions and covenant waivers (primarily C&I); 2021 also included receipt of assets in partial satisfaction (C&I).
  - Impact of new TDRs was not material for the firm for the three and six months ended Jun 30, 2022 and 2021.
  - Carrying value of TDRs: $852M at Jun 30, 2022 vs $607M at Dec 31, 2021.

nodes.title: Nonaccrual loans
nodes.heading: Nonaccrual loans
nodes.start_phrase: The following table provides information on retained wholesale nonaccrual loans.
nodes.summary:
- Retained loans secured by real estate: Balances increased to $123.4 billion at June 30, 2022 (from $118.8 billion at December 31, 2021), split between Multifamily and Other Commercial. Criticized balances were $3.9 billion with a total criticized rate of 3.14% (down from 3.34%). Criticized nonaccruals were $328 million, steady at 0.27% of total real estate–secured loans. Multifamily criticized rate was 2.22% (vs. 2.26%); Other Commercial was 4.69% (vs. 5.11%).

- Geographic distribution of retained wholesale loans: Provides U.S. vs. non-U.S. breakout across loan types (Secured by Real Estate, Commercial & Industrial, Other). Total retained loans rose to $584.3 billion (from $560.4 billion), with $458.0 billion U.S.-domiciled and $126.3 billion non-U.S.

- Delinquency profile: Majority of loans are current. As of June 30, 2022, 30–89 days past due totaled $3.3 billion; 90+ days past due and still accruing (well-collateralized) were $480 million. Criticized nonaccrual loans were $2.083 billion. Footnote notes exclusion of certain PPP loans 90+ days past due that are SBA-guaranteed ($33 million at June 30, 2022; $127 million at December 31, 2021), predominantly in C&I.

- Nonaccrual loans detail: Breaks out nonaccruals with and without allowance by loan category. Totals at June 30, 2022: $1.425 billion with allowance and $658 million without, for $2.083 billion overall (vs. $2.054 billion at year-end 2021). Explains that no allowance is required when discounted cash flows or collateral meet/exceed amortized cost, often after partial charge-offs or interest payments. Notes cash-basis interest income on nonaccruals was not material.

- Loan modifications and TDRs: Defines TDRs and notes typical concessions (maturity extensions, covenant waivers; 2021 also included receipt of assets in partial satisfaction). New TDRs were $60 million for Q2 2022 (vs. $224 million in Q2 2021) and $479 million for the first half of 2022 (vs. $652 million in the first half of 2021). The impact was not material. Carrying value of TDRs increased to $852 million at June 30, 2022 (from $607 million at December 31, 2021).

nodes.title: Loan modifications
nodes.heading: Loan modifications
nodes.start_phrase: Certain loan modifications are considered to be TDRs as they provide various concessions to borrowers who are experiencing financial difficulty.
nodes.summary:
- Presents detailed data on retained loans secured by real estate (split between multifamily and other commercial) as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021, showing portfolio growth and a slight decline in criticized loan percentages.
- Reports criticized and criticized nonaccrual balances and their ratios to total real estate–secured loans; criticized levels are modest and relatively stable period over period.
- Provides a U.S. versus non-U.S. geographic distribution for retained wholesale loans across three categories (secured by real estate, commercial and industrial, and other), noting that most exposure is U.S.-based and that total retained loans increased year over year.
- Breaks down loan delinquency status (current/<30 days, 30–89 days, 90+ days past due but still accruing, and criticized nonaccrual) across the same categories, with an increase in 90+ days past due but still accruing balances, attributed to well-collateralized positions.
- Notes that nonaccrual loan totals are relatively stable across periods, with detail on amounts with and without allowances; explains that no allowance is required when discounted cash flows or collateral value meet or exceed amortized cost.
- States that interest income recognized on a cash basis for nonaccrual loans was not material for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021.
- Discloses that PPP loans 90+ days past due and guaranteed by the SBA are excluded from nonaccrual totals ($33 million at June 30, 2022 versus $127 million at December 31, 2021), predominantly in commercial and industrial.
- Defines troubled debt restructurings (TDRs) and clarifies that short-term or insignificant modifications are not TDRs.
- Quantifies new TDRs: $60 million (Q2 2022) vs. $224 million (Q2 2021) and $479 million (H1 2022) vs. $652 million (H1 2021), primarily driven by maturity extensions and covenant waivers in commercial and industrial; 2021 also included receipt of assets in partial satisfaction.
- Indicates the impact of new TDRs was not material and reports the carrying value of TDRs increased to $852 million at June 30, 2022 from $607 million at December 31, 2021.

nodes.title: Allowance for credit losses
nodes.heading: Note 12 – Allowance for credit losses
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm's allowance for credit losses represents management's estimate of expected credit losses over the remaining expected life of the Firm's financial assets measured at amortized cost and certain off-balance sheet lending-related commitments.
nodes.summary:
- Defines the allowance for credit losses as management’s estimate of expected credit losses over the remaining life of financial assets measured at amortized cost and certain off‑balance sheet lending-related commitments.
- Directs readers to Note 13 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10‑K for detailed methodology and related accounting policies.

nodes.title: Allowance for credit losses and related information
nodes.heading: Allowance for credit losses and related information
nodes.start_phrase: The table below summarizes information about the allowances for credit losses and includes a breakdown of loans and lending-related commitments by impairment methodology.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and structure: Summary of JPMorgan Chase’s allowance for credit losses for the six months ended June 30, 2022 vs. 2021, broken out by portfolio segment (consumer excluding credit card, credit card, wholesale) and by impairment methodology (asset-specific vs. portfolio-based). Includes loan loss allowances, lending-related commitments, and investment securities allowances, plus collateral-dependent loan data and footnotes.

- Allowance for loan losses (rollforward):
  - Ending balance: $17.75B in 2022 vs. $19.50B in 2021.
  - Net charge-offs/(recoveries): $1.239B in 2022 vs. $1.791B in 2021.
  - Provision for loan losses: $2.598B build in 2022 vs. $(7.038)B release in 2021.
  - Segment notes: Credit card allowance declined ($10.4B vs. $12.5B); wholesale increased ($5.421B vs. $5.102B); consumer ex-CC slightly higher ($1.929B vs. $1.898B).

- Allowance for lending-related commitments (rollforward):
  - Ending balance: $2.222B in 2022 vs. $2.998B in 2021.
  - Provision: $(39)M in 2022 vs. $588M in 2021.

- Total allowance for credit losses (loans + lending commitments + securities):
  - $20.019B in 2022 vs. $22.585B in 2021.
  - Investment securities allowance: $47M in 2022 vs. $87M in 2021.

- Impairment methodology detail:
  - Allowance for loan losses:
    - Asset-specific: $(117)M total in 2022 vs. $374M in 2021 (segment mix shows negative in consumer ex-CC, positive in credit card and wholesale).
    - Portfolio-based: $17.867B in 2022 vs. $19.126B in 2021.
  - Loans by methodology:
    - Total retained loans: $1.052T in 2022 vs. $0.964T in 2021; predominantly portfolio-based ($1.036T in 2022).
  - Lending-related commitments allowance:
    - Asset-specific: $78M in 2022 vs. $150M in 2021.
    - Portfolio-based: $2.144B in 2022 vs. $2.848B in 2021.
  - Lending-related commitments outstanding:
    - Total: $475.568B in 2022 vs. $496.021B in 2021; largely portfolio-based.

- Collateral-dependent loans:
  - Net charge-offs: $(7)M in 2022 vs. $29M in 2021 (total).
  - Measured at fair value of collateral less cost to sell: $4.542B in 2022 vs. $5.030B in 2021.

- Key footnotes and definitions:
  - Asset-specific includes collateral-dependent loans, TDRs (or expected TDRs), modified PCD loans, and certain nonaccrual wholesale loans; credit card asset-specific TDR allowance uses original contractual rates.
  - Allowance for lending-related commitments recorded in accounts payable and other liabilities.
  - Significant portions of lending-related commitments are excluded from the allowance calculation: at June 30, 2022, excluded $13.7B (consumer ex-CC), $774.0B (credit card), and $38.7B (wholesale); at June 30, 2021, excluded $20.8B, $682.5B, and $42.7B, respectively.

- Overall themes:
  - Year-over-year decline in total allowance for credit losses driven by lower credit card and commitment allowances.
  - 2022 shows a reserve build versus large reserve releases in 2021.
  - Portfolio-based methodology remains the dominant driver of allowances and balances.

nodes.title: Discussion of changes in the allowance
nodes.heading: Discussion of changes in the allowance
nodes.start_phrase: The allowance for credit losses as of J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2 was $20.0 billion , an increas e of $ 1 . 3 b i l l i o n from D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 1, consisting of: $1.0 billion in wholesale and $311 million in consumer.
nodes.summary:
- Allowance for credit losses (ACL) was $20.0B at June 30, 2022, up $1.3B from December 31, 2021, driven by a $1.0B increase in wholesale and $311M in consumer.
- Key drivers of the increase: higher weighting of adverse scenarios tied to inflation, monetary policy changes, and geopolitical risks (including the war in Ukraine); modest deterioration in the firm’s macroeconomic outlook; loan growth in Card and Commercial Banking in 2Q22; and client-specific Russia/Russia-associated downgrades in CIB and AWM in 1Q22.
- ACL is estimated using a weighted average of five internally developed macroeconomic scenarios; adverse scenarios assume more punitive conditions than the central case, resulting in weighted-average U.S. unemployment above 4% through 4Q23 and a U.S. real GDP level 1.1% lower by 4Q23.
- Central case assumptions (as of June 30, 2022): U.S. unemployment 3.6% (4Q22), 3.6% (2Q23), 3.7% (4Q23); YoY U.S. real GDP growth 1.3%, 1.7%, 1.2%. Prior assumptions (as of December 31, 2021): unemployment 4.2% (2Q22), 4.0% (4Q22), 3.9% (2Q23); YoY GDP growth 3.1%, 2.8%, 2.1%.
- Future changes to forecasts will be reflected in the provision for credit losses.
- References provided to Notes and sections for detailed policies, portfolio information, and critical accounting estimates.

nodes.title: Variable interest entities
nodes.heading: Note 13 – Variable interest entities
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 1 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for a further description of JPMorgan Chase’s accounting policies regarding consolidation of VIEs.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of Note 13 on Variable Interest Entities (VIEs), with references to JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for consolidation and securitization accounting policies (Notes 1 and 14).
- Definition of “Firm-sponsored” VIEs, including entities where JPMorgan Chase is the primary beneficiary, uses the VIE to securitize Firm assets, the VIE issues JPMorgan-branded instruments, or is a JPMorgan-administered asset-backed commercial paper conduit.
- Summary of major Firm-sponsored VIE types by business segment:
  - CCB: Credit card securitization trusts (securitization of originated credit card receivables); Mortgage securitization trusts (servicing and securitization of originated and purchased residential mortgages).
  - CIB: Mortgage and other securitization trusts (securitization of originated and purchased residential and commercial mortgages and other consumer loans); Multi-seller conduits (client access to markets and tailored transactions); Municipal bond vehicles (financing municipal bond investments). Page references 152–154.
- Note that JPMorgan Chase also invests in, finances, and provides services to third-party sponsored VIEs; see pages 155–157 for consolidated VIE assets/liabilities and third-party VIE details.
- Significant Firm-sponsored VIEs:
  - Credit card securitizations: JPMorgan Chase is the primary beneficiary of the Chase Issuance Trust due to its continuing involvement.
  - Mortgage and other securitization trusts: The Firm securitizes originated and purchased residential and commercial mortgages and other consumer loans, primarily in CCB and CIB, and may act as servicer and/or retain beneficial interests depending on the transaction.

nodes.title: Credit card securitizations
nodes.heading: Credit card securitizations
nodes.start_phrase: As a result of the Firm’s continuing involvement, the Firm is considered to be the primary beneficiary of its Firm- sponsored credit card securitization trust, the Chase Issuance Trust.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of JPMorgan Chase’s variable interest entities (VIEs), with references to the Firm’s broader consolidation and securitization accounting policies in the 2021 Form 10-K (Notes 1 and 14).
- Definition of “Firm-sponsored” VIEs, including entities where JPMorgan Chase is the primary beneficiary, securitizes Firm assets, issues instruments under the JPMorgan Chase name, or is an administered asset-backed commercial paper conduit.
- Summary of the most significant Firm-sponsored VIE types by business segment:
  - CCB: credit card securitization trusts; mortgage securitization trusts (servicing and securitization of originated and purchased residential mortgages).
  - CIB: mortgage and other securitization trusts (residential, commercial mortgages, and other consumer loans); multi-seller conduits (client financing/market access); municipal bond vehicles (financing municipal bond investments).
  - Related Form 10-Q page references: 152–154 (securitizations, conduits) and 154 (municipal bond vehicles).
- Statement that the Firm also invests in, finances, and provides services to third-party-sponsored VIEs, with additional details and consolidated VIE assets/liabilities on pages 155–157.
- Significant Firm-sponsored VIEs:
  - Credit card securitizations: JPMorgan Chase is the primary beneficiary of the Chase Issuance Trust due to continuing involvement.
  - Mortgage and other securitization trusts: conducted primarily in CCB and CIB; the Firm may act as servicer and/or retain beneficial interests in the trusts.

nodes.title: Firm-sponsored mortgage and other securitization trusts
nodes.heading: Firm-sponsored mortgage and other securitization trusts
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm securitizes (or has securitized) originated and purchased residential mortgages, commercial mortgages and other consumer loans primarily in its CCB and CIB businesses.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Note 13 covers JPMorgan Chase’s involvement with variable interest entities (VIEs), referencing the 2021 Form 10-K for consolidation and securitization accounting policies (Notes 1 and 14).
- Definition of Firm‑sponsored VIEs: Includes entities where JPMorgan Chase is the primary beneficiary; uses the VIE to securitize Firm assets; the VIE issues instruments bearing the JPMorgan Chase name; or the VIE is a Firm‑administered ABCP conduit.
- Types by business segment (with page references): 
  - CCB: Credit card securitization trusts (securitization of originated card receivables; p.152); mortgage securitization trusts (servicing and securitization of originated and purchased residential mortgages; pp.152–154).
  - CIB: Mortgage and other securitization trusts (residential, commercial mortgages, and other consumer loans; pp.152–154); multi‑seller conduits (client funding/access to markets; p.154); municipal bond vehicles (financing municipal bond investments; p.154).
- Third‑party VIEs: The Firm also invests in, finances, and provides services to VIEs sponsored by others; see pp.155–157 for consolidated VIE assets/liabilities and third‑party‑sponsored VIE details.
- Significant Firm‑sponsored VIEs:
  - Credit card securitizations: The Firm is the primary beneficiary of the Chase Issuance Trust due to continuing involvement.
  - Mortgage and other securitization trusts: The Firm securitizes originated and purchased residential and commercial mortgages and other consumer loans (primarily in CCB and CIB), may act as servicer, and may retain beneficial interests.
- Continuing involvement and risk: Continuing involvement includes servicing, retained senior/subordinated interests (including risk‑retention), recourse/guarantees, and derivatives; in some cases involvement is only servicing. Maximum loss exposure on retained/purchased interests equals their carrying value.
- Quantitative disclosures for Firm‑sponsored private‑label securitizations (excludes GSE/agency):
  - June 30, 2022: Total assets in securitization VIEs $231.3B; consolidated VIE assets $0.8B; nonconsolidated with continuing involvement $172.2B; JPMorgan interests in nonconsolidated VIEs $9.1B (primarily investment securities) across prime/Alt‑A, subprime, and commercial/other.
  - December 31, 2021: Total assets $216.7B; consolidated $1.0B; nonconsolidated with continuing involvement $150.8B; JPMorgan interests $6.2B.
- Credit quality of retained interests: 86% (June 30, 2022) and 79% (December 31, 2021) rated A or better (S&P‑equivalent); investment‑grade vs. non‑investment‑grade amounts disclosed for prime residential and commercial/other retained interests.
- Footnote highlights: Excludes GSE/agency securitizations, retained servicing, and certain derivatives; “commercial and other” includes CRE‑backed and non‑mortgage consumer receivables purchased from third parties; includes re‑securitizations; excludes certain market‑making positions.

nodes.title: Residential mortgage
nodes.heading: Residential mortgage
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm securitizes residential mortgage loans originated by CCB, as well as residential mortgage loans purchased from third parties by either CCB or CIB.
nodes.summary:
- The Firm’s securitization activities include:
  - Residential mortgages: Securitizes loans originated by CCB and loans purchased from third parties by CCB or CIB.
  - Commercial mortgages and other consumer securitizations: CIB originates and securitizes commercial mortgage loans and underwrites/trades securities issued by securitization trusts.

- Re-securitizations:
  - Transfers to re-securitization VIEs of U.S. GSE and government agency securities totaled $7.373B (Q2 2022) vs $18.794B (Q2 2021); $13.449B (H1 2022) vs $31.899B (H1 2021).
  - No transfers of private-label securities during the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021; retained interests in any Firm-sponsored VIEs were not material as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021.
  - Interests in nonconsolidated U.S. GSE/government agency re-securitization VIEs were $2.470B at June 30, 2022 vs $1.947B at December 31, 2021.
  - The Firm did not consolidate any U.S. GSE/government agency or Firm-sponsored private-label re-securitization VIEs as of those dates.

- Multi-seller conduits:
  - The Firm makes markets in and invests in commercial paper issued by Firm-administered conduits; holdings were $12.1B (June 30, 2022) and $13.7B (December 31, 2021), eliminated in consolidation.
  - Investments reflect funding needs/capacity, not market illiquidity; no obligation to purchase conduit commercial paper beyond credit risk retention requirements.
  - Deal-specific and program-wide liquidity facilities and credit enhancement provided by the Firm are eliminated in consolidation.
  - The Firm or its conduits provide lending-related commitments to certain clients; unfunded commitments were $13.1B (June 30, 2022) and $13.4B (December 31, 2021), reported off-balance sheet (see Note 22).

- Municipal bond vehicles:
  - TOB (tender option bond) trusts facilitate financing municipal bond investments at short-term rates.
  - Customer TOB trusts are sponsored by third parties; the Firm sponsors all non-customer TOB transactions.

nodes.start_phrase: MSRs represent the fair value of expected future cash flows for performing servicing activities for others.
nodes.summary:

- Summarizes MSR activity for Q2 and first half of 2022 vs 2021, including:
  - Beginning and ending fair values (ending June 30, 2022: $7.4B vs $4.5B in 2021).
  - Originations, purchases, and dispositions (including transfers of excess MSRs to agency trusts in exchange for SMBS).
  - Changes due to collection/realization of expected cash flows.
  - Valuation changes driven by market interest rates/prepayment dynamics and by other model inputs (projected cash flows, discount rates, and non-rate prepayment changes).
  - Unrealized gains/losses recognized in income.
- Provides servicing portfolio metrics:

nodes.title: Accumulated other comprehensive income/(loss)
nodes.heading: Note 19 – Accumulated other comprehensive income/(loss)
nodes.start_phrase: AOCI includes the after-tax change in unrealized gains and losses on investment securities, foreign currency translation adjustments (including the impact of related derivatives), fair value changes of excluded components on fair value hedges, cash flow hedging activities, net loss and prior service costs/(credit) related to the Firm’s defined benefit pension and OPEB plans, and fair value option-elected liabilities arising from changes in the Firm’s own credit risk (DVA).
nodes.summary:
- Scope and definition: Note 19 explains what comprises Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income (AOCI): after-tax unrealized gains/losses on investment securities; foreign currency translation adjustments (including related hedges); fair value changes of excluded components on fair value hedges; cash flow hedging activities; net loss and prior service cost/(credit) for defined benefit pension and OPEB plans; and changes in the Firm’s own credit risk on fair value option–elected liabilities (DVA).

- Periods covered: Detailed reconciliations for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021, showing beginning balances, net changes by component, and ending AOCI balances.

- AOCI balances:
  - June 30, 2022: total AOCI of $(14,369) million (down from $(9,567) million at April 1, 2022 and from $(84) million at January 1, 2022).
  - June 30, 2021: total AOCI of $2,570 million (up from $1,041 million at April 1, 2021; down from $7,986 million at January 1, 2021).

- Key drivers of Q2 2022 after-tax OCI movement (net change of $(4,802) million):
  - Significant losses: unrealized losses on investment securities $(4,031) million; cash flow hedges $(1,348) million; translation adjustments $(679) million.
  - Offsets: DVA +$1,185 million; fair value hedges (excluded components) +$51 million; pension/OPEB +$20 million.

- Key drivers of 1H 2022 after-tax OCI movement (net change of $(14,285) million):
  - Significant losses: unrealized losses on investment securities $(11,484) million; cash flow hedges $(4,139) million; translation adjustments $(741) million.
  - Offsets: DVA +$1,831 million; fair value hedges (excluded components) +$161 million; pension/OPEB +$87 million.

- Comparative 2021 movements:
  - Q2 2021 after-tax OCI gain of $1,529 million driven by gains on investment securities and cash flow hedges, partially offset by translation and fair value hedge losses; DVA contributed positively.
  - 1H 2021 after-tax OCI loss of $(5,416) million, primarily from unrealized losses on investment securities and cash flow hedges, partly offset by translation hedge gains and DVA.

- Translation adjustments and hedges: The note discloses separate lines for translation effects and related hedges, showing offsets (e.g., Q2 2022 translation after-tax $(3,357) million versus hedge after-tax +$2,678 million).

- Reclassification adjustments and presentation:
  - Realized gains/losses on investment securities reclassified to Investment securities gains/(losses).
  - Translation and related hedge reclassifications recorded in other income/expense (amounts not material for the periods shown).
  - Fair value hedges line reflects changes in cross-currency basis spreads excluded from effectiveness; initial costs recognized in interest accruals.
  - Cash flow hedge reclassifications primarily recorded in noninterest revenue, net interest income, and compensation expense.

- AFS-to-HTM transfers: As of June 30, 2022 and 2021, AOCI includes after-tax net unamortized unrealized gains/(losses) related to AFS securities transferred to HTM of $(1.4) billion and $3.0 billion, respectively.

- Overall takeaway: In 2022, AOCI declined sharply into a larger accumulated loss, driven mainly by sizable unrealized losses on investment securities and adverse cash flow hedge marks, partially offset by positive DVA; 2021 showed mixed results with Q2 positive OCI but a year-to-date decline versus beginning of year.

nodes.title: Regulatory capital
nodes.heading: Note 21 – Regulatory capital
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 27 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for a detailed discussion on regulatory capital.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Note 21 – Regulatory capital, with further detail cross-referenced to Note 27 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K.
- Regulators and scope: The Federal Reserve sets capital requirements for the consolidated bank holding company (BHC); the OCC sets minimums and standards for the Firm’s principal insured depository institution (IDI), JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.; FDIC standards apply for IDI well-capitalized thresholds.
- Required ratios: The Firm and its IDI subsidiaries must meet risk-based (CET1, Tier 1, Total capital) and leverage-based (Tier 1 leverage, SLR) minimums; failure to meet minimums may prompt regulatory action.
- Risk-based capital ratio requirements and well-capitalized thresholds (as of June 30, 2022 and Dec 31, 2021):
  - BHC (Standardized): CET1 11.2%, Tier 1 12.7%, Total 14.7%.
  - IDI (Standardized): CET1 7.0%, Tier 1 8.5%, Total 10.5%.
  - BHC (Advanced): CET1 10.5%, Tier 1 12.0%, Total 14.0%.
  - IDI (Advanced): CET1 7.0%, Tier 1 8.5%, Total 10.5%.
  - Well-capitalized: BHC—Tier 1 6.0%, Total 10.0% (no CET1 threshold); IDI—CET1 6.5%, Tier 1 8.0%, Total 10.0%.
- Buffer components and surcharges:
  - BHC requirements include minimums plus a 3.5% GSIB surcharge (Method 2) and a 3.2% SCB for Standardized ratios; Advanced ratios include a fixed 2.5% capital conservation buffer; the countercyclical buffer is 0%.
  - IDI requirements include a fixed 2.5% capital conservation buffer; IDIs are not subject to the GSIB surcharge.
- Leverage-based requirements and well-capitalized thresholds:
  - Tier 1 leverage minimum: 4.0% for both BHC and IDI; well-capitalized: IDI 5.0% (no BHC threshold).
  - SLR requirements: BHC 5.0% and IDI 6.0% (built from a 3.0% minimum plus supplementary leverage buffers of 2.0% and 3.0%, respectively); well-capitalized: IDI 6.0% (no BHC threshold).
- CECL regulatory capital transition:
  - The two-year CECL capital transition expired Dec 31, 2021.
  - Starting Jan 1, 2022, the $2.9 billion CET1 capital benefit recognized at Dec 31, 2021 is being phased out 25% per year over three years; CET1 as of June 30, 2022 reflects a remaining $2.2 billion benefit.
  - Effective Jan 1, 2022, 25% of other CECL transition effects were also phased out from Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, and total leverage exposure.
- Dates of applicability: Tables reflect requirements applicable as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021.

nodes.title: CECL regulatory capital transition
nodes.heading: CECL regulatory capital transition
nodes.start_phrase: On December 31, 2021, the CECL capital transition provisions ,	which delayed the effects of CECL on regulatory capital for two years, expired.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and regulators: Outlines U.S. regulatory capital requirements applicable to JPMorgan Chase & Co. (as a bank holding company, BHC, supervised by the Federal Reserve) and its principal insured depository institution (IDI), JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. (supervised by the OCC), with FDIC involvement for IDI standards. References Note 27 of the 2021 Form 10‑K for additional detail.

- Required capital measures: Describes minimum and “well-capitalized” thresholds the Firm and its IDI must meet for:
  - Risk-based ratios: CET1 capital, Tier 1 capital, and Total capital.
  - Leverage-based ratios: Tier 1 leverage ratio and Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR).
  - Notes that failing to meet minimums could prompt regulatory action.

- Risk-based ratio thresholds (as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021):
  - Presents tables of required ratios under both Basel III Standardized and Advanced approaches for the BHC and IDI, plus well-capitalized thresholds.
  - BHC requirements include: minimums plus a 3.5% GSIB surcharge (Method 2), a 3.2% Stress Capital Buffer (SCB) for Standardized ratios, and a fixed 2.5% capital conservation buffer for Advanced ratios; the countercyclical buffer is 0%.
  - IDI requirements include a fixed 2.5% capital conservation buffer; IDIs are not subject to the GSIB surcharge.
  - Notes well-capitalized thresholds for BHCs (risk-based) and IDIs per applicable regulations.

- Leverage-based thresholds:
  - Provides minimum Tier 1 leverage and SLR requirements for BHC and IDI, including composition of the SLR (3.0% minimum plus supplementary leverage buffers of 2.0% for BHCs and 3.0% for IDIs).
  - Lists well-capitalized leverage thresholds for IDIs; Fed regulations do not set well-capitalized thresholds for BHC leverage measures.

- CECL regulatory capital transition:
  - The two-year delay of CECL’s impact on regulatory capital expired December 31, 2021.
  - Starting January 1, 2022, the $2.9 billion CET1 benefit recognized at year-end 2021 is being phased out 25% per year over three years; $2.2 billion remained in CET1 at June 30, 2022.
  - Also phases out 25% of other CECL transition amounts from Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, and total leverage exposure.
  - References Note 27 of the 2021 Form 10‑K for more on CECL transition.

- Reported capital metrics:
  - Provides detailed tables (for June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021) of CET1, Tier 1, and Total capital; risk-weighted assets; and resulting capital ratios under both Basel III Standardized and Advanced for the Firm and the Bank.
  - Presents leverage metrics: adjusted average assets, Tier 1 leverage ratio, total leverage exposure, and SLR.
  - Notes that metrics reflect CECL transition provisions and that PPP loans receive a 0% risk weight.

- Capital status: Confirms that as of both dates, JPMorgan Chase & Co. and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. were well-capitalized and met all applicable capital requirements.

nodes.title: Litigation
nodes.heading: Note 24 – Litigation
nodes.start_phrase: As of June 30, 2022, the Firm and its subsidiaries and affiliates are defendants or respondents in numerous legal proceedings, including private, civil litigations, government investigations or regulatory enforcement matters.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Note 24 – Litigation Contingencies as of June 30, 2022, detailing the Firm’s legal exposures, estimation of potential losses, and summaries of material proceedings.

- Overall legal exposure:
  - The Firm and affiliates are involved in numerous legal proceedings globally, including civil litigations, government investigations, and regulatory enforcement matters, spanning all business lines.
  - Matters range from single-plaintiff cases to large class actions and cover tort, contract, antitrust, securities, and consumer protection claims, some with novel legal theories.
  - Estimated aggregate range of reasonably possible losses in excess of reserves: $0 to approximately $1.2 billion at June 30, 2022.
  - Not all matters are estimable; estimates involve significant judgment due to early case stages, multiple defendants, unresolved issues (e.g., class certification, claim scope), and uncertain outcomes. Estimates may change, and actual losses could differ significantly; outcomes considered remote may still occur.

- Material legal proceedings:
  - Amrapali (India):
    - India’s Enforcement Directorate (ED) is investigating J.P. Morgan India Private Limited regarding 2010 and 2012 investments by two offshore funds formerly managed by JPMorgan entities in Amrapali residential projects.
    - 2017: Multiple creditor and homebuyer civil claims; homebuyer matters overseen by India’s Supreme Court and ongoing.
    - Aug 2021: ED fined J.P. Morgan India approximately $31.5 million; the Firm is appealing.
    - July 2019: India’s Supreme Court made preliminary findings of violations of PMLA and FEMA by Amrapali and others, including unspecified JPMorgan entities and the offshore funds; directed further ED inquiry.
    - May 2020: ED attached approximately $25 million from J.P. Morgan India in the PMLA investigation; the Firm is cooperating.
  - Federal Republic of Nigeria litigation:
    - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. operated an escrow/depository account holding about $1.1 billion for Nigeria’s federal government and two oil companies during an oil field rights dispute.
    - Following settlement, funds were paid out in 2011 and 2013 per client instructions.
    - Nov 2017: Nigeria sued in the English High Court for approximately $875 million, alleging the payments were part of a complex fraud (not involving JPMorgan), and the bank should have been on notice.
    - Trial held Feb–Apr 2022; in June 2022 the Court ruled fully in favor of JPMorgan and dismissed the case.
    - Nigeria has sought permission to appeal relating solely to the 2013 payment of approximately $75 million.
  - Foreign Exchange investigations and litigation:
    - References prior settlements with authorities related to FX sales and trading activities and related controls; notes a May 2015 plea by the Firm (details truncated in the excerpt).

Morgan India Private Limited approximately $31.5 million (under appeal).   - Governmental: Prior settlements include a 2015 guilty plea to a federal antitrust violation; the Department of Labor granted a five-year QPAM exemption under ERISA through January 2023, with a further exemption needed thereafter. - Interchange litigation: Merchant antitrust cases against Visa, Mastercard, and certain banks over interchange fees and network rules.
  - Monetary class: A 2018 amended settlement added $900 million to ~ $5.3 billion from the original settlement; approved in 2019, with appeals pending. Based on opt-outs, $700 million was returned to defendants.

nodes.title: Inquiries Concerning Preservation Requirements.
nodes.heading: Inquiries Concerning Preservation Requirements.
nodes.start_phrase: In December 2021 certain of the Firm’s subsidiaries entered into resolutions with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC”) and the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (“CFTC”) to resolve their respective civil investigations of compliance with records preservation requirements applicable to broker-dealer firms, swap dealers and futures commission merchants.
nodes.summary:
- Antitrust and FX matters: The Firm pled guilty to a single federal antitrust violation. The U.S. Department of Labor granted a five-year ERISA QPAM exemption through January 2023; the Firm will seek a further exemption for the remainder of the ten-year disqualification period. The only remaining FX-related governmental inquiry is a South Africa Competition Commission case pending before the South Africa Competition Tribunal.
- FX civil litigation: A 2018 SDNY settlement of a U.S. class action alleging FX rate manipulation was approved; some class members opted out and filed separate suits that remain pending. Additional putative classes include consumers alleging inflated currency purchase rates and purported indirect purchasers of FX instruments, the latter settled in 2020 for $10 million with 11 other defendants. Related actions are pending outside the U.S. (U.K., Israel, Netherlands, Brazil, Australia); the U.K. tribunal denied opt-out class certification.
- Records preservation inquiries: In December 2021, the Firm resolved SEC and CFTC investigations into failures to retain required communications sent over unapproved electronic messaging, with findings of related supervision failures. Penalties included $125 million to the SEC (J.P. Morgan Securities LLC) and $75 million to the CFTC (J.P. Morgan Securities LLC, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., and J.P. Morgan Securities plc). The Firm is cooperating with ongoing information requests.
- Shareholder derivative action: Filed March 2022 in EDNY alleging the Board failed to oversee records preservation compliance, seeking damages, restitution, disgorgement, and governance reforms; defendants moved to dismiss.
- Interchange litigation: Merchant antitrust suits against Visa, Mastercard, and banks over credit/debit card interchange and rules. After a 2012 settlement was reversed on appeal in 2017, the case was split into monetary and injunctive classes. A 2018 amended monetary settlement added $900 million to about $5.3 billion in escrow; approved in December 2019, with appeals pending. Based on opt-outs, $700 million was returned to defendants. The injunctive case continues, with partial class certification granted in September 2021. Some individual merchant actions remain pending.

nodes.title: Interchange Litigation.
nodes.heading: Interchange Litigation.
nodes.start_phrase: Groups of merchants and retail associations filed a series of class action complaints alleging that Visa and Mastercard, as well as certain banks, conspired to set the price of credit and debit card interchange fees and enacted related rules in violation of antitrust laws.
nodes.summary:
- Criminal antitrust matter (FX): The Firm pled guilty to a federal antitrust violation, triggering a 10-year ERISA QPAM disqualification. The Department of Labor granted a five-year exemption through January 2023; a further exemption is needed for the remaining period. The only outstanding FX-related governmental inquiry is a South Africa Competition Commission case before the Competition Tribunal.
- Civil FX litigation: A U.S. consolidated class action settlement was finally approved in August 2018, but some class members opted out and filed new suits in November 2018. Additional putative class actions include consumer claims over allegedly inflated retail foreign currency rates and indirect purchaser claims (the latter settled in 2020 for $10 million with 11 other defendants). Similar actions are pending outside the U.S. (U.K., Israel, the Netherlands, Brazil, Australia); in the U.K., the Competition Appeal Tribunal denied opt-out class certification.
- Records preservation inquiries: In December 2021, resolutions with the SEC and CFTC addressed failures to preserve required records and supervise use of unapproved electronic messaging. Penalties totaled $200 million ($125 million to the SEC; $75 million to the CFTC), involving J.P. Morgan Securities LLC, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., and J.P. Morgan Securities plc. The Firm is responding to ongoing regulatory information requests and is cooperating.
- Shareholder derivative action: Filed March 2022 in the Eastern District of New York against the Firm’s Board for alleged oversight failures regarding records preservation and related securities law violations, seeking damages, restitution, disgorgement, and governance reforms. Defendants moved to dismiss.
- Interchange fee litigation: Merchants allege Visa/Mastercard and certain banks conspired to fix credit/debit card interchange fees and impose anticompetitive rules. After an initial 2012 settlement was reversed on appeal, the case was split into monetary and injunctive classes. A 2018 amended monetary settlement added $900 million to about $5.3 billion in escrow; it was approved in December 2019, with appeals pending. Based on opt-outs, $700 million was returned to defendants. The injunctive class was certified in part in September 2021. Some individual merchant actions remain pending.

nodes.title: LIBOR and Other Benchmark Rate Investigations and Litigation.
nodes.heading: LIBOR and Other Benchmark Rate Investigations and Litigation.
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase has responded to inquiries from various governmental agencies and entities around the world relating primarily to the British Bankers Association’s (“BBA”) London Interbank Offered Rate (“LIBOR”) for various currencies and the European Banking Federation’s Euro Interbank Offered Rate (“EURIBOR”).
nodes.summary:
- JPMorgan Chase is addressing global regulatory inquiries into benchmark rates, focusing on BBA-administered LIBOR (multiple currencies) and EBF’s EURIBOR.
- The Swiss Competition Commission’s EURIBOR investigation remains ongoing; the European Commission issued a 2016 antitrust decision against the Firm and others regarding EURIBOR, which the Firm has appealed to the European General Court.
- The Firm faces multiple individual and putative class actions tied to benchmark rates, including U.S. dollar LIBOR:
  - Some cases related to BBA-era USD LIBOR have been dismissed or resolved; others continue.
  - The SDNY certified antitrust class claims involving bonds and interest rate swaps sold directly by defendants, including the Firm.
  - A consolidated putative class action covering the ICE-administered USD LIBOR period was dismissed.
  - Individual plaintiffs filed antitrust claims alleging a conspiracy to set USD LIBOR and to monopolize markets for LIBOR-based consumer loans and credit cards; defendants moved to dismiss, and in Dec 2021 the court denied plaintiffs’ motions for a preliminary injunction to halt LIBOR setting and enforcement of LIBOR-linked instruments.
  - Settlements of putative class actions concerning Swiss franc LIBOR, SIBOR, SOR, and Australia’s BBSW are pending court approval.
- Metals and U.S. Treasuries matters:
  - The Firm and subsidiaries resolved DOJ, CFTC, and SEC investigations into historical trading practices in precious metals and U.S. Treasuries (2008–2016).
  - The Firm entered a Deferred Prosecution Agreement with the DOJ on two wire fraud counts; the criminal information will be dismissed after three years if obligations are met.
  - Across the DOJ, CFTC, and SEC resolutions, the entities agreed to pay approximately $920 million, including victim compensation.
  - Putative class actions alleging precious metals futures/options manipulation were consolidated in SDNY; final settlement approval was granted in July 2022.
  - Putative class actions alleging manipulation of U.S. Treasury futures/options were consolidated in SDNY; final settlement approval was granted in June 2022.
  - Related putative class actions have been filed in Canada regarding precious metals.
- Securities litigation:
  - Two putative class actions in EDNY allege the Firm’s SEC filings were materially false or misleading for not disclosing aspects of the above investigations; plaintiffs later added allegations that certain precious metals futures orders during the class period were false and misleading; defendants moved to dismiss.
- Shareholder derivative action:
  - Filed in May 2022 in New York state court, alleging breach of fiduciary duty and unjust enrichment by certain current and former officers and directors, asserting wrongful rejection of a shareholder’s demand to commence litigation, and seeking relief.

nodes.title: Metals and U.S. Treasuries Investigations and Litigation and Related Inquiries.
nodes.heading: Metals and U.S. Treasuries Investigations and Litigation and Related Inquiries.
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm previously reported that it and/or certain of its subsidiaries had entered into resolutions with the U.S. Department of Justice (“DOJ”), the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (“CFTC”) and the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC”), which, collectively, resolved those agencies’ respective investigations relating to historical trading practices by former employees in the precious metals and U.S. treasuries markets and related conduct from 2008 to 2016.

- Benchmark rate investigations and litigation:

  - European Commission issued a 2016 antitrust decision against the firm and others regarding EURIBOR; JPMorgan Chase has appealed to the European General Court.
  - Multiple U.S. actions tied to U.S. dollar LIBOR: some dismissed or resolved; others ongoing. Antitrust class claims certified in SDNY for bonds and interest rate swaps sold directly by defendants, including the firm.

  - Individual plaintiffs brought antitrust claims alleging unlawful agreement to set U.S. dollar LIBOR and conspiracy to monopolize LIBOR-based consumer loans/credit cards; court denied preliminary injunction in Dec 2021.
  - Settlements for class actions related to Swiss franc LIBOR, SIBOR/SOR, and Australian BBSW remain subject to court approval.

- Metals and U.S. Treasuries investigations and related litigation:
  - Resolutions reached with DOJ, CFTC, and SEC regarding historical trading practices in precious metals and U.S. Treasuries (2008–2016).
  - Deferred Prosecution Agreement with DOJ: criminal information charging two counts of wire fraud against JPMorgan Chase & Co.; dismissal after three years contingent on compliance by JPMorgan Chase & Co., JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., and J.P. Morgan Securities LLC.
  - Aggregate monetary amount of approximately $920 million, including victim compensation.
  - Precious metals CEA putative class actions consolidated in SDNY; final settlement approval granted July 2022.
  - U.S. Treasury futures/options CEA putative class actions consolidated in SDNY (transferred from N.D. Ill.); final settlement approval granted June 2022.
  - Related Canadian putative class actions filed concerning precious metals conduct.
  - Securities Exchange Act putative class actions (EDNY) alleging material misstatements/omissions in SEC filings related to investigations; cases consolidated; second amended complaint filed May 2021 adding allegations of false precious metals futures orders; motion to dismiss pending.
  - May 2022 shareholder derivative suit in NY state court alleging breach of fiduciary duty and unjust enrichment by certain officers/directors; challenges Board’s rejection of shareholder demand; seeks damages, disgorgement, and governance reforms tied to spoofing-related conduct (subject of Sept 2020 DOJ/CFTC/SEC resolutions) and separate OCC fiduciary resolution (Nov 2020).

- Securities lending antitrust litigation:
  - JPMorgan entities named in SDNY putative class action alleging conspiracy to block anonymous exchange trading in securities lending; motion to dismiss denied; plaintiffs seek class certification, which defendants oppose.

- Broader litigation posture and financial impact:
  - JPMorgan Chase and subsidiaries are involved in numerous additional legal proceedings; the firm asserts meritorious defenses and intends vigorous defense; new matters may arise.
  - Litigation reserves established for several hundred proceedings; accruals follow U.S. GAAP contingency standards and are reviewed quarterly.
  - Legal expense: $73 million (Q2 2022) vs. $185 million (Q2 2021); $192 million (six months ended June 30, 2022) vs. $213 million (six months ended June 30, 2021).
  - Outcomes are uncertain; while current knowledge, reserves, and estimated loss ranges suggest pending matters should not materially adversely affect consolidated financial condition, ultimate resolutions may exceed reserves or have reputational impacts and could be material to results in a given period.

nodes.title: Securities Lending Antitrust Litigation.

- Explains litigation reserve practices: reserves established for several hundred matters; accrual under U.S. GAAP when loss is probable and reasonably estimable; reserves reviewed and adjusted quarterly with counsel input.

nodes.title: Business segments

nodes.title: Segment results
nodes.heading: Segment results
nodes.start_phrase: The following table provides a summary of the Firm’s segment results as of or for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021 , on a managed basis.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of business segmentation: The firm is managed by lines of business (LOBs) with four reportable segments—Consumer & Community Banking (CCB), Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB), Commercial Banking (CB), and Asset & Wealth Management (AWM)—plus a Corporate segment. Segments are defined by products/services or customer type and align with how the Operating Committee evaluates performance.

- Managed basis presentation: Segment results are shown on a managed, fully tax-equivalent (FTE) basis. Revenue from tax-advantaged investments and tax‑exempt securities is grossed up for comparability with taxable items; corresponding tax effects are recorded in income tax expense. Reconciling items remove these FTE adjustments to arrive at reported U.S. GAAP results.

- Capital allocation: Equity capital is assigned to each LOB; methodologies and assumptions are periodically reassessed, which can change LOB capital.

- Change in tax allocation: In 1Q22 the firm changed its methodology for allocating income taxes to LOBs; prior periods were revised for comparability with no impact on firmwide net income.

- Segment performance highlights (three months ended June 30, 2022 vs. 2021):
  - Firmwide: Total net revenue was approximately flat (30.7bn vs. 30.5bn). Provision for credit losses swung to a 1.1bn expense from a 2.3bn release. Noninterest expense rose to 18.7bn from 17.7bn. Net income declined to 8.65bn from 11.95bn. ROE fell to 13% from 18%; overhead ratio increased to 61 from 58.
  - CCB: Total net revenue essentially flat (12.6bn vs. 12.8bn) with higher net interest income and lower noninterest revenue; provision moved to a 761mm expense from a 1.87bn release; expenses increased. Net income fell to 3.10bn from 5.65bn; ROE 24% vs. 44%.
  - CIB: Revenue decreased (11.95bn vs. 13.21bn); slight provision expense vs. a prior release; higher expenses. Net income declined to 3.73bn from 5.02bn; ROE 14% vs. 23%. Average equity rose significantly (103bn vs. 83bn).
  - CB: Revenue increased (2.68bn vs. 2.48bn); provision expense vs. prior release; expenses up. Net income declined to 994mm from 1.42bn; ROE 15% vs. 23%.
  - AWM: Revenue increased (4.31bn vs. 4.11bn); modest provision expense vs. prior release; expenses up. Net income declined to 1.00bn from 1.16bn; ROE 23% vs. 32%.
  - Corporate: Revenue improved (80mm vs. -1.17bn). Net loss narrowed (-174mm vs. -1.30bn). Total assets rose to 1.46tn from 1.38tn.

- Balance sheet and efficiency metrics: Average equity increased notably in CIB and AWM; total assets grew across major segments. Overhead ratios rose in all operating segments, indicating higher expense-to-revenue levels.

- Reconciliation to GAAP: Segment-level FTE adjustments are eliminated in reconciling items; the Corporate reconciling column shows offsetting tax effects to align managed results with reported GAAP. References are made to the firm’s 2021 Form 10‑K (Note 32 and page 93) for additional details on segment definitions, managed basis, and capital allocation.

Metrics shown: noninterest revenue, net interest income, total net revenue, provision for credit losses, noninterest expense, income before income tax, income tax expense/benefit, net income, average equity, total assets, return on equity (ROE), and overhead ratio.

- Provides average equity by segment (e.g., CIB average equity higher in 2022 vs 2021) and total assets by segment and Firm totals as of June 30, 2022 vs 2021.

- Purpose and scope: Executive overview of JPMorgan Chase’s Q2 2022 MD&A, emphasizing that full 10-Q and 2021 10-K should be read for complete context, trends, risks, and critical accounting estimates; several non-GAAP measures referenced.

- Firmwide Q2 2022 results:

Noninterest revenue $15.6B (-12%), driven by lower Investment Banking fees, Credit Adjustments & Other loss vs prior gain, equity investment losses, lower Card income, and $337MM bridge financing markdowns; partially offset by higher Markets revenue.
  - Noninterest expense up 6% due to continued investments (technology, marketing) and higher structural compensation, partly offset by lower revenue-related compensation.
  - Provision for credit losses $1.1B vs prior-year net benefit of $2.3B; includes $428MM allowance build (loan growth, modest macro deterioration) and $657MM net charge-offs (down YoY, driven by Card).

  - Average loans $1.1T (+7%); average deposits $2.5T (+9%), with Q2 declines in certain areas due to migration to higher-yield alternatives and increased consumer spending.

- Capital and metrics:

  - Book value per share $86.38; tangible book value per share $69.53 (+1% YoY).

- Segment highlights (Q2 2022):

  - Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB): ROE 14%; #1 global IB fees with 8.1% YTD wallet share; Markets revenue $7.8B (+15%) with both Fixed Income and Equity Markets +15%.
  - Commercial Banking (CB): ROE 15%; gross IB revenue $788MM (-32%); average loans +7% YoY/+4% QoQ; average deposits +4%.
  - Asset & Wealth Management (AWM): ROE 23%; AUM $2.7T (-8%); average loans +11% YoY/+1% QoQ; average deposits +22%.

- Credit provided and capital raised (1H 2022):

- Recent event:

- 2022 outlook (forward-looking):

  - Card net charge-off rate expected to be <2%.

- Business developments:
