structure.title: Consolidated Results of Operations
structure.heading: Consolidated Results of Operations
structure.start_phrase:
This section provides a comparative discussion of JPMorgan Chase’s Consolidated Results of Operations on a reported basis for the 
three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021 , unless otherwise specified.
structure.summary:
- Scope: Comparative discussion of JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated results for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 vs. 2021; segment-specific drivers referenced to segment sections; notes on critical accounting estimates.

- Total net revenue:
  - Q2 2022: $30.7B, up 1% YoY; noninterest revenue down 12% to $15.6B; net interest income (NII) up 19% to $15.1B.
  - YTD 2022: $61.4B, down 2% YoY; noninterest revenue down 13% to $32.4B; NII up 13% to $29.0B.

- Revenue line items and drivers (Q2 unless noted):
  - Investment banking fees: down 54% (YTD down 44%) on lower debt/equity underwriting due to volatile markets and reduced advisory from fewer announced deals (CIB).
  - Principal transactions: up 22% Q2 on strong Fixed Income Markets (macro/Currencies & EM) and Equity Markets (derivatives), offset by:
    - $218M loss in Credit Adjustments & Other vs. $233M gain prior year, and
    - $337M markdowns on held-for-sale bridge financing positions (CIB/CB).
    - Q2 also included net gains on certain legacy PE investments in Corporate.
    - YTD down 5% due to CAO losses (funding spread widening, commodities and Russia-related exposures), bridge loan markdowns, and net losses on legacy PE in Corporate; partially offset by stronger Markets (FICC macro and equities derivatives/prime).
  - Lending- and deposit-related fees: up 6% Q2; YTD up on higher deposit fees in CCB and higher cash management fees in CIB/CB.
  - Asset management, administration and commissions: flat Q2; YTD up on higher AWM fees from cumulative net inflows and removal of most money market fund fee waivers; Q2 tempered by lower markets and performance fees.
  - Investment securities losses: roughly flat Q2; higher YTD losses from repositioning Treasury and CIO securities (U.S. Treasuries, GSE/government agency MBS).
  - Mortgage fees and related income: down Q2 and YTD on lower production margins/volume; largely offset by higher MSR risk management results (slower prepayment expectations) and higher servicing revenue on more third-party loans.
  - Card income: down Q2 and YTD on higher amortization of new account origination costs and lower net interchange from a co-brand contract renegotiation.
  - Other income: down Q2 on net equity investment losses in CIB and lower auto operating lease income; partially offset by gains on an equity-method investment in CB and higher gains on certain Corporate investments. YTD also benefited from insurance proceeds, absence of prior-year weather-related write-downs in CIB, offset by lower auto operating lease income and investment losses in AWM/CIB.

- Net interest income and balance sheet metrics:
  - Q2 average interest-earning assets $3.4T (+$209B); yield 2.22% (+43 bps); net yield (FTE) 1.80% (+18 bps); net yield excluding Markets 2.26% (+36 bps). NII up on higher rates and balance sheet growth; offset by lower Markets NII and lower PPP loan NII.
  - YTD average interest-earning assets $3.4T (+$242B); yield 2.04% (+21 bps); net yield (FTE) 1.74% (+9 bps); excluding Markets 2.11% (+19 bps).

- Provision for credit losses (PCL):
  - Q2 PCL $1.1B vs. $(2.3)B prior year; includes $657M net charge-offs and $428M net ACL build:
    - Wholesale: +$238M from modest macro deterioration and CB loan growth, partly offset by client-specific reductions.
    - Consumer: +$184M, mainly Card loan growth.
    - Net charge-offs down $77M YoY, driven by Card; prior-year included $3.0B ACL release and $734M net charge-offs.
  - YTD PCL $2.6B vs. $(6.4)B prior year; includes $1.3B net ACL build and $1.2B net charge-offs:
    - Wholesale: +$1.0B from increased weight on adverse scenarios (inflation, monetary policy shifts, geopolitical risks incl. Ukraine), modest macro deterioration, CB loan growth, and Russia-related downgrades in CIB/AWM.
    - Consumer: +$311M (Card loan growth; Home Lending adverse-scenario weighting).
    - Net charge-offs down $552M YoY, driven by Card; prior year had $8.2B ACL release and $1.8B net charge-offs.

- Noninterest expense:
  - Q2 total $18.7B, up 6% YoY; compensation up 5% on investments and higher structural expense, partly offset by lower revenue-related comp in CIB. Noncomp up 8% on higher investments (marketing, technology) and structural expense (travel/entertainment); partly offset by lower volume-related expense (auto lease depreciation in CCB) and lower legal expense.
  - YTD total $37.9B, up 4% YoY; compensation up 3% with similar drivers; noncomp up 5% on investments and higher structural/regulatory assessments; prior year included a $550M Foundation contribution; partially offset by lower volume-related expense (lower auto lease depreciation) and higher operating losses in CCB. Firmwide legal expense down vs. prior year.

- Income taxes:
  - Q2 pretax income $10.9B (down 28%); tax expense $2.2B (down 30%); effective tax rate 20.4% vs. 20.9%, lower due to benefits from tax audit settlements, partly offset by mix effects; prior year included tax audit settlement expenses.
  - YTD pretax income $20.9B (down 36%); tax $4.0B (down 39%); ETR 19.1% vs. 20.0%, lower on tax audit settlement benefits and the relative impact of certain tax items on lower pretax income, partly offset by mix; prior year included settlement expenses.

- Additional notes:
  - CIB Markets performance is assessed on total revenue, as principal transactions and NII can offset each other.
  - Several items cite segment-level detail and accounting/measurement notes referenced elsewhere in the filing.

structure.title: Consolidated Balance Sheets and Cash Flows Analysis
structure.heading: Consolidated Balance Sheets and Cash Flows Analysis
structure.start_phrase: The following is a discussion of the significant changes between J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2, and D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 1.
structure.summary:
- Scope and purpose: Provides an analysis of changes in consolidated balance sheets between June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021, and a consolidated cash flows analysis for the six months ended June 30, 2022 versus 2021.
- Scale: Total assets rose 3% to $3.84T; total liabilities rose 3% to $3.56T; stockholders’ equity fell 3% to $286.1B.

Assets
- Cash and due from banks and deposits with banks: Declined, driven by Markets activities and loan growth; deposits with central banks decreased.
- Securities financing: Federal funds sold and securities purchased under resale agreements up 23% on higher collateral needs, demand to cover shorts, and netting effects in client market-making; securities borrowed slightly down.
- Trading assets: Up 7% on higher FX and commodity derivative receivables, higher debt instruments, and additional deployment in Treasury and CIO; partially offset by lower equities.
- Investment securities: Mix shifted with $73.2B transferred from AFS to HTM. AFS down (paydowns, unrealized losses in AOCI, partly offset by net purchases). HTM up (purchases partly offset by paydowns).
- Loans: Up 2%. Drivers: higher CB utilization and originations; higher retained residential real estate in AWM and Home Lending; higher Card balances on strong spending; higher CIB wholesale loans. Offsets: lower Home Lending mortgage warehouse balances (higher rates); CCB decline from PPP forgiveness.
- Allowance for loan losses: Up $1.4B (wholesale +$1.1B; consumer +$314MM) reflecting greater weight on adverse scenarios (inflation, monetary policy shifts, geopolitical risks incl. Ukraine), modest macro deterioration, loan growth in Card and CB, and Russia-related downgrades in CIB/AWM; $39MM reduction in allowance for lending-related commitments (other liabilities).
- Accrued interest and receivables: Up 42% on higher client receivables, including prime brokerage.
- Goodwill/MSRs/intangibles: Up on higher MSRs (rate changes and net additions) and acquisitions (Frosch Travel Group in CCB; Volkswagen Payments S.A. in CIB).
- Other assets: Up due to higher cash collateral and securities financing in Markets.

Liabilities and equity
- Deposits: Flat overall. Growth in new CCB accounts and higher deposits in Securities Services and Payments offset by CB outflows as non-operating deposits migrated to higher-yielding alternatives and seasonal declines in AWM/CB.
- Federal funds purchased and securities loaned/sold under repos: Up 15% from higher secured financing of trading assets and netting effects; partly offset by lower secured financing of AFS in Treasury and CIO.
- Short-term borrowings: Up 9% due to higher commercial paper issuance for short-term liquidity in Treasury and CIO.
- Trading liabilities: Up 16% on client-driven Fixed Income Markets short positions.
- Accounts payable and other liabilities: Up 19% on higher client payables, including prime brokerage.
- Beneficial interests in consolidated VIEs: Slightly down.
- Long-term debt: Down 4% due to fair value hedge accounting adjustments from higher rates and lower fair value of structured notes, largely offset by net issuances.
- Stockholders’ equity: Down 3% on net unrealized AOCI losses from higher rates impacting AFS securities and cash flow hedges.

Cash flows (six months ended June 30)
- Net change in cash and deposits with banks: Decrease of $71.6B in 2022 vs increase of $177.8B in 2021; adverse FX impact of $18.8B in 2022 vs $5.9B in 2021.
- Operating activities: 2022 provided $24.1B (higher payables, trading liabilities, proceeds from loans held-for-sale, offset by higher trading assets and receivables). 2021 used $(30.3)B (higher receivables and securities borrowed, partly offset by higher payables).
- Investing activities: 2022 used $(125.8)B (higher resales, net loan originations, net investment securities purchases). 2021 provided $33.1B (lower resales, partly offset by net loan originations).
- Financing activities: 2022 provided $49.0B (higher repos and net proceeds from long- and short-term borrowings). 2021 provided $181.0B (higher deposits and repos, and net borrowing proceeds). Both periods used cash for share repurchases and dividends.

Overall themes
- Balance sheet growth driven by securities financing, trading-related activities, and moderate loan growth.
- Credit provisioning increased amid a more adverse macro outlook and geopolitical uncertainty.
- Equity reduced by rate-driven AOCI losses; funding mix stable with flat deposits and higher secured financing/short-term borrowings.
- Cash flows reflect deployment into securities financing, loans, and investment securities in 2022, funded by repos and borrowings.

structure.title: Explanation and Reconciliation of the Firm’s Use of Non-GAAP Financial Measures
structure.heading: Explanation and Reconciliation of the Firm’s Use of Non-GAAP Financial Measures
structure.start_phrase:
The Firm prepares its Consolidated Financial Statements in 
accordance with U.S. GAAP and this presentation is referred 
to as “reported” basis; these financial statements appear on 
page 88-92 .
structure.summary:
- Purpose: Explains JPMorgan Chase’s use of non-GAAP financial measures and reconciles them to U.S. GAAP (“reported”) results.
- Non-GAAP measures covered:
  - Firmwide “managed” basis results (including fully taxable-equivalent, or FTE, adjustments) and the overhead ratio.
  - Pre-provision profit (total net revenue less total noninterest expense).
  - Net interest income (NII), net yield, and noninterest revenue excluding Markets.
  - Tangible common equity (TCE), return on TCE (ROTCE), and tangible book value per share (TBVPS).
  - Adjusted expense (excluding Firmwide legal expense).
  - Allowance for loan losses to period-end loans retained (excluding trade finance and conduits).
- Reference: Points to the 2021 Form 10-K (pages 58–60) for further discussion of these non-GAAP and key performance measures.
- Reconciliations: Provides summary tables reconciling U.S. GAAP to managed basis for:
  - Three months ended June 30, 2022 vs. 2021:
    - Managed total net revenue: $31.6B (2022) vs. $31.4B (2021).
    - NII (managed): up 19% to $15.2B; noninterest revenue (managed): down 12% to $16.4B.
    - Pre-provision profit (managed): $12.9B vs. $13.7B (down year-over-year).
    - Provision for credit losses: build of $1.1B vs. release of $(2.3)B in 2021.
    - Net income: $8.6B vs. $11.9B; overhead ratio: 59% managed (vs. 56%).
  - Six months ended June 30, 2022 vs. 2021:
    - Managed total net revenue: $63.2B vs. $64.5B.
    - NII (managed): up 13% to $29.2B; noninterest revenue (managed): down 12% to $34.0B.
    - Pre-provision profit (managed): $25.3B vs. $28.1B.
    - Provision for credit losses: build of $2.6B vs. release of $(6.4)B in 2021.
    - Net income: $16.9B vs. $26.2B; overhead ratio: 60% managed (vs. 56%).
- NII, yield, and noninterest revenue excluding Markets:
  - Q2 2022 vs. Q2 2021:
    - NII excluding Markets (managed): up 26% to $13.7B.
    - Net yield on average interest-earning assets excluding Markets: 2.26% vs. 1.90%.
    - Noninterest revenue excluding Markets: down 26% to $10.2B.
    - Memo: Total Markets net revenue up 15% to $7.8B.
  - Six months 2022 vs. 2021:
    - NII excluding Markets: up 18% to $25.4B; yield excluding Markets: 2.11% vs. 1.92%.
    - Noninterest revenue excluding Markets: down 21% to $21.2B.
    - Memo: Total Markets net revenue up 4% to $16.5B.
- TCE reconciliation:
  - Bridge from common stockholders’ equity to TCE by subtracting goodwill and other intangibles and adding certain deferred tax liabilities (related to tax-deductible goodwill/intangibles).
  - Period-end (6/30/22 vs. 12/31/21): TCE $203.9B vs. $210.6B; TBVPS $69.53 vs. $71.53.
  - ROTCE: 17% (Q2 2022) vs. 23% (Q2 2021); 16% (1H22) vs. 26% (1H21).
- Notes:
  - FTE adjustments are used to make tax-exempt items comparable and are predominantly recognized in CIB, CB, and Corporate.
  - Interest figures include effects of related hedges.
  - Additional Markets detail referenced elsewhere in the report.

structure.title: Business Segment Results
structure.heading: Business Segment Results
structure.start_phrase: The Firm is managed on an LOB basis.
structure.summary:
- Purpose and structure
  - Presents JPMorgan Chase’s business segment results on a managed (non-GAAP) basis for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022, with comparisons to 2021.
  - Describes the Firm’s line-of-business (LOB) reporting methodology, including revenue sharing between segments, funds transfer pricing (FTP), centralized management of certain foreign exchange risk by Treasury and CIO, and capital allocation to segments.
  - Notes a 2022 change in methodology for allocating income taxes to LOBs (no impact to firmwide net income).

- Firmwide summary (managed basis)
  - Q2 2022: Total net revenue $31.6B (+1% YoY), noninterest expense $18.7B (+6%), provision for credit losses $1.1B vs. prior-year net benefit, net income $8.6B (-28%), ROE 13%.
  - 1H 2022: Total net revenue $63.2B (-2%), noninterest expense $37.9B (+4%), provision for credit losses $2.6B vs. prior-year net benefit, net income $16.9B (-35%), ROE 13%.

- Consumer & Community Banking (CCB)
  - Q2 2022: Net income $3.1B (-45%); revenue $12.6B (-1%). NII up on deposit growth and higher card revolve; noninterest revenue down on lower card income (higher amortization, co-brand renegotiation), weaker mortgage production, and lower auto lease income; partially offset by higher MSR servicing revenue and deposit fees.
  - Expenses up on investments and structural costs (compensation, technology, marketing); provision reflects net charge-offs down YoY and an allowance build tied to card growth; prior year included large reserve releases.
  - 1H 2022 mirrors Q2 themes; detailed business metrics provided (deposits up, card loans up, digital/mobile customers up, mortgage and auto originations down, MSR value higher, stable-to-strong credit metrics).

- Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB)
  - Q2 2022: Net income $3.7B (-26%); revenue $11.9B (-10%).
  - Banking revenue down 37%: investment banking fees -54% amid market volatility and markdowns on bridge financing; underwriting fees sharply lower; advisory down. Payments flat reported (up strongly excluding markdowns). Lending up on fair value gains and higher NII.
  - Markets & Securities Services up 8%: Fixed Income +15% (macro strength), Equities +15% (derivatives), Securities Services +6%; Credit Adjustments & Other a loss on funding spread widening.
  - Expenses modestly higher; small provision build reflecting a softer macro outlook (vs. prior-year benefit). 1H 2022 shows similar trends; retains top-tier league table positions (#1 global IB fees YTD).

- Commercial Banking (CB)
  - Q2 2022: Net income $994MM (-30%); revenue $2.68B (+8%).
  - NII up on higher deposit margins and loan growth (partly offset by funding costs); noninterest revenue down on lower IB revenue and bridge financing markdowns, offset by a gain on an equity method investment and higher payments.
  - Expenses up on structural and volume/revenue-related costs; provision is a net addition tied to loan growth (vs. prior-year release). Loans up ~10% YoY; credit quality strong.

- Asset & Wealth Management (AWM)
  - Q2 2022: Net income $1.0B (-13%); revenue $4.31B (+5%).
  - NII up strongly; noninterest revenue slightly down. Asset Management revenue down on investment valuation losses and lower performance fees, partly offset by higher management fees (fewer money market fee waivers). Global Private Bank revenue up on deposit/loan growth and improved margins, partly offset by lower placement fees.
  - Expenses up on structural, investment, and volume-related costs; small provision. Client assets $3.8T (-6%) and AUM $2.74T (-8%) driven by market declines, partially offset by net inflows; regional detail provided.

- Corporate segment (Treasury and CIO; Other Corporate)
  - Q2 2022: Net loss $174MM vs. $1.3B loss prior year; revenue $80MM vs. prior-year loss, driven by higher NII from rising rates and slower prepayments.
  - Noninterest revenue pressured by FX impacts and losses (including hedging costs) tied to international consumer initiatives; offset by gains on legacy private equity and other investments. Expenses lower on structural and legal costs, partly offset by investments in international consumer growth (Chase U.K., Nutmeg, C6 Bank).
  - Treasury & CIO securities portfolio composition and AFS-to-HTM transfers disclosed for capital/liquidity management.

- Credit and risk context
  - Across LOBs, 2022 reflects a shift from prior-year reserve releases to net additions to the allowance for credit losses due to macro outlook changes and loan growth, while net charge-offs remain low.

- Additional disclosures and metrics
  - Extensive segment-level tables for revenue/expense, provisions, ROE, balance sheets, headcount, business activity (e.g., digital users, card sales, payments volume), international splits, markets revenue composition, investment banking fee breakdowns, credit quality statistics, and AUC/AUM/client assets.

structure.title: Firmwide Risk Management
structure.heading: Firmwide Risk Management
structure.start_phrase: Risk is an inherent part of JPMorgan Chase’s business activities.
structure.summary:
The excerpt outlines JPMorgan Chase’s firmwide approach to risk management, emphasizing that risk is inherent across its businesses and must be managed to balance client, customer, and investor interests while safeguarding the Firm’s safety and soundness. Effective risk management is framed around three pillars: individual accountability for identifying and escalating risks; ownership of risk identification, assessment, data, and management within each line of business and Corporate; and strong firmwide risk governance structures. The Firm’s compensation practices are designed to reinforce prudent risk-taking, with disciplined governance, independent Board oversight, and explicit consideration of risk and control outcomes in performance evaluations and incentives. The risk governance and oversight framework focuses on understanding risk drivers, types, and impacts, and directs readers to detailed discussions in the 2021 Form 10-K. The document lists the key risk categories covered and where they are governed and overseen, including:
- Strategic risk
- Capital risk
- Liquidity risk
- Reputation risk
- Consumer credit risk
- Wholesale credit risk
- Investment portfolio risk
- Market risk
- Country risk
- Operational risk
- Compliance risk
- Conduct risk
- Legal risk
- Estimations and model risk

structure.title: Capital Risk Management
structure.heading: Capital Risk Management
structure.start_phrase: Capital risk is the risk the Firm has an insufficient level or composition of capital to support the Firm’s business activities and associated risks during normal economic environments and under stressed conditions.
structure.summary:
- Defines capital risk and points to related 10-K, 10-Q Note 21, and Pillar 3 disclosures.
- Basel III overview: explains Standardized vs Advanced RWA approaches; Firm’s Standardized risk-based ratios are currently more binding than Advanced. SLR requirement applies and is currently more binding than Standardized risk-based ratios.
- Key regulatory developments:
  - CECL capital transition: two-year delay expired 12/31/21; starting 1/1/22 the $2.9B CET1 benefit is being phased out 25% per year (remaining $2.2B at 6/30/22); parallel phaseout effects in Tier 2, adjusted average assets, and total leverage exposure.
  - Adoption of SA-CCR on 1/1/22 replacing CEM for derivatives exposure under both RWA frameworks and SLR: increased Standardized RWA by ~$40B (based on 12/31/21 exposures), reducing CET1 ratio ~30 bps; modest SLR leverage exposure decrease; Advanced RWA also rose but less.
- Risk-based and leverage capital metrics (6/30/22 vs 12/31/21):
  - CET1 capital $207.4B; Tier 1 $239.7B; Total capital (Std) $268.3B.
  - RWA: Standardized $1.705T; Advanced $1.613T.
  - Ratios: Standardized CET1 12.2% (down from 13.1%); Advanced CET1 11.2% (down from 12.9%).
  - Leverage: Tier 1 leverage 6.2%; SLR 5.3% (vs 5.0% requirement).
  - Target: Standardized CET1 ratio of 12.5% by end of 4Q22, reflecting an expected SCB increase.
- Capital components and rollforward:
  - Reconciliation from stockholders’ equity to CET1/Tier 1/Total capital, including deductions for goodwill/intangibles and inclusion of CECL transition benefit.
  - 1H22 drivers of CET1 change: net income, common dividends, share repurchases, AOCI losses (including cash flow hedges and DVA), other adjustments; CET1 down $6.5B to $207.4B; Tier 1 down $6.5B; Standardized Tier 2 roughly flat; Advanced Tier 2 down ~$2.0B.
- RWA rollforward (1H22):
  - Increases driven by SA-CCR adoption, portfolio growth/changes, market movements, and operational risk updates.
  - Standardized total RWA up to $1.705T; Advanced total RWA up to $1.613T.
- Supplementary leverage ratio details:
  - Presents components (Tier 1 capital, adjusted average assets, off-balance sheet exposures) and notes inclusion of SA-CCR from 1/1/22; Firm SLR at 5.3%.
- Line of business equity (allocated capital as of 6/30/22):
  - CCB $50B; CIB $103B; CB $25B; AWM $17B; Corporate $58.3B; total common equity $253.3B.
- Capital actions:
  - Common dividend $1.00 per share, subject to board approval.
  - New $30B share repurchase authorization effective 5/1/22; repurchases temporarily suspended due to expected higher SCB in 4Q22 and GSIB surcharge in 1Q23.
  - Reports quarterly and year-to-date repurchase amounts; preferred dividends disclosed.
- Capital planning and stress testing (CCAR 2022):
  - Indicative SCB increased to 4.0% (from 3.2%); expected Standardized CET1 requirement (including buffers) to 12.0% effective 10/1/22 through 9/30/23.
- Other capital requirements (TLAC/LTD):
  - Presents eligible external TLAC and eligible LTD amounts and surpluses versus RWA and total leverage exposure as of 6/30/22; Firm exceeds regulatory minimums.
- U.S. broker-dealer regulatory capital:
  - J.P. Morgan Securities net capital of ~$20.5B vs ~$6.0B minimum; subject to SEC/CFTC/FINRA/NFA rules.
- Non-U.S. subsidiary regulatory capital:
  - J.P. Morgan Securities plc (U.K.): regulated by PRA/FCA; subject to CRR; compliant with fully phased-in MREL as of 1/1/22; strong CET1 (21.9%) and total capital ratios (28.1%).
  - J.P. Morgan SE (EU): regulated by ECB and local authorities; compliant with MREL; CET1 18.2%; total capital ratio 29.1%.

structure.title: Liquidity Risk Management
structure.heading: Liquidity Risk Management
structure.start_phrase: Liquidity risk is the risk that the Firm will be unable to meet its contractual and contingent financial obligations as they arise or that it does not have the appropriate amount, composition and tenor of funding and liquidity to support its assets and liabilities.
structure.summary:
- Defines liquidity risk and points to JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K and U.S. LCR disclosures for fuller detail.
- Explains LCR and HQLA requirements: minimum 100% LCR at both the Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.; excess HQLA at the bank that is not transferable to non‑bank affiliates is excluded from Firm-level HQLA.
- Presents average LCR metrics for the three months ended June 30, 2022 (and prior periods):
  - Firm: HQLA $742B (eligible cash ~$634B; eligible securities ~$107B), net cash outflows ~$676B, LCR 110%, net excess eligible HQLA ~$65.7B.
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.: LCR 169%, net excess eligible HQLA ~$487.9B.
  - Notes that LCRs fluctuate with changes in eligible HQLA and estimated net cash outflows.
- Attributes the bank’s LCR decline in 2Q22 vs 1Q22 to lower HQLA from reduced cash due to loan growth and declines in the market value of HQLA‑eligible investment securities in Treasury and CIO.
- Details other liquidity sources: unencumbered marketable securities of ~$826B at 6/30/22 (down from ~$914B at 12/31/21, largely due to lower excess eligible HQLA at the bank); available borrowing capacity of ~$308B at FHLBs and the Federal Reserve discount window (not viewed as a primary liquidity source).
- States NSFR compliance: both the Firm and the bank met the 100% minimum NSFR at 6/30/22; public NSFR disclosure to begin semiannually in 2023.
- Describes funding strategy and sources: diversified mix of stable deposits, secured/unsecured market funding, and equity; deposits are the primary funding for the bank; non‑bank subsidiaries rely mainly on long‑term unsecured and short‑term secured borrowings; excess funding is managed by Treasury and CIO.
- Summarizes deposits by line of business and trends:
  - Period‑end Firm deposits ~$2.472T (6/30/22) vs ~$2.462T (12/31/21).
  - Deposits = 70% of total liabilities; loans‑to‑deposits ratio 45%.
  - Average deposits increased YoY in 2Q22 and 1H22 due to prior‑year government actions and CCB account growth; 2Q22 saw declines in some areas (e.g., CB non‑operating deposits migrating to higher‑yielding alternatives, higher consumer spending in CCB). Corporate increases reflect international consumer initiatives.
- Outlines non‑deposit funding mix and levels:
  - Short‑term secured funding (primarily repos) up vs year‑end due to higher secured financing of trading assets; balances fluctuate with client activity and portfolio management.
  - Short‑term unsecured funding (e.g., commercial paper) increased, driven by short‑term liquidity management.
  - Long‑term unsecured funding (senior notes, subordinated, structured notes), largely issued by the Parent Company to support bank and non‑bank needs and TLAC requirements; Parent advances proceeds to the IHC.
- Provides issuance and maturity activity:
  - Parent long‑term unsecured: 2Q22 issuance included $13B of U.S. senior notes; YTD 2022 senior note issuance ~$23.9B; structured notes issued at both parent and subsidiaries; maturities/redemptions detailed for senior and structured notes.
  - Secured long‑term activity modest: limited FHLB advance movements, minimal credit card securitization issuance in 2Q22.
- Discusses credit ratings: importance to funding cost/availability; potential impacts of downgrades are incorporated in liquidity risk metrics; lists current ratings (e.g., Parent: Moody’s A2/P‑1, S&P A‑/A‑2, Fitch AA‑/F1+; bank rated higher) and notes stable/positive outlooks.
- Introduces Credit and Investment Risk Management scope and references to deeper discussions (consumer, wholesale, investment portfolio risk).
- Presents a credit portfolio snapshot (as of 6/30/22 unless noted):
  - Total loans ~$1.104T (retained ~$1.052T; HFS ~$4.7B; at fair value ~$47.1B).
  - Derivative receivables ~$81.3B; receivables from customers ~$58.3B.
  - Total credit‑related assets ~$1.244T; lending‑related commitments ~$1.302T.
  - Nonperforming assets provided, with exclusions for government‑guaranteed items (e.g., FHA/VA and PPP).
  - Net protection via credit derivatives and credit‑related notes used in portfolio management; liquid collateral held against derivatives.
  - Credit performance: 2Q22 net charge‑offs $657M; average retained loans ~$$1.036T; net charge‑off rate 0.25% (vs 0.31% in 2Q21).

structure.title: Consumer Credit Portfolio
structure.heading: Consumer Credit Portfolio
structure.start_phrase:
The Firm’s retained consumer portfolio consists primarily of residential real estate loans, credit card loans, scored auto and 
business banking loans, as well as associated lending-related commitments.
structure.summary:
- Scope and focus: Describes JPMorgan Chase’s retained consumer credit portfolio—primarily prime residential real estate, credit card, scored auto, and business banking loans—and related lending commitments across CCB, AWM, CIB, and Corporate. Points to relevant 10‑Q/10‑K notes for policies and additional detail.

- Portfolio size and composition (as of June 30, 2022 vs. Dec 31, 2021):
  - Consumer excluding credit card exposure: $357.7B vs. $368.6B; nonaccrual loans declined to $4.67B from $5.35B.
  - Credit card exposure (loans plus commitments): $939.5B vs. $884.8B; card loans $165.5B vs. $154.3B; commitments $774.0B vs. $730.5B.
  - Total consumer credit portfolio exposure: $1.297T vs. $1.253T.
  - Notes on credit-related risk transfer: $1.56B of credit-related notes outstanding.

- Credit performance (charge-offs/recoveries):
  - Q2 2022 vs. Q2 2021 net charge-off rates (retained): residential real estate net recoveries (-0.12% vs. -0.15%), auto and other higher charge-offs (0.56% vs. 0.24%), total consumer ex-card slightly higher (0.04% vs. -0.04%), credit card improved (1.47% vs. 2.24%), total consumer improved (0.53% vs. 0.67%).
  - First half 2022 vs. 2021: similar themes; card charge-offs materially lower (1.42% vs. 2.60%); total consumer improved (0.52% vs. 0.80%).

- Consumer excluding credit card—portfolio analysis:
  - Overall: Loans decreased due to lower loans at fair value and “auto and other,” partially offset by higher retained residential real estate.
  - Residential real estate:
    - Predominantly prime mortgages and HELOCs.
    - Retained loans up on originations net of paydowns; nonaccruals down on improved credit.
    - Net recoveries lower in Q2 on reduced prepayments amid higher rates.
    - Loans at fair value down as Home Lending warehouse sales outpaced originations due to higher rates and lower CIB purchase activity; related nonaccruals down.
    - HELOCs outstanding $16.9B; includes $5.5B recast/modified and $5.5B interest‑only balloon HELOCs (mostly post‑2030 maturities); risk managed by line reductions/closures when credit deteriorates.
    - Interest‑only mortgages $34.4B (higher‑balance, higher‑income borrowers, mainly AWM); performance comparable to prime mortgages, minimal charge-offs.
    - Government‑insured/guaranteed mortgage exposure $1.16B; such loans generally excluded from nonaccrual due to guarantees.
    - Modified residential real estate with concessions (TDRs and certain PCD): retained $12.2B; nonaccrual within these $3.54B.
  - Auto and other:
    - Portfolio down primarily from PPP forgiveness in business banking; auto loans down on paydowns partially offset by originations.
    - Higher net charge-offs in 2022 driven by overdrafts and auto; prior year benefited from stimulus and payment assistance.
    - Scored auto net charge-off rates: Q2 2022 0.12% vs. -0.11% prior year; 1H 2022 0.15% vs. 0.00% prior year.

- Asset quality and nonperforming assets:
  - Nonperforming assets down to $4.83B from $5.48B; nonaccrual loans $4.67B (mostly residential real estate), plus $154M assets acquired in loan satisfactions.
  - Six‑month nonaccrual loan activity: additions $1.15B; reductions $1.83B (payments, charge-offs, returns to performing, liquidations); ending balance down $678M.

- Purchased credit deteriorated (PCD) loans (residential real estate):
  - Balance $12.35B; 30+ day delinquency ratio improved to 5.54% from 7.24%; nonaccruals $1.33B.
  - Net recoveries in Q2 2022; improved net charge-off/recovery rates vs. prior year.

- Credit card portfolio:
  - Loans up on higher consumer spending; delinquency rates stable (30+ days ~1.05%, 90+ days ~0.51%).
  - Net charge-offs decreased year over year; metrics supported by consumer financial strength.
  - Policy: credit card loans generally remain on accrual until charge-off; allowance covers uncollectible accrued interest/fees.
  - Credit card TDRs outstanding $827M, down from $1.0B.

- Key footnote themes:
  - Exclusions of government‑insured mortgages and SBA‑guaranteed PPP loans from nonaccrual measures.
  - COVID‑19 deferral program treatment for delinquency reporting.
  - The Firm can reduce/cancel certain revolving commitments per policy and law.

structure.title: Wholesale Credit Portfolio
structure.heading: Wholesale Credit Portfolio
structure.start_phrase:
In its wholesale businesses, the Firm is exposed to credit 
risk primarily through its underwriting, lending, market-
making, and hedging activities with and for clients and 
counterparties, as well as through various operating 
services (such as cash management and clearing activities), 
securities financing activities and cash placed with banks.
structure.summary:
- Scope and sources of risk: Describes the Firm’s wholesale credit risk across underwriting, lending, market-making, hedging, operating services, securities financing, and cash placed with banks; a portion of originations is retained while significant volumes are syndicated to manage concentrations.
- Portfolio coverage: Includes exposures in CIB, CB, AWM, Corporate, and certain risk-rated CCB exposures (business banking and auto dealer).
- 1H22 performance and trends: Credit performance remained strong with historically low charge-offs; nonperforming exposure decreased on lower lending-related commitments (mainly CIB), partly offset by higher nonperforming derivatives; Russia-related downgrades in 1Q22 with subsequent paydowns in 2Q22; retained loans rose $23.9B (CB and CIB up, AWM down).
- Size and composition (6/30/22 vs 12/31/21): Total wholesale credit portfolio $1.249T ($1.203T prior); loans $621.4B; derivative receivables $81.3B; receivables from customers $58.3B; lending-related commitments $487.5B; total nonperforming $3.4B (down from $3.6B). Liquid securities and cash collateral held against derivatives increased; net credit protection used in credit portfolio management decreased to $15.4B (from $18.7B).
- Maturity and ratings profile: Investment-grade share remains high—loans retained 72% IG; derivative receivables net of collateral 72% IG; lending-related commitments 68% IG. Total exposure net of liquid collateral rose to ~$1.229T.
- Industry concentrations and criticized exposure: Criticized exposure fell to $31.3B (2.7% of wholesale exposure) from $38.2B (3.5%), driven by net portfolio activity and upgrades, partly offset by downgrades; largest decreases in Consumer & Retail and TMT. Top industry exposures include Real Estate ($165.5B), Individuals & Individual Entities ($138.2B), Consumer & Retail ($119.3B), Asset Managers ($97.7B), TMT ($77.8B), Industrials ($71.7B), Healthcare ($57.7B), Banks & Finance ($55.9B), Oil & Gas ($46.5B), and Utilities.
- Deeper industry detail:
  - Real Estate: $165.5B total, $95.2B multifamily; criticized exposure down $913M to $4.3B; ~78% secured; unsecured ~76% IG.
  - Consumer & Retail: $119.3B; criticized down $2.9B to $6.9B; ~56% secured; unsecured ~77% IG.
  - Oil & Gas: $46.5B; E&P and Oilfield Services $27.4B; derivative receivables up on commodity price moves; criticized down $708M to $978M; ~48% secured; unsecured ~57% IG.
- Loans and credit quality:
  - Nonaccruals: Ending balance $2.49B; down $924M vs 6/30/21; activity driven by paydowns and upgrades in Real Estate and Oil & Gas, offset by Russia downgrades.
  - Net charge-offs: Remain very low; 1H22 wholesale NCOs $80M, NCO rate 0.03% (vs 0.02% 1H21).
- Commitments and customer receivables: Explains that contractual amounts overstate expected usage; margin loans to brokerage clients are collateralized and typically require no allowance; margin monitored via ongoing margining.
- Derivative contracts and collateral: Derivatives used by clients and the Firm; significant collateralization (about 87–88% of OTC trades under collateral agreements, excluding FX spot and cleared trades). Derivative receivables increased (FX and commodities); substantial liquid securities and other collateral held; exposure net of all collateral $59.8B with 72% IG.
- Credit portfolio management: Firm uses credit derivatives/credit-related notes to manage loan, commitment, and derivative counterparty exposures; net protection outstanding $15.4B (split ~$4.6B on loans/commitments and ~$10.8B on derivatives).
- Allowance for credit losses (ACL):
  - Level and change: ACL $20.0B at 6/30/22, up $1.3B since year-end (+$1.0B wholesale, +$311M consumer), driven by heavier weighting of adverse scenarios (inflation, tightening, geopolitical risks), modest macro deterioration, loan growth in Card and CB, and Russia-related downgrades.
  - Scenario framework: Five internally developed macro scenarios; adverse scenarios imply U.S. unemployment above 4% through 4Q23 and lower U.S. real GDP vs central case. Central case at 6/30/22: U.S. unemployment ~3.6–3.7%, YoY real GDP growth ~1.2–1.7% over forecast horizon.
  - Composition and ratios (6/30/22): Allowance for loan losses $17.75B (consumer $12.33B; wholesale $5.42B); allowance for lending-related commitments $2.22B (mostly wholesale); total ACL including securities $20.02B. Wholesale ALL/loans 0.93%; ALL/nonaccrual wholesale 260%; consolidated NCO rate 0.24% (1H22). Allocation by wholesale class: secured by real estate $1.53B, commercial & industrial $2.69B, other $1.20B.

structure.title: Investment Portfolio Risk Management
structure.heading: Investment Portfolio Risk Management
structure.start_phrase:
Investment portfolio risk is the risk associated with the loss 
of principal or a reduction in expected returns on 
investments arising from the investment securities portfolio 
or from principal investments.
structure.summary:
- Defines investment portfolio risk as potential loss of principal or reduced expected returns from the securities portfolio and principal investments; notes investments are generally long-term with no expectation of short-term realized gains.
- Describes the investment securities portfolio as predominantly held by Treasury and CIO for balance sheet and asset-liability management; risk centers on default of principal and interest but is mitigated by high-quality holdings.
- Provides portfolio metrics as of June 30, 2022: investment securities (net of allowance for credit losses) totaled $661.9 billion with an average AA+ credit rating (based on external ratings where available, otherwise internal ratings).
- References related sections for more detail: Corporate segment results and Note 9 (securities portfolio and internal ratings), Liquidity Risk Management (pages 50–54), and Market Risk Management (pages 75–79).
- Defines principal investments as largely privately-held ownership or junior capital instruments (including tax-oriented investments) made by dedicated investing businesses or within broader strategies; managed within LOBs and Corporate; excludes consolidated investments.
- Notes strategic evolution of principal investments, including commitments to underserved communities and minority-owned businesses.
- Reports carrying values of principal investments: total $33.3B at June 30, 2022 vs. $30.5B at Dec 31, 2021; breakdown—tax-oriented (alternative energy, affordable housing) $23.7B vs. $23.2B; private equity/debt/real assets $9.6B vs. $7.3B, including a 40% stake in C6 Bank.
- Points to the firm’s governance and oversight of Investment Portfolio Risk Management in JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K (page 132).

structure.title: Market Risk Management
structure.heading: Market Risk Management
structure.start_phrase:
Market risk is the risk associated with the effect of changes 
in market factors such as interest and foreign exchange 
rates, equity and commodity prices,
structure.summary:
- Defines market risk as exposure to changes in interest rates, FX rates, equity/commodity prices, credit spreads, and implied volatilities affecting assets and liabilities, and points to the firm’s 2021 Form 10-K for broader context on governance, measurement, monitoring, and business drivers.
- Notes inherent model uncertainty, especially under sudden or severe market shifts, and references the firm’s model risk management framework.
- Describes JPMorgan Chase’s single Value-at-Risk (VaR) framework:
  - Risk Management VaR: one-day holding period, expected tail-loss methodology approximating a 95% confidence level, aligned to day-to-day risk management.
  - Regulatory VaR: calculated per regulatory rules for Basel III market risk capital.
  - VaR models are periodically enhanced; changes can affect historical comparisons.
  - References to limitations of VaR and to Pillar 3 disclosures for regulatory components and backtesting.
- Presents firmwide Risk Management VaR results (95% confidence) for Q2 2022, Q1 2022, and Q2 2021, including:
  - CIB trading VaR by risk type (fixed income, FX, equities, commodities), Credit Portfolio VaR, business-line VaR (CCB, Corporate/other), and diversification benefits.
  - Key figures for Total VaR (average/min/max): 
    - Q2 2022: $54m / $41m / $71m
    - Q1 2022: $63m / $34m / $242m
    - Q2 2021: $43m / $35m / $52m
  - Explanatory notes:
    - Early 2022 removal of certain CVA credit risk components (and related hedges) from Credit Portfolio VaR due to elevated credit spreads; now captured in sensitivity-based measures.
    - Nickel market dislocation in March 2022 elevated Credit Portfolio VaR; exposures reduced by Q2 2022 but still elevated vs prior year.
    - Decrease in Corporate/other VaR tied to lower market values of a legacy publicly traded private equity position.
- Performance commentary:
  - Quarter over quarter: Average Total VaR down $9m in Q2 2022 vs Q1 2022, driven by reductions in nickel-related credit exposures, partly offset by higher fixed income volatility.
  - Year over year: Average Total VaR up $11m vs Q2 2021, largely from higher fixed income volatility and nickel-related effects in March 2022.
  - Daily VaR movements in March 2022 linked to nickel-related counterparty exposure in the Credit portfolio.
- VaR backtesting:
  - Compares daily Risk Management VaR to daily backtesting gains/losses (excluding intraday activity, fees, certain valuation adjustments, and NII), consistent with Basel III.
  - Expected frequency: ~5 exceptions per 100 trading days if volatility matches VaR’s historical window.
  - Results: 
    - Trailing 12 months ended June 30, 2022: backtesting gains on 148 of 261 days; 22 exceptions.
    - Q2 2022: backtesting gains on 37 of 65 days; 3 exceptions.
- Earnings-at-risk (interest rate risk in banking activities):
  - Methodology estimates 12-month net interest income sensitivity to rate scenarios (parallel, steepeners, flatteners), incorporating modeled prepayments, deposit betas, forecasted balance sheet, and FTP, but excluding management/client actions in response to rate shocks.
  - U.S. dollar sensitivities (change vs Dec 31, 2021 reflects higher baseline rates and balance sheet changes):
    - +100 bps parallel: $(1.4)b (was +$5.0b)
    - -100 bps parallel: $(1.0)b (not meaningful at 12/31/21)
    - Steeper (+100 bps long end): +$0.5b (was +$1.8b)
    - Flatter (+100 bps short end): $(1.8)b (was +$3.2b)
    - Commentary: +100 bps parallel/short-end hurts more due to faster liability repricing; +100 bps long-end and -100 bps parallel benefit more from asset repricing.
  - Non-U.S. dollar sensitivities:
    - +100 bps parallel: +$0.9b (was +$0.8b)
    - -100 bps parallel: $(0.8)b (not meaningful at 12/31/21)
    - Flatter (+100 bps short end): +$0.8b (unchanged)
    - Steeper scenario with long-end move not material.
- Other sensitivity-based measures (exposures not captured in VaR or earnings-at-risk) and their estimated impacts on net revenue, OCI, or noninterest expense:
  - Debt and equity positions:
    - Asset management seed capital, co-investments, and deferred comp (10% market decline).
    - Other debt/equity at fair value, including real estate-related FVO loans and private equity (10% market decline).
  - Credit/funding-related exposures:
    - Cross-currency basis risk on non-USD long-term debt hedges (1 bp basis tightening).
    - FX revaluation on non-USD LTD hedges (10% currency depreciation).
    - Derivatives funding valuation adjustment spread risk (1 bp increase).
    - CVA counterparty credit risk (10% spread widening) now reported here after removal from Credit Portfolio VaR.
    - DVA on FVO-elected liabilities and interest rate sensitivity tied to own credit spread (1 bp increase), with OCI vs net revenue distinctions.
- Emphasizes ongoing review and enhancement of models, measures, and simulations; acknowledges limitations of statistical and sensitivity-based metrics; and points to 10-K and Pillar 3 reports for further details.

structure.title: Country Risk Management
structure.heading: Country Risk Management
structure.start_phrase:
The Firm, through its LOBs and Corporate, may be exposed 
to country risk resulting from financial, economic, political 
or other significant developments which adversely affect 
the value of the Firm’s exposures related to a particular 
country or set of countries.
structure.summary:
- Focus: Overview of JPMorgan Chase’s internal country risk management practices, including monitoring, measurement, and reporting of exposures by country across lines of business and Corporate. The aim is to assess diversification relative to strategy and risk tolerance. Reference is made to the 2021 Form 10-K (pp. 141–142) for more detail.
- Sources of country risk: Exposures arise from lending and deposits, investing, and market‑making activities, both cross‑border and locally funded, and include government and private‑sector counterparties.
- Country attribution methodology: Exposures are assigned to the country where the largest share of a counterparty’s assets is located or revenue is derived, which may differ from domicile/incorporation. Reported exposure aggregates risk to an immediate default with zero recovery. Contingent/indirect exposures (e.g., clearing services, secondary exposure to collateral) are excluded. Assumptions are used for certain products (e.g., non‑linear or index), and different approaches could change reported amounts.
- Measurement framework:
  - Lending: total committed (funded and unfunded) net of allowance for credit losses and eligible cash/marketable securities collateral.
  - Deposits: cash balances with central and commercial banks.
  - Securities financing: receivable balance net of eligible collateral.
  - Debt and equity securities: fair value of long and short positions.
  - Derivative receivables: fair value net of eligible collateral.
  - Credit derivatives: net notional protection purchased/sold for the same reference entity, inclusive of derivative fair values, reflecting management view.
- Reporting differences: Internal country risk reporting differs from FFIEC regulatory reporting.
- Risk reporting and key observations:
  - Presents the top 20 non‑U.S. country exposures as of June 30, 2022, with comparisons to December 31, 2021; these represent 88% and 87% of total attributable non‑U.S. exposure, respectively.
  - Rankings are not an assessment of credit conditions; exposures fluctuate with client activity and market flows.
  - Notable changes: increase in Germany and decrease in the U.K. driven by shifts in cash placements at central banks due to balance sheet/liquidity management; decrease in Australia due to reduced cash at the central bank tied to client market‑making and lower client deposits amid rate hikes.
  - Russia exposure approximately $600 million as of June 30, 2022.
  - Category definitions: “Lending and deposits” includes loans, commitments (net of collateral and ACL), bank deposits, acceptances, other monetary assets, and letters of credit net of participations; excludes intraday/operational exposures. “Trading and investing” includes market‑making inventory, investment securities, and net counterparty exposures on derivatives and securities financing (including single‑name and index exposures by underlying country). “Other” is predominantly physical commodity inventory.
  - Note: December 31, 2021 country rankings are presented using the June 30, 2022 ordering.

structure.title: Operational Risk Management
structure.heading: Operational Risk Management
structure.start_phrase: Operational risk is the risk of an adverse outcome resulting from inadequate or failed internal processes or systems, human factors, or external events impacting the Firm’s processes or systems.
structure.summary: The excerpt defines operational risk as losses from failed processes, systems, people, or external events, encompassing compliance, conduct, legal, and model/estimation risks. It outlines how such risks can manifest (fraud, business disruptions, cyberattacks, employee misconduct, regulatory non-compliance, and third-party failures) and notes that management aims to keep these risks at appropriate levels given the firm’s business, financial position, and regulatory context. It references JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K (pages 143–149) for broader detail. The section highlights heightened operational risks from evolving sanctions related to the war in Ukraine and the firm’s added controls to manage sanctions compliance, including blocking or restricting payments. It describes the Firmwide Business Resiliency Program to prepare for and recover from disruptions such as pandemics, severe weather, infrastructure outages, third-party failures, cyberattacks, and terrorism through governance, training, planning, and testing. It also addresses elevated cybersecurity risk tied to potential retaliation for sanctions, noting enhanced threat monitoring and other measures, while acknowledging that absolute protection cannot be guaranteed.

structure.title: Critical Accounting Estimates Used by the Firm
structure.heading: Critical Accounting Estimates Used by the Firm
structure.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase ’s accounting policies and use of estimates are integral to understanding its reported results.
structure.summary:
The excerpt outlines JPMorgan Chase’s critical accounting estimates, governance, and key judgments:

- Estimation governance: The Firm emphasizes robust policies, controls, independent reviews, and consistency in applying estimation methods across businesses, with controlled processes for methodology changes.

- Allowance for credit losses (ACL): Management estimates expected losses over the remaining life of amortized-cost financial assets and certain off-balance sheet commitments, comprising:
  - Allowance for loan losses (scored and risk-rated portfolios)
  - Allowance for lending-related commitments
  - Allowance for credit losses on investment securities
  Key judgments include macroeconomic forecasts and their weighting, historical loss experience, risk characteristics and ratings, collateral valuation, and remaining life. An eight-quarter forecast uses hundreds of macroeconomic variables (MEVs); primary drivers vary by portfolio/geography.
  - Consumer key MEVs: U.S. unemployment, home price index (HPI), U.S. real GDP
  - Wholesale key MEVs: U.S. real GDP, unemployment, equity prices, credit spreads, oil prices, commercial real estate prices, HPI
  The Firm considers multiple scenarios (including central and relative adverse). Compared with the central scenario, the relative adverse scenario assumes higher unemployment (avg. +2.2%, peak +3.7% in 2Q23), lower GDP (roughly 2.9% lower at the end of the horizon; peak difference 5.8% in 2Q23), and lower HPI (peak difference 17.6% in 1Q24). Sensitivity of modeled losses (excluding offsetting qualitative effects) under the adverse vs. central scenario shows increases of about:
  - $0.6 billion for residential real estate loans and related commitments
  - $2.0 billion for credit card loans
  - $3.0 billion for wholesale loans and related commitments
  The Firm cautions that MEV impacts are interrelated and nonlinear, the allowance already reflects weighting to adverse scenarios, and portfolio/behavioral changes and qualitative adjustments can materially affect outcomes. Management deems ACL estimates reasonable as of June 30, 2022.

- Fair value measurements: A portion of assets and liabilities is carried at fair value on a recurring basis (e.g., derivatives, structured notes, certain securities financing) and nonrecurring basis (e.g., certain loans measured via collateral fair value).
  - As of June 30, 2022, total assets measured at fair value were $1,156.7 billion, including $24.0 billion of Level 3; Level 3 represented 0.6% of total Firm assets and 2.1% of fair value assets.
  - Notable Level 3 items include derivative receivables ($8.9 billion), mortgage servicing rights ($7.4 billion), and loans ($2.0 billion). Derivative receivables Level 3 amounts are shown without netting for classification transparency.
  Valuation requires significant judgment, especially for Level 3 instruments, including model selection and unobservable inputs (e.g., rates, credit curves, prepayments, defaults, volatilities, correlations, prices, FX). Management applies valuation adjustments for counterparty and Firm credit, funding, liquidity, unobservable parameters, and position size. Heightened volatility widens reasonable valuation ranges; alternative methods/assumptions could yield different fair values.

- Other critical estimates:
  - Credit card rewards liability: $10.6 billion at June 30, 2022 (up from $9.8 billion at December 31, 2021), recorded in accounts payable and other liabilities.
  - Income taxes: Significant assumptions, judgments, and interpretations.
  - Goodwill impairment: Significant valuation judgments; assessment performed as of June 30, 2022.
  - Litigation reserves: Significant estimates and judgments in establishing reserves.

structure.title: Accounting and Reporting Developments
structure.heading: Accounting and Reporting Developments
structure.start_phrase: •Provides optional expedients and exceptions to current accounting guidance when financial instruments, hedge accounting relationships, and other transactions are amended due to reference rate reform.
structure.summary:
- Section overview: Accounting and Reporting Developments outlining FASB standards adopted since January 1, 2021 and standards issued but not yet adopted.
- Adopted standard: Reference Rate Reform (issued March 2020; updated January 2021).
  - Optional expedients for contract modifications and hedge accounting to facilitate transition from reference rates (e.g., LIBOR), including treating certain amendments as modifications, permitting hedge term changes without termination, and a one-time transfer out of held-to-maturity.
  - January 2021 update allows derivatives modified for discounting/margining alignment to be accounted for as modifications.
  - Effective upon issuance; the firm elected certain expedients beginning Q3 2020 (discounting transition applied retrospectively); no material impact on Consolidated Financial Statements.
- Issued but not yet adopted (March 2022):
  - Derivatives and Hedging: Fair Value Hedging – Portfolio Layer Method
    - Expands portfolio hedging (including non-prepayable assets), clarifies eligible derivatives, and updates balance sheet presentation and disclosures.
    - Effective January 1, 2023; the firm is evaluating impact and adoption timing.
  - Financial Instruments – Credit Losses: Troubled Debt Restructurings and Vintage Disclosures
    - Eliminates TDR accounting/disclosure (including DCF requirement); requires disclosures for certain loan modifications to borrowers in financial difficulty and charge-offs by origination year.
    - Adoption may be prospective or modified retrospective with a retained earnings adjustment; effective January 1, 2023; early adoption permitted; the firm plans to adopt January 1, 2023 and is evaluating impact.
