- Consolidation policy: Financial statements include entities where the Firm has a controlling financial interest; intercompany balances/transactions are eliminated; client assets held in agency/fiduciary capacity are excluded from the balance sheet; control assessed via voting interest vs. variable interest entities; references Notes 1 and 14 of the 2021 Form 10-K for more detail.
- Offsetting assets and liabilities: Explains netting of derivative receivables/payables and related cash collateral, and netting for securities financing activities when legally enforceable master netting agreements exist; the Firm has elected to net where conditions are met; references the 2021 Form 10-K for further information.
- Note 2 – Fair value measurement: Directs to Note 2 of the 2021 Form 10-K for valuation methodologies, fair value measurements, and the fair value hierarchy.

nodes.title: Fair value measurement
nodes.heading: 7.2 Note 2 – Fair value measurement
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 2 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for a discussion of the Firm’s valuation methodologies for assets, liabilities and lending-related commitments measured at fair value and the fair value hierarchy.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and reference: Summarizes JPMorgan Chase’s fair value measurement disclosures, referencing Note 2 of the 2021 Form 10-K for valuation methodologies and the fair value hierarchy.

- Fair value hierarchy presentation: Provides detailed tables of assets and liabilities measured at fair value on a recurring basis by Level 1, Level 2, and Level 3, including derivative netting adjustments, as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021.

- Key totals:
  - June 30, 2022: Total assets at fair value $1,153,408 million; total liabilities at fair value $452,617 million; Level 3 assets $22,290 million; Level 3 liabilities $36,588 million.
  - December 31, 2021: Total assets at fair value $1,154,549 million; total liabilities at fair value $403,073 million; Level 3 assets $17,479 million; Level 3 liabilities $41,471 million.

- Major product categories covered:
  - Assets: Federal funds sold and securities purchased under resale agreements; securities borrowed; trading assets (debt instruments including MBS—U.S. GSE/government and nonagency residential/commercial, U.S. Treasury/GSE/government, municipals, CDs/BA/CP, non-U.S. government, corporate debt, loans, ABS; equity securities; physical commodities; other); derivative receivables by risk type (interest rate, credit, FX, equity, commodity) with netting; available-for-sale securities (MBS, U.S. Treasury/government, municipals, non-U.S. government, corporate debt, ABS); loans; mortgage servicing rights; other assets.
  - Liabilities: Deposits; repos and securities loaned/sold under repurchase agreements; short-term borrowings; trading liabilities (debt and equity instruments); derivative payables by risk type with netting; accounts payable and other liabilities; beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs; long-term debt.

- Derivative netting: Discloses gross derivative receivables and payables with significant netting adjustments under legally enforceable master netting agreements; notes that applying netting would also reduce reported Level 3 balances.

- Footnote highlights:
  - GSE obligations: U.S. GSE mortgage-related obligations included in totals ($70.0 billion at 6/30/22; $73.9 billion at 12/31/21).
  - Physical commodities: Inventories generally recorded at lower of cost or net realizable value, which approximates fair value; fair value hedge accounting can align carrying values with fair value; all such inventories included for consistency.
  - Trading long/short presentation: Debt and equity trading balances are shown net of identical long and short positions.
  - Investments measured using NAV practical expedient: Excluded from hierarchy; fair values of $856 million (6/30/22) and $801 million (12/31/21), split between trading assets and other assets.
  - Loans at fair value: Include specified amounts of residential and commercial first‑lien mortgages; identifies conforming mortgages originated for sale to U.S. GSEs.
  - Derivatives netting policy: Election to net derivatives and related cash collateral where legally enforceable.

- Level 3 valuations overview:
  - Describes forthcoming table (not shown here) of primary Level 3 instruments, valuation techniques, significant unobservable inputs, and input ranges/weighted averages.
  - Notes Level 3 instruments often include observable components; risks of observable portions are managed with Level 1/2 instruments.
  - Clarifies that input ranges and averages reflect instrument characteristics and portfolio mix, not input uncertainty; these metrics vary across periods and parameters (illustrated with options and implied volatility differences).

nodes.title: Level 3 valuations
nodes.heading: 7.2.a Level 3 valuations
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 2 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for further information on the Firm’s valuation process and a detailed discussion of the determination of fair value for individual financial instruments.
nodes.summary:
- Explains footnotes related to fair value disclosures:
  - Long positions are reduced by identical short positions when presenting balances.
  - Investments measured using NAV practical expedient (e.g., certain hedge funds, private equity, real estate and other funds) are excluded from the fair value hierarchy; these totaled $856 million at June 30, 2022 and $801 million at December 31, 2021, including trading assets of $45 million and $51 million, and other assets of $811 million and $750 million, respectively.
  - Loan balances included $13.5 billion and $26.2 billion of residential first-lien mortgages and $7.7 billion and $8.2 billion of commercial first-lien mortgages at June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021, respectively; residential loans included conforming mortgages intended for sale to U.S. GSEs/government agencies of $4.4 billion and $13.6 billion, respectively.
  - Under U.S. GAAP, derivative receivables/payables and related cash collateral are netted when a legally enforceable master netting agreement exists; level 3 balances would be reduced if such netting were applied, including the benefit of cash collateral.

- Outlines the firm’s approach to level 3 valuations:
  - References JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K (Note 2) for detailed valuation processes and fair value determinations.
  - Describes a table (not shown) that lists primary level 3 instruments, valuation techniques, significant unobservable inputs, ranges for those inputs, and weighted or arithmetic averages.
  - Notes that level 3 instruments often contain observable components; level 1/2 inputs are excluded from the table, and risks of observable components are managed with level 1 or 2 positions.
  - Clarifies that input ranges and averages reflect instrument characteristics and portfolio mix, not input uncertainty or the reasonableness of estimates; these metrics vary over time and by parameter.

nodes.title: Level 3 inputs(a) June 30, 2022
nodes.heading: 7.2.b Level 3 inputs(a) June 30, 2022
nodes.start_phrase: (a)The categories presented in the table have been aggregated based upon the product type, which may differ from their classification on the Consolidated balance sheets.
nodes.summary:
- Discloses Level 3 fair value measurements as of June 30, 2022, detailing for each product/instrument the fair value (in millions), principal valuation technique (discounted cash flows, market comparables, option pricing), and significant unobservable inputs with their ranges and average values.
- Instruments covered: 
  - Residential mortgage-backed securities and loans ($1,731)
  - Commercial mortgage-backed securities and loans ($418)
  - Corporate debt securities ($760)
  - Loans ($1,596)
  - Non-U.S. government debt securities ($205)
  - Net interest rate derivatives ($415 option pricing; $5 discounted cash flows)
  - Net credit derivatives ($227 discounted cash flows; $22 market comparables)
  - Net foreign exchange derivatives ($338 option pricing; $(93) discounted cash flows)
  - Net equity derivatives ($(1,234) option pricing)
  - Net commodity derivatives ($26)
  - Mortgage servicing rights (MSRs) ($7,439; inputs referenced to Note 14)
  - Long-term debt, short-term borrowings, and deposits ($26,284 option pricing; $926 discounted cash flows), including structured notes with embedded derivatives
  - Other Level 3 assets and liabilities, net ($1,057)
- Key unobservable inputs include: yields; prepayment speeds; conditional default rates; loss severity; security/loan prices; interest rate and spread volatilities; interest rate curve; multiple correlations (interest rate, FX, equity, cross-asset); credit correlation, credit spreads, and recovery rates; forward equity price; commodity forwards (oil and industrial metals), volatilities, and correlations. Input ranges and averages are presented (weighted averages generally; arithmetic averages for derivative-related inputs).
- Footnotes clarify:
  - Categories are aggregated by product type and may differ from Consolidated balance sheet classifications; not all listed inputs apply to every instrument within a technique.
  - Composition details for RMBS/CMBS/loans (GSE/government agency vs nonagency; trading vs non-trading).
  - Structured notes’ fair value includes embedded derivative features; significant unobservable inputs align with those for derivative receivables.
  - “Price” inputs assume $100 par; forward equity price is a percentage of current equity price.
  - Other Level 3 assets include equity securities valued with internal techniques (e.g., EBITDA multiples, comparable analysis); remaining Level 3 items are individually and in aggregate insignificant.

nodes.title: Changes in and ranges of unobservable inputs
nodes.heading: 7.2.c Changes in and ranges of unobservable inputs
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 2 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K f or a discussion of the impact on fair value of changes in unobservable inputs and the relationships between unobservable inputs as well as a description of attributes of the underlying instruments and external market factors that affect the range of inputs used in the valuation of the Firm’s positions.
nodes.summary:
- Discusses changes in and ranges of unobservable inputs used in fair value measurements, with a reference to Note 2 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for detailed discussion of their impact, interrelationships, instrument attributes, and external market factors influencing input ranges.
- Presents rollforward information (including changes in fair value) for Level 3 recurring fair value measurements on the Consolidated balance sheets for the three- and six-month periods ended June 30, 2022 and 2021.
- Clarifies that classification into Level 3 is based on the significance of unobservable inputs, though Level 3 instruments often also contain observable components.
- Notes that gains and losses shown include effects from observable factors within the valuation methodologies.
- Explains that the firm manages risks of the observable components of Level 3 instruments using Level 1 and Level 2 securities and derivatives, which are not included in the rollforward tables; therefore, reported gains/losses do not reflect the effects of these risk management activities.

nodes.title: Changes in level 3 recurring fair value measurements
nodes.heading: 7.2.d Changes in level 3 recurring fair value measurements
nodes.start_phrase: The following tables include a rollforward of the Consolidated balance sheets amounts (including changes in fair value) for financial instruments classified by the Firm within level 3 of the fair value hierarchy for the three and six months ended J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2 and 2021 .
nodes.summary:
- Scope and purpose: The excerpt details JPMorgan Chase’s Level 3 fair value measurements (instruments valued using significant unobservable inputs). It references Note 2 of the 2021 Form 10-K for discussion of how unobservable inputs and market factors affect fair value and the ranges/relationships of those inputs.

- Rollforward disclosures: Comprehensive tables present Level 3 rollforwards for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021, showing:
  - Beginning fair value, total realized/unrealized gains and losses, transfers into/out of Level 3, purchases/sales/issuances/settlements, ending fair value, and the change in unrealized gains/losses on instruments still held at period-end.
  - Asset categories: trading assets (debt instruments including MBS, U.S. states/municipal, non-U.S. government, corporate, loans, ABS; equity securities; physical commodities; other), net derivative receivables by risk class (interest rate, credit, FX, equity, commodity), available-for-sale securities, loans, mortgage servicing rights (MSRs), and other assets.
  - Liability categories: deposits, short-term borrowings, trading liabilities, accounts payable and other liabilities, long-term debt, and beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs (none reported in these periods).

- Presentation and measurement notes:
  - Level 3 instruments can include observable components; gains/losses reflect both observable and unobservable factors.
  - Related Level 1/Level 2 risk management hedges are excluded from the tables, so reported gains/losses do not reflect hedge effects.
  - Level 3 derivatives are presented on a net basis.
  - Income statement/OCI classification: principal transactions revenue for most changes; mortgage-related items (certain CCB loans/commitments and MSRs) in mortgage fees and related income; AFS unrealized changes in OCI; DVA on fair value option liabilities recognized in OCI (realized in principal transactions).
  - Operational notes: loan originations included in purchases; settlements include maturities, repayments, modifications, VIE deconsolidations, and other items.

- Magnitude of Level 3 positions:
  - Level 3 assets were 2% of total firm assets at fair value at both June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021.
  - Level 3 liabilities were 8% and 10% of total firm liabilities at fair value at June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021, respectively.

- Key changes in Level 3 assets (narrative analysis):
  - Level 3 assets totaled $22.3 billion at June 30, 2022, up $329 million from March 31, 2022 and up $4.8 billion from December 31, 2021.
  - Six-month 2022 drivers: approximately $1.6 billion increase in gross derivative receivables (gains and purchases) and a $1.9 billion increase in MSRs.

- Transfers between fair value hierarchy levels (based on changing observability/significance of inputs; assumed at the start of the quarter):
  - Three months ended June 30, 2022: no significant transfers from Level 2 into Level 3; significant transfers from Level 3 into Level 2 included about $930 million of gross interest rate derivative receivables due to increased observability.
  - Six months ended June 30, 2022: significant transfers into Level 3 included about $1.6 billion of total debt and equity instruments (notably $959 million of equity securities due to restricted market access) and $1.3 billion of gross equity derivative payables; significant transfers out of Level 3 included about $965 million of gross interest rate derivative receivables and $920 million and $1.4 billion of gross equity derivative receivables and payables, respectively, due to increased observability.
  - 2021 comparisons: no significant transfers from Level 2 into Level 3 in Q2 or first half; transfers out of Level 3 included in Q2 2021 about $1.0 billion of gross equity derivative receivables; for the first half of 2021, about $800 million of total debt and equity instruments (largely trading loans) and $1.3 billion and $1.1 billion of gross equity derivative receivables and payables, respectively.

- Additional footnote highlights:
  - AFS securities realized gains/losses recognized in investment securities gains/losses; unrealized OCI impacts were immaterial in 2021 and small in 2022.
  - DVA-related realized results were not material in the periods; unrealized DVA recognized in OCI showed gains in 2022 versus small changes in 2021.

nodes.title: Level 3 analysis
nodes.heading: 7.2.e Level 3 analysis
nodes.start_phrase: The following describes significant changes to level 3 assets since December 31, 2021, for those items measured at fair value on a recurring basis.
nodes.summary:
- Presentation and accounting notes:
  - Most fair value changes are reported in principal transactions revenue, except for CCB mortgage loans and lending-related commitments originated with intent to sell, and mortgage loan purchase commitments, which are reported in mortgage fees and related income.
  - AFS securities: realized gains/losses are in investment securities gains/losses; unrealized gains/losses are in OCI. No realized gains/losses in income for the three or six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021. Unrealized OCI impact: $(19) million (Q2 2022) vs $0 (Q2 2021); $8 million (H1 2022) vs $0 (H1 2021).
  - MSR fair value changes are reported in mortgage fees and related income.
  - DVA on fair value option liabilities: realized effects (in principal transactions revenue) were not material for Q2 and H1 in both 2022 and 2021; unrealized effects recorded in OCI were $(344) million (Q2 2022) vs $5 million (Q2 2021) and $(574) million (H1 2022) vs $(17) million (H1 2021).
  - Loan originations are included in purchases.
  - “Other changes” include maturities, partial/full repayments, modifications, VIE deconsolidations, and other items.

- Level 3 analysis (recurring fair value):
  - Level 3 assets totaled $22.3 billion at June 30, 2022, up $329 million from March 31, 2022 and up $4.8 billion from December 31, 2021.
  - Six-month drivers to June 30, 2022:
    - $1.6 billion increase in gross derivative receivables (gains and purchases, largely offset by net transfers).
    - $1.9 billion increase in MSRs.

- Transfers between fair value hierarchy levels (based on changes in observability/significance of inputs; assumed at the start of the quarter):
  - Three months ended June 30, 2022:
    - No significant transfers from Level 2 to Level 3.
    - From Level 3 to Level 2: $930 million of gross interest rate derivative receivables (greater input observability; reduced unobservable significance).
  - Six months ended June 30, 2022:
    - From Level 2 to Level 3:
      - $1.6 billion of total debt and equity instruments, driven largely by $959 million of equity securities due to decreased observability/restricted market access.
      - $1.3 billion of gross equity derivative payables (decreased observability; increased unobservable input significance).
    - From Level 3 to Level 2:
      - $965 million of gross interest rate derivative receivables.
      - $920 million of gross equity derivative receivables and $1.4 billion of gross equity derivative payables (all due to increased observability/reduced unobservable input significance).
  - 2021 comparatives:
    - No significant Level 2 to Level 3 transfers in Q2 or H1 2021.
    - Q2 2021: From Level 3 to Level 2, $1.0 billion of gross equity derivative receivables.
    - H1 2021: From Level 3 to Level 2, $800 million of total debt and equity instruments (largely trading loans), plus $1.3 billion of gross equity derivative receivables and $1.1 billion of gross equity derivative payables.

nodes.title: Transfers between levels for instruments carried at fair value on a recurring basis
nodes.heading: 7.2.f Transfers between levels for instruments carried at fair value on a recurring basis
nodes.start_phrase: For the three months ended J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2, there were no significant transfers from level 2 into level 3.
nodes.summary:
- Clarifies income statement classification for fair value changes:
  - Most fair value changes are reported in principal transactions revenue, except CCB mortgage loans and lending-related commitments originated with intent to sell, and mortgage loan purchase commitments, which are in mortgage fees and related income.
  - AFS securities: realized gains/losses go to investment securities gains/(losses); unrealized gains/losses go to OCI. No realized gains/losses for the three or six months ended June 30, 2022 or 2021. Unrealized OCI impact: $(19) million (Q2’22) vs $0 (Q2’21); $8 million (6M’22) vs $0 (6M’21).
  - MSR fair value changes are reported in mortgage fees and related income.
  - DVA on fair value option liabilities: realized effects in principal transactions revenue (not material for Q2 and 6M of 2022 and 2021); unrealized effects in OCI of $(344) million (Q2’22) vs $5 million (Q2’21) and $(574) million (6M’22) vs $(17) million (6M’21).
  - Loan originations are included in purchases.
  - Other changes include maturities, repayments, modifications, VIE deconsolidations, and miscellaneous items.

- Level 3 assets (recurring fair value) overview:
  - Level 3 assets totaled $22.3 billion at June 30, 2022, up $329 million from March 31, 2022, and up $4.8 billion from December 31, 2021.
  - 6M’22 increase primarily driven by:
    - $1.6 billion rise in gross derivative receivables (gains and purchases, largely offset by net transfers).
    - $1.9 billion increase in MSRs. References provided to Note 14 and to nonrecurring fair value disclosures.

- Transfers between Level 2 and Level 3 (recurring fair value):
  - Q2’22:
    - No significant transfers from Level 2 to Level 3.
    - Transfers from Level 3 to Level 2: $930 million of gross interest rate derivative receivables due to increased observability and reduced reliance on unobservable inputs.
  - 6M’22:
    - Transfers from Level 2 to Level 3: $1.6 billion of total debt and equity instruments (including $959 million of equity securities) due to decreased observability, predominantly from restricted access to certain markets; and $1.3 billion of gross equity derivative payables due to decreased observability and increased significance of unobservable inputs.
    - Transfers from Level 3 to Level 2: $965 million of gross interest rate derivative receivables, and $920 million (receivables) and $1.4 billion (payables) of gross equity derivatives, all due to increased observability and reduced significance of unobservable inputs.
  - 2021 comparatives:
    - No significant transfers from Level 2 to Level 3 in Q2 or 6M’21.
    - Q2’21: $1.0 billion of gross equity derivative receivables moved from Level 3 to Level 2.
    - 6M’21: $800 million of total debt and equity instruments (largely trading loans) and $1.3 billion/$1.1 billion of gross equity derivative receivables/payables transferred from Level 3 to Level 2 due to increased observability.
  - Policy note: Transfers reflect changes in observability/significance of valuation inputs and are assumed to occur at the beginning of the reporting quarter.

nodes.title: Gains and losses
nodes.heading: 7.2.g Gains and losses
nodes.start_phrase: The following describes significant components of total realized/unrealized gains/(losses) for instruments measured at fair value on a recurring basis for the periods indicated.
nodes.summary:
- Overview: Presents significant components of realized/unrealized gains and losses for instruments measured at fair value on a recurring basis, excluding effects of the Firm’s risk management activities for Level 1 and Level 2 instruments. References Level 3 rollforward tables (pp. 99–104).

- Three months ended June 30, 2022:
  - Assets: $3.4 billion net gains, driven by net equity derivative receivables (market movements) and mortgage servicing rights (MSRs) from lower prepayment speeds due to higher rates.

- Three months ended June 30, 2021:
  - Assets: $1.3 billion net losses, from net equity derivative receivables (market movements) and MSRs reflecting faster prepayment speeds on lower rates.
  - Liabilities: $468 million net losses, from long-term debt losses partly offset by gains in short-term borrowings, due to market movements.

- Six months ended June 30, 2022:
  - Assets: $5.5 billion net gains, mainly from net equity derivative receivables (market movements) and MSRs due to lower prepayment speeds on higher rates.
  - Liabilities: $5.0 billion net gains, primarily from long-term debt due to market movements.

- Six months ended June 30, 2021:
  - Assets: $282 million net losses, driven by losses in net derivative receivables (market movements) largely offset by MSR gains from lower prepayment speeds on higher rates. Reference to Note 14 for MSRs.

- Credit and funding adjustments — derivatives: Discloses CVA and FVA impacts on principal transactions revenue (excluding hedges). FVA includes the Firm’s own credit quality at inception and changes over time.

  - Six months ended June 30: 2022 total loss $(424) million (Loans $(91) million; Other assets $(45) million; Liabilities $(288) million) vs. 2021 total gain $67 million.
  - Measurement alternative impacts within Other assets: $(387) million (Q2 2022) vs. $102 million (Q2 2021); $(29) million (H1 2022) vs. $107 million (H1 2021).
- Reference: Note 11 for additional information on collateral-dependent loan measurement.

nodes.title: Equity securities without readily determinable fair values
nodes.heading: 7.2.k Equity securities without readily determinable fair values
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm measures certain equity securities without readily determinable fair values at cost less impairment (if any), plus or minus observable price changes from an identical or similar investment of the same issuer (i.e., measurement alternative), with such changes recognized in other income.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Equity securities without readily determinable fair values measured under the ASC 321 measurement alternative (cost minus impairment, plus/minus observable price changes in identical/similar investments of the same issuer), with changes recognized in other income.
- Valuation approach: The Firm may adjust observable transaction prices to reflect differences in rights/obligations and to align with its valuation techniques for private equity direct investments. Securities with observable price changes are included in nonrecurring fair value disclosures.
- Balances:
  - Carrying value in other assets at June 30: $4.196 billion (2022) vs. $2.798 billion (2021).
  - Carrying value at December 31, 2021: $3.6 billion (reflects cumulative purchases, sales, and remeasurement changes).
- Period changes:
  - Upward carrying value changes: $76 million (Q2 2022) vs. $109 million (Q2 2021); $445 million (H1 2022) vs. $116 million (H1 2021).
  - Downward carrying value changes/impairments: $(463) million (Q2 2022) vs. $(7) million (Q2 2021); $(474) million (H1 2022) vs. $(9) million (H1 2021).
- Cumulative since January 1, 2018:
  - Upward carrying value changes: $1.5 billion.
  - Downward carrying value changes/impairments: $(844) million.
- Notable holding: Approximately 40 million Visa Class B common shares held at a nominal carrying value; subject to transfer restrictions; convertible into Visa Class A shares upon resolution of certain litigation. The conversion rate was 1.6059 as of June 30, 2022 and may be adjusted by Visa depending on litigation developments.

nodes.title: Additional disclosures about the fair value of financial instruments that are not carried on the Consolidated balance sheets at fair value
nodes.heading: 7.2.l Additional disclosures about the fair value of financial instruments that are not carried on the Consolidated balance sheets at fair value
nodes.start_phrase: The following table presents, by fair value hierarchy classification, the carrying values and estimated fair values at J u n e 3 0 , 2022 , and D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 1, of financial assets and liabilities, excluding financial instruments that are carried at fair value on a recurring basis, and their classification within the fair value hierarchy.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose: Additional disclosures on the fair value of financial instruments not carried at fair value on the Consolidated balance sheets.
- Scope and presentation: A table shows, as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021, the carrying amounts and estimated fair values of selected financial assets and liabilities, categorized by the fair value hierarchy (Levels 1, 2, and 3).
- Assets covered: Cash and due from banks; deposits with banks; accrued interest and accounts receivable; federal funds sold and securities purchased under resale agreements; securities borrowed; investment securities held-to-maturity (mix of Level 1 and Level 2); loans net of allowance (significant Level 3 component); and other assets.
- Liabilities covered: Deposits; federal funds purchased and securities loaned or sold under repurchase agreements; short‑term borrowings; accounts payable and other liabilities (includes a Level 3 component); beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs; and long‑term debt (primarily Level 2 with a small Level 3 portion).
- Key observations: Differences between carrying values and estimated fair values are presented, with notable gaps for held‑to‑maturity securities and loans; deposits and short‑term instruments generally approximate carrying values.
- Valuation methodology for loans: Fair value primarily estimated via discounted cash flow models incorporating loan characteristics and key inputs such as expected lifetime credit losses, interest rates, prepayment rates, and market spreads; certain loans valued based on collateral. Carrying value reflects the allowance for loan losses; differences versus fair value largely reflect changes in market rates, credit spreads, and liquidity premiums.
- Lending-related commitments: Most are not carried at fair value. The table discloses carrying value and estimated fair value for wholesale lending‑related commitments (classified in Level 3), with fair values exceeding carrying values at both dates. Disclosures exclude the guarantee liability and offsetting asset recognized at inception and include the wholesale allowance for lending‑related commitments.
- Consumer commitments: The Firm does not estimate fair value for consumer off‑balance sheet lending‑related commitments because they can typically be reduced or canceled; a 2021 Form 10‑K reference is provided for further detail.

nodes.title: Note 3 – Fair value option
nodes.heading: 7.3 Note 3 – Fair value option
nodes.start_phrase: The fair value option provides an option to elect fair value for selected financial assets, fina ncial liabilities, unrecognized firm commitments, and written loan commitments.
nodes.summary:
- Topic: Note 3 – Fair value option (FVO) describing the firm’s election to measure certain financial instruments at fair value.
- Purpose of FVO: To reduce income statement volatility from mixed measurement bases (accrual vs. fair value) and to align accounting with how instruments are risk-managed and managed on a fair value basis.
- Scope of election: Applies selectively to
  - Loans tied to securitization warehousing, subject to bifurcation, or otherwise managed on a fair value basis, including lending-related commitments
  - Certain securities financing agreements
  - Owned beneficial interests in securitized financial assets with embedded credit derivatives (that would otherwise require separate derivative accounting)
  - Structured notes and other hybrid instruments with embedded derivatives, issued or transacted in client-driven activities
  - Certain long-term beneficial interests issued by CIB’s consolidated securitization trusts when underlying assets are at fair value
- Earnings impact disclosure: Provides a table of changes in fair value recognized in the Consolidated statements of income for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021, limited to instruments for which FVO was elected; related risk management instruments (already at fair value) are excluded.
- Presentation detail: Changes in fair value are split between “Principal transactions” and “All other income,” with separate disclosure of instrument-specific credit risk vs. other fair value changes for loans (including loans reported as trading assets).
- Key categories shown (example for the three months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021): federal funds and resale agreements, securities borrowed, trading assets (debt and equity), loans (credit risk and other changes), other assets, deposits, repos/reverse repos, short-term borrowings, trading liabilities, beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs (no change shown), other liabilities, and long-term debt.
- Notable figures in the excerpt: 2022 Q2 long-term debt shows a significant positive fair value change; deposits and short-term borrowings show gains; several asset categories show losses; 2021 Q2 shows a large negative change in long-term debt.
- Footnote indicators (a–f) appear in the table referencing classification details, but their full explanations are not included in the excerpt.

nodes.title: Changes in fair value under the fair value option election
nodes.heading: 7.3.a Changes in fair value under the fair value option election
nodes.start_phrase: The following table presents the changes in fair value included in the Consolidated statements of income for the three and six months ended J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2 and 2021 , for items for which the fair value option was elected.
nodes.summary:
- Note 3 explains the firm’s use of the fair value option (FVO), which allows election of fair value measurement for selected financial assets and liabilities, unrecognized firm commitments, and written loan commitments.
- Rationale for electing FVO: reduce income-statement volatility from mixed measurement bases and align accounting with risk management and how certain instruments are managed (on a fair value basis).
- Instruments for which FVO is elected include:
  - Loans purchased/originated for securitization warehousing, subject to bifurcation, or managed on a fair value basis (including lending-related commitments)
  - Certain securities financing agreements
  - Owned beneficial interests in securitized financial assets with embedded credit derivatives
  - Structured notes and other hybrid instruments with embedded derivatives issued/transacted for client-driven activities
  - Certain long-term beneficial interests issued by CIB’s consolidated securitization trusts where underlying assets are at fair value
- The note presents changes in fair value recognized in the income statement for FVO-elected items (excluding related risk management instruments) for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021, split between principal transactions and all other income.
- Key period comparisons:
  - Three months ended June 30, 2022 vs 2021:
    - Long-term debt (predominantly structured notes): gain of approx. $5.4B vs loss of approx. $2.2B
    - Loans (other changes in fair value): loss of approx. $0.8B vs gain of approx. $0.9B
    - Deposits: gain of approx. $0.4B vs loss of approx. $0.3B
    - Short-term borrowings: gain of approx. $0.5B vs loss of approx. $0.5B
    - Trading assets (debt/equity, excl. loans): loss of approx. $1.3B vs gain of approx. $0.4B
    - Securities financing (federal funds sold/resale; securities borrowed): losses
  - Six months ended June 30, 2022 vs 2021:
    - Long-term debt: gain of approx. $9.4B vs loss of approx. $0.9B
    - Loans (other changes in fair value): loss of approx. $2.0B vs gain of approx. $1.0B
    - Deposits: gain of approx. $0.8B vs loss of approx. $0.1B
    - Short-term borrowings: gain of approx. $0.8B vs loss of approx. $0.6B
    - Trading assets (debt/equity, excl. loans): loss of approx. $0.9B vs gain of approx. $1.1B
- Instrument-specific credit risk (own-credit/DVA) and classification details:
  - For liabilities under FVO, unrealized gains/losses from instrument-specific credit risk are recorded in OCI; realized amounts are in principal transactions (realized DVA not material in Q2; six months was approximately $(9)M in 2022 and $(2)M in 2021).
  - Certain gains/losses are presented in mortgage fees and related income or other income, as applicable.
  - Reported changes in fair value exclude contractual interest (reported in interest income/expense).
  - Related risk management instruments used to hedge structured notes and other exposures are excluded from the table.
  - Prior-period amounts were revised to conform to current presentation.
- Minimal or no activity reported for beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs during the periods shown.

nodes.title: Difference between aggregate fair value and aggregate remaining contractual principal balance outstanding
nodes.heading: 7.3.b Difference between aggregate fair value and aggregate remaining contractual principal balance outstanding
nodes.start_phrase: The following table reflects the difference between the aggregate fair value and the aggregate remaining contractual principal balance outstanding as of J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2, and D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 1, for loans, long-term debt and long-term beneficial interests for which the fair value option has been elected.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt presents a fair value option disclosure comparing aggregate fair value to aggregate remaining contractual principal outstanding for loans, long-term debt, and long-term beneficial interests as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021. It shows:
- Loans: Total contractual principal of $60.3 billion vs fair value of $54.9 billion at 6/30/22, reflecting fair value $5.4 billion below principal (vs $3.9 billion below at 12/31/21). Breakdowns include nonaccrual loans (notably large discounts on loans reported as trading assets), government-guaranteed loans 90+ days past due (small discounts and excluded from nonaccrual), and all other performing loans (trading assets at a discount; other loans near par in 2021 but at a discount in 2022).
- Long-term debt: Principal-protected notes show fair value $8.3 billion below contractual principal at 6/30/22 (vs $2.2 billion below at 12/31/21). Nonprincipal-protected structured notes report fair value only (no applicable contractual principal), with fair values of $38.5 billion (2022) and $41.1 billion (2021). Total long-term debt fair value was $66.1 billion (2022) and $74.9 billion (2021); contractual principal totals are not applicable due to the presence of nonprincipal-protected notes.
- Long-term beneficial interests: Only nonprincipal-protected amounts are presented, with fair values of $5 million (2022) and $12 million (2021); contractual principal is not applicable.
- Footnotes clarify that government-guaranteed 90+ day past due loans are excluded from nonaccrual; there were no performing loans 90+ days past due at either date; nonprincipal-protected instruments do not obligate return of stated principal; and principal amounts for zero-coupon/discount notes reflect the maturity or next call date amount.
- Off-balance sheet: Lending-related commitments under the fair value option totaled $10.0 billion (fair value $30 million) at 6/30/22 and $11.9 billion (fair value $10 million) at 12/31/21.

nodes.title: Structured note products by balance sheet classification and risk component
nodes.heading: 7.3.c Structured note products by balance sheet classification and risk component
nodes.start_phrase: The following table presents the fair value of structured notes, by balance sheet classification and the primary risk type.
nodes.summary: The excerpt presents a table of the fair value of structured notes by balance sheet classification (long-term debt, short-term borrowings, deposits) and primary risk exposure (interest rate, credit, foreign exchange, equity, commodity) at June 30, 2022 versus December 31, 2021 (in millions). Total structured notes declined to $85,158 from $92,642. By risk, interest rate was roughly flat/slightly lower ($38,378 vs $38,988), equity decreased ($37,876 vs $41,269), credit decreased ($4,743 vs $7,210), foreign exchange decreased ($3,366 vs $4,767), while commodity increased ($795 vs $408). By classification, long-term debt fell ($64,804 vs $73,587), short-term borrowings were slightly lower ($7,490 vs $8,001), and deposits increased ($12,864 vs $11,054), largely driven by higher interest rate–linked deposits ($8,929 vs $4,860). A footnote notes that deposits linked to precious metals not under the fair value option are excluded ($583 at June 30, 2022 and $692 at December 31, 2021).

nodes.title: Note 4 – Derivative instruments
nodes.heading: 7.4 Note 4 – Derivative instruments
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase makes markets in derivatives for clients and also uses derivatives to hedge or manage its own risk exposures.
nodes.summary:
- Describes JPMorgan Chase’s use of derivatives both for client market-making and for hedging/managing the Firm’s own risk, with a reference to the 2021 Form 10-K (Note 5) for accounting policies.
- Explains that disclosures are organized by accounting treatment and purpose: derivatives designated in hedge accounting (fair value, cash flow, net investment) versus those not designated.
- Summarizes qualifying hedge accounting uses:
  - Interest rate derivatives hedging fixed-rate items (fair value hedges) and floating-rate items (cash flow hedges) in Corporate.
  - Foreign exchange derivatives hedging FX-denominated assets/liabilities (fair value hedges) and forecasted revenues/expenses (cash flow hedges) in Corporate.
  - Net investment hedges for non-USD functional currency entities in Corporate.
  - Commodity derivatives hedging inventory (fair value hedges) in CIB and AWM.
- Outlines non-designated “specified risk management” uses:
  - Interest rate risk for mortgage commitments, warehouse loans, and MSRs in CCB.
  - Credit risk on wholesale lending exposures in CIB.
  - Interest rate and FX risks on other specified assets/liabilities in Corporate.
- Identifies market-making and other derivative activities:
  - Various derivatives for market-making and related risk management primarily in CIB.
  - Other derivatives used across CIB, AWM, and Corporate.
- Notes that the table links each derivative type to its purpose, hedge designation/category, affected business segments (Corporate, CIB, AWM, CCB), and provides 10-Q page references (pages 119–123).

nodes.title: Notional amount of derivative contracts
nodes.heading: 7.4.a Notional amount of derivative contracts
nodes.start_phrase: The following table summarizes the notional amount of free-standing derivative contracts outstanding as of J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2, and D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 1.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose: Summarizes the notional amounts of the firm’s outstanding free-standing derivative contracts as of June 30, 2022, versus December 31, 2021 (in billions).

  - Additional details on credit derivatives are referenced elsewhere (page 124).

nodes.title: Impact of derivatives on the Consolidated balance sheets
nodes.heading: 7.4.b Impact of derivatives on the Consolidated balance sheets
nodes.start_phrase: The following table summarizes information on derivative receivables and payables (before and after netting adjustments) that are reflected on the Firm’s Consolidated balance sheets as of J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2, and D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 1, by accounting designation (e.g., whether the derivatives were designated in qualifying hedge accounting relationships or not) and contract type.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of how derivatives impact the Firm’s Consolidated balance sheets, presenting derivative receivables and payables both gross and net (after legally enforceable netting and cash collateral) under U.S. GAAP.
- Data shown as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021, broken out by:
  - Accounting designation: not designated as hedges vs. designated as hedges.
  - Contract type: interest rate, credit, foreign exchange, equity, and commodity.
- Scope limited to trading assets and liabilities; structured notes with the fair value option are excluded.
- Key totals:
  - June 30, 2022: Gross derivative receivables $653.5B; net receivables $81.3B. Gross derivative payables $627.5B; net payables $52.4B.
  - December 31, 2021: Gross derivative receivables $545.3B; net receivables $57.1B. Gross derivative payables $535.0B; net payables $50.1B.
- Composition and changes:
  - Most activity is not designated as hedges; hedge designations are concentrated in foreign exchange and commodities, minimal in interest rate, equity, and credit.
  - From 12/31/21 to 6/30/22, notable increases in foreign exchange and commodity gross balances; interest rate gross balances slightly declined; equity receivables rose while equity payables fell.
- Netting note: The Firm offsets derivative receivables/payables and related cash collateral when a legally enforceable master netting agreement exists.

nodes.title: Derivatives netting
nodes.heading: 7.4.c Derivatives netting
nodes.start_phrase: The following tables present, as of J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2, and D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 1, gross and net derivative receivables and payables by contract and settlement type.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Discloses gross and net derivative receivables and payables by contract type (interest rate, credit, foreign exchange, equity, commodity) and by settlement type (OTC, OTC-cleared, exchange-traded) as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021.
- Netting policy: Derivative assets/liabilities and related cash collateral are netted on the Consolidated balance sheets only when supported by an appropriate legal opinion under a master netting agreement. Positions without such an opinion are not eligible for netting and are shown separately.
- Collateral treatment:
  - Additional collateral (liquid securities per the LCR rule and other cash held at third-party custodians) mitigates counterparty risk but is not eligible for net presentation; it is shown as “Collateral not nettable on the Consolidated balance sheets,” limited to the fair value exposure.
  - Collateral exceeding exposure or tied to positions without a qualifying legal opinion is excluded from the tables.
  - Derivative collateral applies only to OTC and OTC-cleared instruments.
- Key totals (June 30, 2022 vs. December 31, 2021):
  - Total derivative receivables recognized: gross $653.5B; net $81.3B vs. gross $545.3B; net $57.1B.
  - Total derivative payables recognized: gross $627.5B; net $52.4B vs. gross $535.0B; net $50.1B.
  - Collateral not nettable: receivables $(19.8)B vs. $(10.1)B; payables $(2.9)B vs. $(5.9)B.
  - Net amounts after non-nettable collateral: receivables $61.5B vs. $47.0B; payables $49.5B vs. $44.2B.
- Composition highlights:
  - Significant balances in interest rate and foreign exchange contracts; notable year-over-year increases in FX and commodity contract balances; interest rate and equity balances are also material.
  - Breakdowns provided for OTC, OTC-cleared, and exchange-traded segments within each asset class.
- Legal opinion segmentation: Tables distinguish between positions with appropriate legal opinions (eligible for U.S. GAAP netting) and those without (presented gross and not netted).
- Footnotes and operational details:
  - Exchange-traded futures are settled daily.
  - For some counterparties, third-party custodied collateral may exceed derivative balances, but reported amounts are capped at net derivative balances.
  - Cash collateral included in netted amounts: net derivatives receivable include $64.6B (6/30/22) and $67.6B (12/31/21); net derivatives payable include $67.6B (6/30/22) and $64.3B (12/31/21).

nodes.title: Liquidity risk and credit-related contingent features
nodes.heading: 7.4.d Liquidity risk and credit-related contingent features
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 5 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for a more detailed discussion of liquidity risk and credit-related contingent features related to the Firm’s derivative contracts.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Liquidity risk and credit-related contingent features tied to JPMorgan Chase’s OTC and OTC-cleared derivative contracts, with references to Note 5 of the 2021 Form 10-K for fuller context.
- Downgrade-triggered features: Many derivatives contain contingent collateral or termination provisions that may be activated upon a ratings downgrade of JPMorgan Chase & Co. or its subsidiaries (primarily JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.).
- Exposure and collateral levels:
  - Aggregate fair value of net derivative payables: $16.0B at June 30, 2022 vs. $20.1B at December 31, 2021.
  - Collateral posted against these: $14.9B at June 30, 2022 vs. $19.4B at December 31, 2021.
- Liquidity impact of potential downgrades (based on a downgrade below the lowest current rating referenced in each contract; a single agency downgrade not below another agency’s corresponding rating generally does not trigger additional collateral or terminations, except possible added initial margin):
  - Additional collateral required:
    - Single-notch: $273M (6/30/22) vs. $219M (12/31/21)
    - Two-notch: $1,552M (6/30/22) vs. $1,577M (12/31/21)
  - Amounts to settle contracts with termination triggers:
    - Single-notch: $85M (6/30/22) vs. $98M (12/31/21)
    - Two-notch: $700M (6/30/22) vs. $787M (12/31/21)
  - Notes: Additional collateral figures include initial margin; termination amounts reflect fair value of derivative payables and exclude collateral already posted.
- Accounting for derivatives executed alongside asset transfers: In some transactions where financial assets are transferred, JPMorgan retains economic exposure via a derivative with the same counterparty. These are generally accounted for as collateralized financings; in limited cases they qualify as a sale plus a derivative under U.S. GAAP. Amounts accounted for as sales with an associated outstanding derivative were not material at June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021.

nodes.title: Derivatives executed in contemplation of a sale of the underlying financial asset
nodes.heading: 7.4.e Derivatives executed in contemplation of a sale of the underlying financial asset
nodes.start_phrase: In certain instances the Firm enters into transactions in which it transfers financial assets but maintains the economic exposure to the transferred assets by entering into a derivative with the same counterparty in contemplation of the initial transfer.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines JPMorgan Chase’s liquidity risk and credit-related contingent features tied to OTC and OTC-cleared derivatives, with a cross-reference to Note 5 of the 2021 Form 10-K. It presents:
- Aggregate fair value of net derivative payables that include downgrade-triggered collateral or termination features and related collateral posted: $16,037 million payables and $14,926 million collateral at June 30, 2022; $20,114 million payables and $19,402 million collateral at December 31, 2021.
- Estimated liquidity impact if the firm or key subsidiaries are downgraded: for June 30, 2022, additional collateral of $273 million (single-notch) and $1,552 million (two-notch), and termination settlement requirements of $85 million and $700 million, respectively; for December 31, 2021, additional collateral of $219 million and $1,577 million, and termination amounts of $98 million and $787 million, respectively. It clarifies that triggers generally apply when ratings fall below the lowest current rating cited in contracts, and that amounts for termination reflect derivative payables at fair value, excluding posted collateral; additional collateral figures include any required initial margin.
- A brief note on transactions where the firm sells financial assets but retains economic exposure via a derivative with the same counterparty: typically accounted for as collateralized financings; in limited cases, as a sale plus a derivative under U.S. GAAP. The volume of such sales with outstanding associated derivatives was not material at June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021.

nodes.title: Impact of derivatives on the Consolidated statements of income
nodes.heading: 7.4.f Impact of derivatives on the Consolidated statements of income
nodes.start_phrase: The following tables provide information related to gains and losses recorded on derivatives based on their hedge accounting designation or purpose.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Impact of derivatives on the Consolidated statements of income, specifically fair value hedge accounting relationships.
- Coverage: Detailed pre-tax gains and losses for derivatives and related hedged items for three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021.
- Breakdown by contract type:
  - Interest rate: Hedges of benchmark rates (e.g., LIBOR, SOFR) on fixed-rate long-term debt and AFS securities; gains/losses recorded in net interest income.
  - Foreign exchange: Hedges of spot foreign currency risk on long-term debt and AFS securities; impacts recorded primarily in principal transactions revenue and net interest income.
  - Commodity: Overall fair value hedges of physical commodities inventories carried at lower of cost or net realizable value; impacts recorded in principal transactions revenue.
- Presentation of results:
  - Tables show derivatives and hedged item gains/losses, the net income statement impact, and the income statement and OCI effects of components excluded from hedge effectiveness.
  - Derivatives and hedged items generally offset, leaving a relatively small net impact on earnings in each period.
  - 2022 shows larger gross interest rate and commodity volatility (notably derivative losses offset by hedged item gains) versus 2021; FX shows similar offsetting patterns.
  - OCI reflects changes in excluded components (predominantly cross-currency basis spreads), with positive OCI in 2022 and negative OCI in 2021.
- Accounting notes and methodology:
  - Effective January 1, 2022, presentation was updated to include amortization of the inception hedge accounting adjustment applied to the hedged item; prior periods were revised for comparability.
  - Accrual of interest on interest rate swaps and related hedged items is excluded from the tables.
  - Excluded components from hedge effectiveness include forward points, time values, and cross-currency basis spreads; recognized in earnings via amortization over the derivative’s life or through current-period fair value changes.
  - OCI line captures period-over-period change in the value of amounts excluded under the amortization approach, which are subsequently recognized in earnings over time.

nodes.title: Fair value hedge gains and losses
nodes.heading: 7.4.g Fair value hedge gains and losses
nodes.start_phrase: The following tables present derivative instruments, by contract type, used in fair value hedge accounting relationships, as well as pre-tax gains/(losses) recorded on such derivatives and the related hedged items for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021 , respectively.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Impact of derivatives on the Consolidated Statements of Income, specifically fair value hedge accounting.
- Coverage periods: Three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021.
- Content of tables:
  - Pre-tax gains/(losses) on derivatives and related hedged items by contract type (interest rate, foreign exchange, commodity).
  - Income statement impact, including the effect of excluded components (amortization approach vs. changes in fair value).
  - Amounts recorded in other comprehensive income (OCI) related to excluded components.
  - Presentation note that derivative gains/(losses) are recorded in the same income statement line as the related hedged item.
- Key accounting explanations:
  - Interest rate hedges target benchmark rate risk (e.g., LIBOR, SOFR) of fixed-rate long-term debt and AFS securities; gains/losses recorded in net interest income.
  - Foreign exchange hedges address spot FX risk of long-term debt and AFS securities; impacts recorded primarily in principal transactions revenue and net interest income.
  - Commodity hedges are overall fair value hedges of physical commodity inventories; impacts recorded in principal transactions revenue.
  - Excluded components (e.g., forward points, time value, cross-currency basis spreads) may affect earnings via systematic amortization or current-period fair value changes; related OCI reflects changes under the amortization approach.
  - 2022 presentation update includes amortization of inception hedge accounting adjustments on hedged items; prior periods conformed.
- Balance sheet impacts:
  - Disclosure of carrying amounts and cumulative fair value hedge basis adjustments for AFS investment securities and liabilities (long-term debt; beneficial interests in consolidated VIEs) as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021.
  - Split between active and discontinued hedge relationships; these basis adjustments are expected to reverse through future earnings as yield adjustments.
  - Sign convention: positive/negative amounts indicate future increases/reductions to net interest income for assets and liabilities, respectively.
- Notable exclusions and clarifications:
  - Physical commodities inventories measured at fair value are excluded from the basis adjustment roll-forward, with no incremental future net income impact from hedge accounting.
  - Items hedged only for foreign currency risk are excluded because their basis adjustments will not reverse through the income statement; specific excluded carrying amounts for AFS securities and long-term debt are provided.
  - Carrying amount for AFS represents amortized cost (net of allowance); certain prior-period amounts revised for consistency.

nodes.title: Cash flow hedge gains and losses
nodes.heading: 7.4.h Cash flow hedge gains and losses
nodes.start_phrase: The following tables present derivative instruments, by contract type, used in cash flow hedge accounting relationships, and the pre-tax gains/(losses) recorded on such derivatives, for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021 , respectively.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Cash flow hedge accounting—derivative instruments by contract type (interest rate and foreign exchange) and related pre-tax gains/losses for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021.
- Presentation: Gains/losses on hedging derivatives are recorded in the same income statement line as the hedged item; tables disaggregate amounts reclassified from AOCI to income, amounts recorded in OCI, and the total change in OCI.
- 2Q22 results: Significant OCI losses driven primarily by interest rate hedges (about $(1.5) billion) with additional FX-related OCI losses (about $(0.2) billion); small net reclassifications from AOCI to income.
- 1H22 results: Larger cumulative OCI losses—interest rate hedges roughly $(4.9) billion and FX roughly $(0.3) billion; total change in OCI about $(5.4) billion.
- 2Q21 results: OCI gains for interest rate hedges (about $1.1 billion) offset by small FX losses; total OCI gain around $1.1 billion.
- 1H21 results: Net OCI loss of approximately $(1.6) billion, driven by interest rate hedges, partially offset by FX gains.
- Contract details:
  - Interest rate hedges primarily cover LIBOR- and SOFR-indexed floating-rate assets; related gains/losses recorded in net interest income.
  - FX hedges cover foreign currency risk of non-USD revenue and expenses; gains/losses follow the hedged item’s line (primarily noninterest revenue and compensation expense).
- Forecasted transactions: None failed to occur in the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021.
- Outlook and timing: About $(1.1) billion after-tax of net losses currently in AOCI as of June 30, 2022, are expected to be recognized in income over the next 12 months.
- Duration:
  - Terminated cash flow hedges: AOCI amortization to earnings over up to ~8 years.
  - Open cash flow hedges: Forecasted transactions hedged for up to ~6 years, tied to core lending and borrowing activities.

nodes.title: Net investment hedge gains and losses
nodes.heading: 7.4.i Net investment hedge gains and losses
nodes.start_phrase: The following table presents hedging instruments, by contract type, that were used in net investment hedge accounting relationships, and the pre-tax gains/(losses) recorded on such instruments for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021 .
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Net investment hedge gains and losses.
- Content: Pre-tax results for hedging instruments used in net investment hedge accounting, by contract type, showing amounts recorded in income and in other comprehensive income (OCI) for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021.
- Instrument: Foreign exchange derivatives (only type presented).
- Results (in millions):
  - Three months ended June 30:
    - 2022: Income $(116); OCI $3,520
    - 2021: Income $(79); OCI $(270)
  - Six months ended June 30:
    - 2022: Income $(247); OCI $3,858
    - 2021: Income $(107); OCI $930
- Notes:
  - Certain derivative components (e.g., forward points) are excluded from hedge effectiveness assessment and their fair value changes are recorded directly in other income.
  - Amounts exclude reclassifications from AOCI to income upon sale or liquidation of hedged entities; such reclassifications for the periods presented were not material (see Note 19).

nodes.title: Gains and losses on derivatives used for specified risk management purposes
nodes.heading: 7.4.j Gains and losses on derivatives used for specified risk management purposes
nodes.start_phrase: The following table presents pre-tax gains/(losses) recorded on a limited number of derivatives, not designated in hedge accounting relationships, that are used to manage risks associated with certain specified assets and liabilities, including certain risks arising from mortgage commitments, warehouse loans, MSRs, wholesale lending exposures, and foreign currency-denominated assets and liabilities.
nodes.summary:
- The excerpt details pre-tax gains and losses on a limited set of derivatives not designated in hedge accounting, used to manage specified risks tied to mortgage commitments, warehouse loans, mortgage servicing rights (MSRs), wholesale lending exposures, and foreign currency-denominated assets and liabilities.
- Results by contract type for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 vs. 2021:
  - Interest rate derivatives: losses of (309) for Q2 2022 and (538) for 1H 2022 vs. gains of 644 and 502 in 2021.
  - Credit derivatives: gains of 89 for Q2 2022 and 122 for 1H 2022 vs. losses of (27) and (67) in 2021.
  - Foreign exchange derivatives: a small gain of 6 for Q2 2022 but a loss of (76) for 1H 2022 vs. losses of (30) and gains of 68 in 2021.
  - Total: net losses of (214) for Q2 2022 and (492) for 1H 2022 vs. net gains of 587 and 503 in 2021.
- Accounting presentation:
  - Interest rate derivative gains/losses recorded predominantly in mortgage fees and related income (hedging interest rate risk in mortgage commitments, warehouse loans, MSRs, and written commitments to originate warehouse loans).
  - Credit and foreign exchange derivative gains/losses recorded in principal transactions revenue (used to mitigate credit risk in wholesale lending and FX risk of specified foreign currency assets/liabilities).
- The document also outlines derivatives related to market-making and other activities: the firm makes markets in derivatives, uses them to manage net open risk and counterparty credit risk from derivative receivables; all derivatives not in hedge accounting or specified risk management fall in this category, with gains/losses primarily recorded in principal transactions revenue (referenced Note 5).

nodes.title: Gains and losses on derivatives related to market-making activities and other derivatives
nodes.heading: 7.4.k Gains and losses on derivatives related to market-making activities and other derivatives
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm makes markets in derivatives in order to meet the needs of customers and uses derivatives to manage certain risks associated with net open risk positions from its market-making activities, including the counterparty credit risk arising from derivative receivables.
nodes.summary:
This section summarizes pre-tax gains and losses on a limited set of derivatives not designated for hedge accounting that are used to manage specified risks tied to certain assets and liabilities, including mortgage commitments, warehouse loans, mortgage servicing rights (MSRs), wholesale lending exposures, and foreign currency–denominated assets and liabilities.

For the three months ended June 30, 2022 versus 2021: interest rate derivatives recorded a loss of $309 million (gain of $644 million in 2021), credit derivatives a gain of $89 million (loss of $27 million in 2021), and foreign exchange derivatives a gain of $6 million (loss of $30 million in 2021), for a total loss of $214 million (total gain of $587 million in 2021). For the six months ended June 30, 2022 versus 2021: interest rate derivatives recorded a loss of $538 million (gain of $502 million in 2021), credit derivatives a gain of $122 million (loss of $67 million in 2021), and foreign exchange derivatives a loss of $76 million (gain of $68 million in 2021), for a total loss of $492 million (total gain of $503 million in 2021).

Accounting presentation: interest rate derivative results are recorded predominantly in mortgage fees and related income. Credit derivative results (which here exclude derivatives used to mitigate counterparty credit risk on derivative receivables) and foreign exchange derivative results are recorded in principal transactions revenue.

The section also describes gains and losses on derivatives related to market-making and other activities. The firm makes markets in derivatives to meet customer needs and uses derivatives to manage risks from net open market-making positions, including counterparty credit risk on derivative receivables. All derivatives not included in hedge accounting or the specified risk management category are included here, with gains and losses primarily recorded in principal transactions revenue (see Note 5).

nodes.title: Credit derivatives
nodes.heading: 7.4.l Credit derivatives
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 5 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for a more detailed discussion of credit derivatives.
nodes.summary:
- Focuses on JPMorgan Chase’s credit derivatives activity, referencing Note 5 of the 2021 Form 10-K for more detail.
- Explains that notional amounts are not the primary risk measure because they ignore credit event probability, recovery values, and offsets from related cash instruments and economic hedges.
- Provides summary tables of maximum payout/notional for June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021, split into:
  - Credit default swaps and other credit derivatives (mainly credit swap options and total return swaps).
  - Protection sold, protection purchased on identical underlyings, net protection (sold)/purchased, and other protection purchased.
  - Credit-related notes (presented as other protection purchased by CIB in market-making).
- Key 6/30/22 figures (in $ millions): total protection sold $526,060; protection purchased on identical underlyings $551,600; net purchased $25,540; other protection purchased $19,378; credit-related notes $9,004; total other protection $28,382.
- Key 12/31/21 figures (in $ millions): total protection sold $499,611; protection purchased on identical underlyings $537,766; net purchased $38,155; other protection purchased $15,704; credit-related notes $9,437; total other protection $25,141.
- Footnotes clarify: “identical underlyings” alignment between sold and purchased protection; net protection does not reflect settlement adjustments from the fair value/recovery of the reference obligation; “other protection purchased” is on non-identical references.
- Presents ratings and maturity profiles of protection sold as of both dates, by investment-grade vs noninvestment-grade and by maturity buckets (<1 year, 1–5 years, >5 years), noting purchased protection has a comparable profile.
- Includes fair value disclosures for protection sold: gross receivables and payables and net fair value, shown before the effect of legally enforceable netting and collateral.
  - 6/30/22: total notional $526,060; IG $390,062; non-IG $135,998; net fair value liability $(5,132) million; concentration in 1–5 year maturities.
  - 12/31/21: total notional $499,611; IG $375,296; non-IG $124,315; net fair value asset $3,649 million; similar maturity concentration.
- Notes that ratings rely primarily on S&P and Moody’s scales.

nodes.title: Note 5 – Noninterest revenue and noninterest expense
nodes.heading: 7.5 Note 5 – Noninterest revenue and noninterest expense
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 6 of JPMorgan Chase ’s 2021 Form 10-K for a discussion of the components of and accounting policies for the Firm’s noninterest revenue.
nodes.summary:
- Note 5 addresses noninterest revenue (and references noninterest expense), directing readers to Note 6 of the 2021 Form 10-K for components and accounting policies.
- Investment banking fees are detailed by category—underwriting (equity and debt) and advisory—with totals for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021.
- Principal transactions present realized and unrealized gains/losses, excluding interest income/expense on trading assets and liabilities. Trading revenue is shown by instrument type (interest rate, credit, foreign exchange, equity, commodity), with totals for the same periods, plus private equity gains/losses and overall principal transactions revenue. Footnotes explain impacts from funding valuation adjustments (FVA), credit valuation adjustments (CVA), and bridge financing portfolio markdowns, and caution that trading revenue by instrument is not indicative of any single line-of-business’s total revenue.
- Lending- and deposit-related fees are broken out between lending-related fees and deposit-related fees, with period totals.
- Asset management, administration and commissions are disaggregated into:
  - Asset management fees (investment management fees and other ancillary asset management fees),
  - Administration fees (custody, securities lending, fund services, securities clearance),
  - Commissions and other fees (brokerage commissions and other commissions),
  with totals for the three- and six-month periods.
- All figures are presented in millions for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021, with explanatory footnotes describing what each fee category represents.

nodes.title: Noninterest revenue
nodes.heading: 7.5.a Noninterest revenue
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 6 of JPMorgan Chase ’s 2021 Form 10-K for a discussion of the components of and accounting policies for the Firm’s noninterest revenue.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Excerpt from Note 5 covering JPMorgan Chase’s noninterest revenue (noninterest expense referenced in the title but not included here). It points readers to Note 6 of the 2021 Form 10-K for components and accounting policies.
- Investment banking fees: Detailed breakdown of underwriting (equity and debt) and advisory. Fees declined materially year over year:
  - Q2 2022 total $1.586B vs $3.470B in Q2 2021; H1 2022 $3.594B vs $6.440B.
  - Underwriting (both equity and debt) drove most of the decline; advisory also lower.
- Principal transactions: Presents realized and unrealized gains/losses, excluding interest income/expense on trading assets/liabilities.
  - Trading revenue by instrument: interest rate, credit, foreign exchange, equity, commodity.
  - Q2 2022 trading revenue $4.882B vs $4.094B (strength in FX and equity); H1 2022 $10.134B vs $10.491B (slightly lower).
  - Private equity gains/losses: Q2 2022 +$108M vs -$18M; H1 2022 -$39M vs +$85M.
  - Total principal transactions: Q2 2022 $4.990B vs $4.076B; H1 2022 $10.095B vs $10.576B.
  - Footnotes note impacts from funding valuation adjustments (FVA) and credit valuation adjustments (CVA) on derivatives, and mark downs on held-for-sale bridge financing positions (primarily unfunded commitments). Caution that trading revenue by instrument isn’t indicative of any single line-of-business total.
- Lending- and deposit-related fees: Both categories and totals provided.
  - Q2 2022 total $1.873B vs $1.760B; H1 2022 $3.712B vs $3.447B (growth driven by deposit-related fees).
- Asset management, administration and commissions: Detailed components and totals.
  - Asset management fees (investment management and other) were flat in Q2 YoY; higher in H1.
  - Administration fees slightly lower YoY.
  - Commissions: brokerage slightly lower in Q2 but roughly flat H1; other commissions higher.
  - Total for this category: Q2 2022 $5.240B vs $5.194B; H1 2022 $10.602B vs $10.223B.
- Footnote clarifications: Define investment management fees (for client assets including funds and separate accounts), ancillary asset management fees (e.g., mutual fund distribution), administration fees (custody, securities lending, fund services, clearance), and brokerage commissions (client trade facilitation).

nodes.title: Investment banking fees
nodes.heading: 7.5.b Investment banking fees
nodes.start_phrase: The following table presents the components of investment banking fees.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Excerpt from JPMorgan Chase’s Note 5 (Noninterest revenue and noninterest expense) focused on noninterest revenue. It references Note 6 of the Firm’s 2021 Form 10-K for component definitions and accounting policies. Periods covered are the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021 (in millions).

- Investment banking fees: Detailed breakdown into underwriting (equity and debt) and advisory. Totals show a significant year-over-year decline, driven largely by lower equity and debt underwriting activity.

- Principal transactions: Presents realized and unrealized gains/losses, with trading revenue by instrument type (interest rate, credit, foreign exchange, equity, commodity). Notes that interest income/expense on trading balances is excluded and that trading revenue by instrument is not a proxy for any single line of business’s total revenue. Includes private equity gains/losses. Footnotes highlight the effects of funding valuation adjustments (FVA) and credit valuation adjustments (CVA) on derivatives and mark-downs on held-for-sale bridge financing positions (primarily unfunded commitments).

- Lending- and deposit-related fees: Breaks out lending-related and deposit-related fees, with total fees rising modestly versus the prior year.

- Asset management, administration and commissions: Components include investment management fees, other asset management fees, administration fees (custody, securities lending, fund services, securities clearance), brokerage commissions, and other commissions. Definitions clarify the nature of each fee stream. Overall totals show a slight increase year over year.

nodes.title: Principal transactions
nodes.heading: 7.5.c Principal transactions
nodes.start_phrase: The following table presents all realized and unrealized gains and losses recorded in principal transactions revenue.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 5 focuses on JPMorgan Chase’s noninterest revenue, referencing Note 6 of the 2021 Form 10-K for component details and accounting policies. The excerpt provides detailed breakdowns for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021.
- Investment banking fees: Significant year-over-year decline driven by lower underwriting activity.
  - Q2 2022 total fees $1,586mm vs $3,470mm in Q2 2021; H1 2022 $3,594mm vs $6,440mm in H1 2021.
  - Underwriting fell sharply (Equity: Q2 $230mm vs $1,073mm; Debt: Q2 $711mm vs $1,473mm). Advisory also declined (Q2 $645mm vs $924mm).
- Principal transactions: Trading revenue by instrument with notes on FVA/CVA impacts and bridge financing markdowns.
  - Total trading revenue increased in Q2 (Q2 2022 $4,882mm vs $4,094mm) but was slightly lower YTD (H1 2022 $10,134mm vs $10,491mm).
  - Notable moves: FX and Commodities up materially; Interest rate and Credit down; Equity roughly flat YTD.
  - Private equity swung to a small YTD loss (H1 2022 $(39)mm vs $85mm); total principal transactions Q2 $4,990mm vs $4,076mm; H1 $10,095mm vs $10,576mm.
  - Excludes interest income/expense on trading assets/liabilities; trading revenue is shown by instrument type and not by line of business totals.
- Lending- and deposit-related fees: Growth led by deposit-related fees.
  - Q2 2022 total $1,873mm vs $1,760mm; H1 $3,712mm vs $3,447mm.
  - Lending-related fees were flat to slightly down; deposit-related fees increased.
- Asset management, administration and commissions: Generally stable to modestly higher overall.
  - Asset management fees were flat in Q2 and up YTD (Investment management fees slightly higher YTD).
  - Administration fees declined.
  - Total commissions rose, with “all other commissions and fees” increasing despite slightly lower brokerage commissions.
  - Total for this category: Q2 $5,240mm vs $5,194mm; H1 $10,602mm vs $10,223mm.

nodes.title: Lending- and deposit-related fees
nodes.heading: 7.5.d Lending- and deposit-related fees
nodes.start_phrase: The following table presents the components of lending- and deposit-related fees.
nodes.summary:
- The excerpt is from Note 5 (Noninterest revenue and noninterest expense) and focuses on Noninterest revenue; it references Note 6 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for components and accounting policies.
- Investment banking fees are broken out into underwriting (equity and debt) and advisory for both the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 vs. 2021. Fees declined materially year over year, driven by lower equity and debt underwriting; advisory also decreased. Q2 total fell to $1.6B from $3.5B; year-to-date fell to $3.6B from $6.4B.
- Principal transactions are detailed, separating trading revenue by instrument type (interest rate, credit, foreign exchange, equity, commodity) and private equity gains/losses.

- Asset management, administration and commissions are disaggregated into:
  - Asset management fees (investment management fees and other ancillary asset management fees),
  - Administration fees (custody, securities lending, fund services, securities clearance),
  - Commissions and other fees (brokerage commissions and all other).
  - Overall, this category was slightly higher year over year in both Q2 and YTD, with strength in investment management fees and “all other” commissions, and modest softness in administration fees.
- The tables present results for both the three- and six-month periods ended June 30, 2022 and 2021, with clarifying definitions for fee categories and a reminder that trading revenue by instrument type is not indicative of total revenue of any single line of business.

nodes.title: Asset management, administration and commissions
nodes.heading: 7.5.e Asset management, administration and commissions
nodes.start_phrase: The following table presents the components of asset management, administration and commissions.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Excerpt from Note 5 covering Noninterest revenue (the “Noninterest expense” portion is not included). It references Note 6 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for component details and accounting policies.
- Investment banking fees: Disaggregation into underwriting (equity and debt) and advisory, with totals for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021.
