nodes.title: Card income
nodes.heading: 7.5.f Card income
nodes.start_phrase: The following table presents the components of card income.
nodes.summary:
- Card income:
  - Provides a breakdown for three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021: interchange and merchant processing income; rewards costs and partner payments; other card income; total card income.
  - Interchange income rose in 2022 vs. 2021, but higher rewards/partner payments and negative other card income led to lower total card income (Q2: $1,133m vs. $1,647m; YTD: $2,108m vs. $2,997m).
  - Other card income is predominantly amortization of account origination costs and annual fees.
  - Cross-references: Note 14 (mortgage fees and related income) and Note 16 (operating lease income within other income).

- Noninterest expense – Other expense:
  - Discloses legal expense for the same periods, lower in 2022 vs. 2021 (Q2: $73m vs. $185m; YTD: $192m vs. $213m).

- Note 6 – Interest income and interest expense:
  - Refers to 2021 Form 10-K Note 7 for accounting policies.
  - Details components of interest income (loans; taxable and non-taxable investment securities; trading assets – debt instruments; federal funds sold and securities purchased under resale agreements; securities borrowed; deposits with banks; all other interest-earning assets) and totals.
  - Details components of interest expense (interest-bearing deposits; federal funds purchased and securities loaned or sold under repurchase agreements; short-term borrowings; trading liabilities – debt and all other interest-bearing liabilities; long-term debt; beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs) and totals.
  - Presents net interest income, provision for credit losses, and net interest income after provision for credit losses. 2022 shows higher interest income and expense, and a positive provision for credit losses vs. releases in 2021, reducing net interest income after provision (Q2: $14,027m vs. $15,026m; YTD: $26,436m vs. $32,071m).

- Footnotes and clarifications:
  - Include amortization/accretion of premiums/discounts and net deferred fees/costs within relevant lines.
  - Identify tax-exempt securities.
  - Explain negative interest income on securities borrowed due to rate/fee dynamics and classification of related expenses within trading liabilities.
  - Note inclusion of commercial paper in short-term borrowings and brokerage-related receivables/payables in respective interest lines.

nodes.title: Other expense
nodes.heading: 7.5.g Other expense
nodes.start_phrase: Other expense on the Firm’s Consolidated statements of income includes the following:
nodes.summary:
- Partial financial statement notes for JPMorgan Chase covering three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021 (in millions).
- Card income: detailed breakdown of interchange and merchant processing income, rewards costs and partner payments, and other card income. Net card income declined year over year for both the quarter and year-to-date as higher rewards/partner payments and more negative “other card income” more than offset higher interchange. “Other card income” is predominantly amortization of account origination costs and annual fees. Cross-references provided to Note 14 (mortgage fees) and Note 16 (operating lease income).
- Noninterest expense – Other expense: presents legal expense only, which decreased year over year for both the quarter and year-to-date.
- Note 6 – Interest income and interest expense: summarizes accounting policy reference and provides a full breakout of interest income (loans; taxable and non-taxable investment securities; trading assets – debt instruments; federal funds sold and securities purchased under resale agreements; securities borrowed; deposits with banks; all other interest-earning assets) and interest expense (interest-bearing deposits; federal funds purchased and securities loaned or sold under repurchase agreements; short-term borrowings; trading liabilities – debt and other interest-bearing liabilities; long-term debt; beneficial interests of consolidated VIEs).
- Results: total interest income and interest expense both rose year over year, yielding higher net interest income for both the quarter and year-to-date. Provision for credit losses increased versus the prior year’s reserve release, resulting in lower net interest income after provision versus the prior year period.
- Footnotes clarify: inclusion of amortization/accretion in loans and securities; tax-exempt securities; causes of negative interest on securities borrowed and related recognition in trading liabilities; what is included in “all other” interest-earning assets and liabilities; and that short-term borrowings include commercial paper.

nodes.title: Note 6 – Interest income and Interest expense
nodes.heading: 7.6 Note 6 – Interest income and Interest expense
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 7 of JPMorgan Chase ’s 2021 Form 10-K for a description of JPMorgan Chase’s accounting policies regarding interest income and interest expense.
nodes.summary:
- Card income components and results for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 vs. 2021:
  - Interchange and merchant processing income increased year over year.
  - Rewards costs and partner payments rose substantially, offsetting interchange gains.
  - Other card income was negative and larger in magnitude in 2022, reflecting predominantly amortization of account origination costs and annual fees.
  - Total card income declined versus 2021 for both the quarter and year-to-date.
  - Cross-references provided to Note 14 (mortgage fees and related income) and Note 16 (operating lease income within other income).

- Noninterest expense – Other expense:
  - Legal expense disclosed for the three and six months ended June 30, showing lower expense in 2022 vs. 2021.

- Interest income and interest expense (Note 6):
  - Breakdown of interest income by category: loans; taxable and non-taxable investment securities; trading assets (debt instruments); federal funds sold and securities purchased under resale agreements; securities borrowed; deposits with banks; and other interest-earning assets.
  - Breakdown of interest expense by category: interest-bearing deposits; federal funds purchased and securities loaned or sold under repurchase agreements; short-term borrowings (including commercial paper); trading liabilities – debt and other interest-bearing liabilities; long-term debt; and beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs.
  - Total interest income and total interest expense both increased in 2022 vs. 2021, resulting in higher net interest income for both the quarter and year-to-date.
  - Provision for credit losses shifted from a net release in 2021 to a net build in 2022, reducing net interest income after provision compared with 2021.
  - Footnotes clarify:
    - Inclusion of amortization/accretion of premiums/discounts and deferred fees/costs.
    - Tax-exempt treatment of certain securities.
    - Negative interest income on securities borrowed due to rate/fee dynamics and where related expenses are reported.
    - Classification of brokerage-related receivables/payables within other lines.
    - Inclusion of commercial paper in short-term borrowings.

nodes.title: Note 7 – Pension and other postretirement employee benefit plans
nodes.heading: 7.7 Note 7 – Pension and other postretirement employee benefit plans

nodes.title: Note 9 – Investment securities
nodes.heading: 7.9 Note 9 – Investment securities
nodes.start_phrase: Investment securities consist of debt securities that are classified as AFS or HTM.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 9 – Investment securities, covering the Firm’s debt securities classified as available-for-sale (AFS) or held-to-maturity (HTM); trading assets are addressed separately in Note 2.
- Purpose/ownership: Predominantly held by Treasury and CIO for asset-liability management; portfolio carried an average AA+ credit rating as of June 30, 2022.
- Reclassification: In Q2 2022, $73.2 billion of securities were transferred from AFS to HTM for capital management; AOCI included $4.6 billion of pretax unrealized losses on the securities at the transfer date.
- Cross-reference: Additional background in Note 10 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K.
- Portfolio detail (as of June 30, 2022 vs. December 31, 2021):
  - AFS: Fair value $222.1 billion (vs. $308.5 billion); gross unrealized losses $10.6 billion (vs. $2.3 billion); gross unrealized gains $0.7 billion (vs. $2.6 billion).
  - HTM: Fair value $415.6 billion (vs. $362.6 billion); gross unrealized losses $26.2 billion (vs. $3.2 billion); gross unrealized gains $0.1 billion (vs. $2.1 billion).
  - Total investment securities (net of ACL): Fair value $637.7 billion (vs. $671.2 billion).
  - Category breakdown provided for: mortgage-backed securities (U.S. GSEs/government agencies, residential, commercial), U.S. Treasury and government agencies, obligations of U.S. states and municipalities, non-U.S. government debt, corporate debt, and asset-backed securities (CLOs and other).
- Notable concentrations: Significant holdings in U.S. Treasury/government agency securities, mortgage-backed securities, and CLOs across both AFS and HTM.
- Footnotes:
  - HTM purchases: $14.3 billion (Q2 2022) and $27.5 billion (YTD 6/30/22) vs. $31.8 billion and $63.1 billion in the respective 2021 periods.
  - Amortized cost reported net of allowance for credit losses: $47 million at 6/30/22 (vs. $42 million at 12/31/21).
  - Accrued interest receivables excluded: $2.0 billion at 6/30/22 (vs. $1.9 billion at 12/31/21); no reversals through interest income in the reported periods; further accounting policy details referenced in the 2021 Form 10-K.

nodes.title: Contractual maturities and yields
nodes.heading: 7.9.d Contractual maturities and yields
nodes.start_phrase: The following table presents the amortized cost and estimated fair value at J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2, of JPMorgan Chase ’s investment securities portfolio by contractual maturity.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Summary table of JPMorgan Chase’s investment securities portfolio at June 30, 2022, showing amortized cost, estimated fair value, and average yield by remaining contractual maturity buckets and by security type. Split between available-for-sale (AFS) and held-to-maturity (HTM).

- Totals:
  - AFS: amortized cost $231.9B; fair value $222.1B; average yield 1.78%.
  - HTM: amortized cost $441.7B; fair value $415.6B; average yield 1.73%.

- Composition and yields:
  - AFS:
    - Mortgage-backed securities (MBS): $76.3B amortized, $71.3B fair value; 2.64% yield; largely due after 10 years.
    - U.S. Treasury and government agencies: $113.8B amortized, $110.0B fair; 0.83% yield; significant 1–5 year concentration.
    - States/municipals: $10.4B amortized, $10.1B fair; 4.36% yield (highest among major AFS buckets).
    - Non-U.S. government debt: $16.2B amortized, $15.8B fair; 1.93% yield.
    - Corporate debt: $0.35B amortized, $0.32B fair; 11.86% yield (small balance).
    - Asset-backed securities (ABS): $14.8B amortized, $14.5B fair; 2.37% yield; meaningful >10-year share.
  - HTM:
    - MBS: $138.4B amortized, $128.3B fair; 2.74% yield; predominantly >10 years.
    - U.S. Treasury and agencies: $226.4B amortized, $212.9B fair; 0.84% yield; large 1–5 year and ≤1 year portions.
    - States/municipals: $19.2B amortized, $18.3B fair; 4.10% yield.
    - ABS: $57.8B amortized, $56.2B fair; 2.02% yield; heavy >10 years.

- Maturity profile:
  - Significant portion of both AFS and HTM portfolios contractually due after 10 years, especially MBS and ABS.
  - Treasuries are more front- to intermediate-dated (≤5 years), particularly in AFS.

- Valuation context:
  - Fair values are generally below amortized cost across categories, indicating unrealized losses consistent with a higher-rate environment at the date.

- Yield methodology and prepayment/call features (footnotes):
  - Average yields are effective yields weighted by amortized cost, reflect coupons, premium/discount amortization, and hedging derivatives; tax-equivalent where applicable.
  - Excludes unscheduled prepayments; callable debt yields calculated to earliest call.
  - Although most U.S. residential MBS/CMOs are contractually >10 years, estimated weighted-average lives are shorter: ~8 years (agency MBS), ~7 years (agency CMOs), ~6 years (nonagency CMOs).

nodes.title: Note 10 – Securities financing activities
nodes.heading: 7.10 Note 10 – Securities financing activities
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 11 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for a discussion of accounting policies relating to securities financing activities.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 10 details JPMorgan Chase’s securities financing activities, with cross-references to accounting policies (2021 Form 10-K Note 11), fair value option elections (Note 3), and assets pledged/collateral received (Note 23).

- Balance sheet presentation and netting:
  - Explains U.S. GAAP netting for securities financing agreements when an enforceable master netting agreement is in place and supported by a legal opinion.
  - Clarifies that exchanged collateral (cash/securities) reduces economic exposure but generally is not eligible for balance sheet netting; such amounts are shown as “Amounts not nettable on the Consolidated balance sheets.”
  - Where no qualifying legal opinion exists, balances are presented gross within the “Net amounts.”
  - Describes accounting for securities-for-securities lending when JPMC is lender: recognizes received securities at fair value in other assets and the related obligation in accounts payable and other liabilities.

- Quantitative disclosures (as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021):
  - Tables summarizing gross amounts, amounts netted, amounts presented on the Consolidated balance sheets, amounts not nettable, and resulting net amounts for:
    - Securities purchased under resale agreements (reverse repos)
    - Securities borrowed
    - Securities sold under repurchase agreements (repos)
    - Securities loaned and other
  - Footnotes highlight:
    - Portions of securities-for-securities lending accounted for at fair value.
    - Limits on “amounts not nettable” when collateral exceeds net positions.
    - Inclusion of positions without obtained legal opinions within net amounts, with specific category breakdowns.

- Collateral composition and maturity profile:
  - Breakout of financial assets pledged in repos and securities loaned by asset class (e.g., U.S. Treasuries/GSEs, non-U.S. government debt, MBS, corporate debt, ABS, equities).
  - Remaining contractual maturity schedules for repos and securities loaned by tenor buckets (overnight/continuous, up to 30 days, 30–90 days, greater than 90 days) for both reporting dates.

- Transfers not qualifying for sale accounting:
  - Discloses assets whose rights were transferred but did not meet sale criteria under U.S. GAAP; recognized as collateralized financings.
  - Notes presentation: assets in trading assets and loans; related liabilities predominantly in short-term borrowings.

nodes.title: Note 11 – Loans
nodes.heading: 7.11 Note 11 – Loans
nodes.start_phrase: The accounting for a loan depends on management’s strategy for the loan.
nodes.summary:
- Overview: Note 11 – Loans outlines the Firm’s loan accounting framework, portfolio segmentation, loan classes, and summarizes loan balances by segment and accounting category at June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021.
- Accounting framework: Loans are accounted for as (1) originated or purchased loans held-for-investment (retained), (2) loans held-for-sale, and (3) loans at fair value. The note cross‑references detailed accounting policies (2021 Form 10-K Note 12), fair value option elections (this Form 10-Q Note 3), and loans at fair value classified as trading assets (this Form 10-Q Note 2).
- Portfolio segmentation: The loan portfolio is divided into three segments used for the allowance for loan losses—Consumer excluding credit card; Credit card; and Wholesale.
- Loan classes within segments:
  - Consumer excluding credit card: Residential real estate (scored mortgage and home equity across CCB, AWM, and scored mortgages in CIB and Corporate); Auto and other (scored auto, business banking loans, and overdrafts).
  - Credit card: Credit card loans.
  - Wholesale: Secured by real estate; Commercial and industrial; Other (loans to financial institutions, states and political subdivisions, SPEs, nonprofits, personal investment companies and trusts, and to individuals/individual entities, predominantly Global Private Bank clients). Wholesale classes align with bank regulatory classifications by collateral, purpose, and borrower type; includes certain risk‑rated loans in CCB (e.g., business banking and auto dealer) where wholesale methodology is used for the allowance.
- Loan balances summary:
  - June 30, 2022 totals (in millions): Consumer ex‑credit card $317,212; Credit card $165,494; Wholesale $621,449; Total $1,104,155, comprising Retained $1,052,390; Held‑for‑sale $4,709; At fair value $47,056.
  - December 31, 2021 totals (in millions): Consumer ex‑credit card $323,306; Credit card $154,296; Wholesale $600,112; Total $1,077,714, comprising Retained $1,010,206; Held‑for‑sale $8,688; At fair value $58,820.
  - Key changes: Total loans increased to $1.104T from $1.078T, driven by higher retained loans (notably Wholesale and Credit card). Held‑for‑sale and at‑fair‑value balances declined; Consumer ex‑credit card fair value loans decreased.
- Footnotes/other presentation:
  - Loan totals exclude accrued interest receivables of $3.2B (6/30/22) and $2.7B (12/31/21). Accrued interest receivable write‑offs were $8M for Q2 2022 and Q2 2021, and $20M and $21M for the six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021, respectively; prior periods revised for consistency.
  - Non‑fair‑value‑option loans are presented net of unamortized discounts/premiums and net deferred fees/costs, which were not material at the reported dates.

nodes.title: Loan accounting framework
nodes.heading: 7.11.a Loan accounting framework
nodes.start_phrase: The accounting for a loan depends on management’s strategy for the loan.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 11 – Loans outlines JPMorgan Chase’s loan accounting framework, portfolio segmentation, risk classes, and period-end loan balances, with cross-references to related notes.
- Accounting framework: Loans are accounted for based on management’s strategy in three categories: originated or purchased loans held-for-investment (retained), loans held-for-sale, and loans at fair value. References provided to: 2021 Form 10-K Note 12 (policies), this Form 10-Q Note 3 (fair value option elections), and Note 2 (loans at fair value classified as trading assets).
- Portfolio segmentation and risk classes: Three portfolio segments aligned with the allowance for loan losses—Consumer (excluding credit card), Credit card, and Wholesale. Classes include:
  - Consumer, excluding credit card: Residential real estate; Auto and other (includes scored auto and business banking loans and overdrafts).
  - Credit card: Credit card loans.
  - Wholesale: Secured by real estate; Commercial and industrial; Other (loans to financial institutions, states/political subdivisions, SPEs, nonprofits, personal investment companies/trusts, and individuals, predominantly Global Private Bank clients). Wholesale classes align with regulatory classifications by collateral, purpose, and borrower; wholesale methodology is applied to certain CCB risk-rated loans (e.g., business banking, auto dealer).
- Loan balances by segment and measurement category:
  - June 30, 2022 (in millions): Retained—Consumer ex-CC $302,631; Credit card $165,494; Wholesale $584,265; Total $1,052,390. Held-for-sale—$4,709 total. At fair value—$47,056 total. Grand total $1,104,155 (Consumer ex-CC $317,212; Credit card $165,494; Wholesale $621,449).
  - December 31, 2021 (in millions): Retained—Consumer ex-CC $295,556; Credit card $154,296; Wholesale $560,354; Total $1,010,206. Held-for-sale—$8,688 total. At fair value—$58,820 total. Grand total $1,077,714 (Consumer ex-CC $323,306; Credit card $154,296; Wholesale $600,112).
  - Notable changes: Total loans increased to $1.10T from $1.08T, driven by growth in retained credit card and wholesale; held-for-sale and at-fair-value balances declined; Consumer ex-CC total decreased slightly.
- Presentation and footnotes:
  - Accrued interest receivable excluded from totals: $3.2B at June 30, 2022 and $2.7B at December 31, 2021; accrued interest write-offs were $8M for the three months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021, and $20M/$21M for the six months ended June 30, 2022/2021; prior periods revised to conform to current presentation.
  - Loans not at fair value are presented net of unamortized discounts/premiums and net deferred fees/costs; amounts not material at both dates.

nodes.title: Loan portfolio
nodes.heading: 7.11.b Loan portfolio
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm’s loan portfolio is divided in to three portfolio segments, which are the same segments used by the Firm to determine the allowance for loan losses: Consumer, excluding credit card; Credit card; and Wholesale.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 11 – Loans outlines JPMorgan Chase’s loan accounting framework, portfolio segmentation, period-end loan balances, loan activity (purchases, sales, reclassifications), and related gains/losses.

- Accounting framework:
  - Loans are categorized as: originated or purchased loans held-for-investment (retained), loans held-for-sale (HFS), and loans measured at fair value.
  - Cross-references: Note 12 of the 2021 Form 10-K for policies; Note 3 (fair value option elections) and Note 2 (loans at fair value classified as trading assets) of the current Form 10-Q.

- Portfolio segmentation and classes used for allowance for loan losses:
  - Consumer, excluding credit card: residential real estate; auto and other (includes scored auto, business banking loans, and overdrafts).
  - Credit card: credit card loans.
  - Wholesale: secured by real estate; commercial and industrial; other (includes loans to financial institutions, states/political subdivisions, SPEs, nonprofits, personal investment companies, trusts, and individuals, notably AWM Global Private Bank clients). Wholesale classes align with bank regulatory definitions. Certain “scored” mortgages/home equity appear in multiple lines of business.

- Loan balances (in millions):
  - June 30, 2022 total loans: $1,104,155, comprising retained $1,052,390; HFS $4,709; at fair value $47,056. By segment: Consumer excl. credit card $317,212; Credit card $165,494; Wholesale $621,449.
  - December 31, 2021 total loans: $1,077,714, comprising retained $1,010,206; HFS $8,688; at fair value $58,820. By segment: Consumer excl. credit card $323,306; Credit card $154,296; Wholesale $600,112.
  - Notes: Accrued interest receivables of $3.2B (6/30/22) and $2.7B (12/31/21) are excluded; small write-offs of accrued interest disclosed. Non–fair value loans are presented net of unamortized discounts/premiums and deferred fees/costs (amounts not material).

- Loan activity (carrying value of retained loans):
  - Three months ended June 30, 2022 vs 2021:
    - Purchases: $1,201 vs $412 (consumer purchases predominantly residential real estate; includes voluntary repurchases of certain delinquent Ginnie Mae loans).
    - Sales: $12,087 vs $8,751 (driven largely by wholesale).
    - Reclassified to HFS: $481 vs $979 (non-cash).
  - Six months ended June 30, 2022 vs 2021:
    - Purchases: $1,486 vs $829 (similar mix/footnotes as above).
    - Sales: $21,841 vs $14,662.
    - Reclassified to HFS: $830 vs $1,913 (non-cash).
  - Exclusions: Significant additional purchases of retained loans sourced via the correspondent channel ($6.0B and $5.0B in 2Q22 and 2Q21; $9.2B and $12.0B in 1H22 and 1H21) are excluded from the purchase lines.

- Gains and losses on sales:
  - Noninterest revenue recognized for three and six months ended June 30, 2022: net losses of $(352)M and $(314)M, respectively; loan-related portions were $(67)M and $(32)M.
  - Comparable 2021 periods: net gains of $62M and $194M; loan-related portions were $47M and $182M.
  - Note that loan sales can also impact provision for credit losses via write-downs, recoveries, or allowance changes.

nodes.title: Gains and losses on sales of loans
nodes.heading: 7.11.c Gains and losses on sales of loans

nodes.summary:
- Scope: Activity in retained loans purchased, sold, and reclassified to held-for-sale (HFS) for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021, broken out by consumer (excluding credit card), credit card, and wholesale portfolios. Sales exclude loans that were previously reclassified to HFS and sold in a later period.

- Activity highlights (carrying values, in millions):
  - Three months ended June 30, 2022: Purchases $1,201 (consumer $973; wholesale $228), Sales $12,087 (predominantly wholesale $12,005), Reclassified to HFS $481.
  - Three months ended June 30, 2021: Purchases $412, Sales $8,751, Reclassified to HFS $979.
  - Six months ended June 30, 2022: Purchases $1,486, Sales $21,841, Reclassified to HFS $830.
  - Six months ended June 30, 2021: Purchases $829, Sales $14,662, Reclassified to HFS $1,913.

- Footnotes/definitions:
  - Reclassifications of loans to HFS are non-cash transactions.
  - Purchases predominantly include residential real estate loans, including voluntary repurchases of certain delinquent loans from Ginnie Mae pools; the firm continues to service/manage foreclosure per Ginnie Mae, FHA, RHS, and VA requirements.
  - Reported purchase amounts exclude large volumes of retained loans sourced via the correspondent origination channel underwritten to firm standards: $6.0B (Q2’22), $5.0B (Q2’21), $9.2B (H1’22), and $12.0B (H1’21).

- Gains and losses:
  - Net gains/(losses) on sales of loans and lending-related commitments (including lower-of-cost-or-fair-value adjustments for HFS) recognized in noninterest revenue:

  - Loan sales may also result in write-downs, recoveries, or changes to the allowance recognized in the provision for credit losses.

- Notable trends: Sales volumes are concentrated in wholesale; purchases increased in 2022 versus 2021; reclassifications to HFS declined in 2022 versus 2021; net performance swung from gains in 2021 to losses in 2022.

nodes.title: Consumer, excluding credit card loan portfolio
nodes.heading: 7.11.d Consumer, excluding credit card loan portfolio
nodes.start_phrase: Consumer loans, excluding credit card loans, consist primarily of scored residential mortgages, home equity loans and lines of credit, auto and business banking loans, with a focus on serving the prime consumer credit market.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and composition: Describes consumer loans excluding credit cards, primarily scored residential mortgages, home equity loans/lines, auto loans, and business banking loans, focused on the prime consumer credit market. Portfolio also includes junior-lien home equity loans, prime mortgages with interest-only periods, and certain payment-option loans that can lead to negative amortization.
- Loan balances (retained, in millions): As of June 30, 2022 vs. December 31, 2021:
  - Residential real estate: $237,142 vs. $224,795
  - Auto and other: $65,489 vs. $70,761
  - Total retained loans: $302,631 vs. $295,556
- PPP exposure: Included within Business Banking were $1.5 billion (June 30, 2022) and $5.4 billion (December 31, 2021) of loans under the Paycheck Protection Program.
- Credit quality: Delinquency rates are the primary credit quality indicator; references Note 12 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for further details.

nodes.title: Residential real estate
nodes.heading: 7.11.e Residential real estate
nodes.start_phrase: The following tables provide information on delinquency, which is the primary credit quality indicator for retained residential real estate loans.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Credit quality of retained residential real estate loans, using delinquency as the primary indicator.
- Scope: Two data snapshots—in millions, except ratios—as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021.
- Breakout: Balances shown by delinquency status (current, 30–149 days past due, 150+ days past due) across:
  - Term loans segmented by origination year/vintage.
  - Revolving loans split into within revolving period and converted to term loans.
- Portfolio size and performance trends:
  - Total retained loans increased to $237.1B (6/30/22) from $224.8B (12/31/21).
  - Delinquent balances declined: 30–149 days past due fell to $780M from $883M; 150+ days past due fell to $870M from $1,449M.
  - Overall delinquency ratio (30+ days past due to total) improved to 0.68% (6/30/22) from 1.02% (12/31/21).
- Vintage and product insights:
  - Newer originations exhibit very low delinquency; older vintages (e.g., prior to 2018/2017) show higher delinquency rates.
  - Revolving loans converted to term have higher delinquency than those still in the revolving period, primarily due to higher fully amortizing payments versus minimum payment options.
- Lien composition:
  - Approximately 37% of revolving loans are senior liens; the remainder are junior liens.

nodes.title: Loan modifications

nodes.title: Financial effects of modifications and redefaults
nodes.heading: 7.11.i Financial effects of modifica tions and redefaults
nodes.start_phrase: The following table provides information about the financial effects of the various concessions granted in modifications of residential real estate loans under the loss mitigation programs described above and about redefaults of certain loans modified in TDRs for the periods presented.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Financial effects of permanent modifications (TDRs) of residential real estate loans under loss mitigation programs, excluding trial mods, Chapter 7 discharge-only cases, and insignificant short-term mods.
- Periods covered: Three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021.
- Interest rate concessions: Weighted-average rates for loans with rate reductions declined after TDRs (e.g., Q2 2022 from 4.76% to 3.36; Q2 2021 from 4.39% to 2.85; H1 2022 from 4.55% to 3.31; H1 2021 from 4.51% to 2.90).
- Term/payment extensions: Weighted-average remaining contractual term increased after TDRs (e.g., Q2 2022 from 22 to 38 years; Q2 2021 from 22 to 36; H1 2022 from 23 to 39; H1 2021 from 24 to 38).
- Loss recognition and concessions:
  - Charge-offs on permanent modification: $1m in Q2 and H1 2022; none in 2021.
  - Principal deferred: $4m (Q2 2022) vs $6m (Q2 2021); $11m (H1 2022) vs $18m (H1 2021).
  - Principal forgiven: $0m in Q2 both years; $1m in H1 2022 and H1 2021.
- Redefaults within one year of permanent modification: Balances of $27m (Q2 2022) vs $21m (Q2 2021); $70m (H1 2022) vs $45m (H1 2021).
- Redefault definition and outcomes: Payment default occurs when two contractual payments past due; typically leads to foreclosure or similar liquidation; recent one-year redefault levels may not represent ultimate outcomes.
- Portfolio life: At June 30, 2022, weighted-average estimated remaining life of permanently modified TDR loans was six years, reflecting expected voluntary and involuntary prepayments.
- Foreclosure pipeline: Residential real estate loans (excluding U.S. government-insured) in active or suspended foreclosure, not in REO, totaled $696m at June 30, 2022 vs $619m at December 31, 2021.

- Scope and exclusions: Presents the financial effects of permanent loan modifications (TDRs) for residential real estate under loss mitigation programs, excluding trial/temporary concessions, Chapter 7 cases where only debt discharge occurred, and short-term or insignificant non-concession modifications. Amounts are in millions except weighted averages.
- Interest rate reductions: For loans with rate reductions, weighted-average rates declined post-modification—Q2 2022 from 4.76% to 3.36% (Q2 2021: 4.39% to 2.85%); six months 2022 from 4.55% to 3.31% (2021: 4.51% to 2.90%).

nodes.title: Loan modifications
nodes.heading: 7.11.o Loan modifications
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm may offer loan modification programs granting concessions to credit card borrowers who are experiencing financial difficulty.

- Default definition and handling: Payment default for modified credit card loans is missing two consecutive payments; defaulted loans remain in the modification program and are charged off per standard policy.

nodes.title: Discussion of changes in the allowance
nodes.heading: 7.12.b Discussion of changes in the allowance
nodes.start_phrase: The allowance for credit losses as of J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2 was $20.0 billion , an increas e of $ 1 . 3 b i l l i o n from D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 1, consisting of: $1.0 billion in wholesale and $311 million in consumer.
nodes.summary:
- Allowance for credit losses totaled $20.0 billion at June 30, 2022, up $1.3 billion from December 31, 2021, driven by a $1.0 billion increase in wholesale and a $311 million increase in consumer.
- Key drivers of the increase: higher weighting of adverse macroeconomic scenarios reflecting elevated inflation, monetary policy changes, and geopolitical risks (including the war in Ukraine); loan growth in Card and Commercial Banking in 2Q22; and client-specific Russia and Russia-associated downgrades in Corporate & Investment Bank and Asset & Wealth Management in 1Q22.
- Methodology: allowance is estimated using a weighted average of five internally developed macroeconomic scenarios. Adverse scenarios are more punitive than the central case and imply weighted average U.S. unemployment rates above 4% through 4Q23 and a U.S. real GDP level 1.1% lower by end-4Q23 than under the central case.
- Central case assumptions at June 30, 2022: U.S. unemployment rate of 3.6% (4Q22), 3.6% (2Q23), 3.7% (4Q23); YoY U.S. real GDP growth of 1.3% (4Q22), 1.7% (2Q23), 1.2% (4Q23). At December 31, 2021: unemployment 4.2% (2Q22), 4.0% (4Q22), 3.9% (2Q23); YoY GDP growth 3.1% (2Q22), 2.8% (4Q22), 2.1% (2Q23).
- Note: as of June 30, 2022, YoY GDP growth is calculated as the percent change in U.S. real GDP levels from the prior year. Future forecast updates will be recognized through the provision for credit losses.
- Cross-references provided to 2021 Form 10-K Notes 13 and 10 for policies and methodologies; Consumer Credit Portfolio (pp. 57–61), Wholesale Credit Portfolio (pp. 62–70), and Note 11 for portfolio details; and Critical Accounting Estimates (pp. 83–85) for allowance and related judgments.

nodes.title: Note 13 – Variable interest entities
nodes.heading: 7.13 Note 13 – Variable interest entities
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 1 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K for a further description of JPMorgan Chase’s accounting policies regarding consolidation of VIEs.
nodes.summary: Note 13 outlines JPMorgan Chase’s involvement with variable interest entities (VIEs), referencing the 2021 Form 10-K for detailed accounting policies on consolidation and securitizations. It defines a “Firm-sponsored” VIE as one where JPMorgan Chase is the primary beneficiary, uses the entity to securitize Firm assets, the entity issues instruments bearing the Firm’s name, or it is a Firm-administered ABCP conduit. The note summarizes key Firm-sponsored VIE types by business segment: in CCB, credit card securitization trusts and mortgage securitization trusts; in CIB, mortgage and other securitization trusts, multi-seller conduits to help clients access markets, and municipal bond vehicles. It highlights that the Firm is the primary beneficiary of the Chase Issuance Trust for credit card securitizations due to continuing involvement. For mortgage and other securitizations, the Firm securitizes originated and purchased residential and commercial mortgages and other consumer loans, primarily in CCB and CIB, and may act as servicer and/or retain beneficial interests. The Firm also invests in and provides financing and other services to third-party–sponsored VIEs, with additional details on consolidated VIE assets and liabilities and third-party VIEs referenced elsewhere in the note.

nodes.title: Credit card securitizations

nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines JPMorgan Chase’s Note 13 on Variable Interest Entities (VIEs), referencing Note 1 and Note 14 of the 2021 Form 10-K for consolidation and securitization accounting policies. It defines “Firm-sponsored” VIEs as entities where JPMorgan Chase is the primary beneficiary, uses the VIE to securitize Firm assets, the VIE issues instruments bearing the Firm’s name, or the entity is a Firm-administered ABCP conduit. It summarizes key Firm-sponsored VIE types by business segment with Form 10-Q page references: in CCB, credit card securitization trusts and mortgage securitization trusts (servicing and securitization of originated and purchased residential mortgages); in CIB, mortgage and other securitization trusts (residential, commercial mortgages, and other consumer loans), multi-seller conduits (client funding and transaction structuring), and municipal bond vehicles (financing municipal bond investments). The Firm also invests in and provides financing/services to third-party sponsored VIEs, with details on consolidated VIE assets and liabilities and third-party VIEs on pages 155–157. Significant Firm-sponsored VIEs include the Chase Issuance Trust for credit card securitizations, where the Firm is the primary beneficiary due to continuing involvement, and various mortgage/other securitization trusts in which the Firm securitizes originated and purchased assets, often serving as loan servicer and/or retaining beneficial interests.

- Note that the Firm also invests in, finances, and provides services to third-party-sponsored VIEs; additional details and consolidated VIE balances on pages 155–157.

  - Mortgage and other securitizations: Firm securitizes originated and purchased residential/commercial mortgages and other consumer loans, may act as servicer, and may retain beneficial interests.
- Explanation of “continuing involvement” (servicing, retained senior/subordinated interests including risk retention, recourse/guarantees, derivatives) and that maximum loss exposure from retained/purchased interests equals their carrying value.
- Presentation of unpaid principal balances in Firm-sponsored private-label securitization entities, distinguishing consolidated vs. nonconsolidated VIEs with continuing involvement.

nodes.title: Regulatory capital

Noncompliance could trigger Federal Reserve action. Cross-reference to Note 27 of the 2021 Form 10-K for more detail.

- Required capital measures: The Firm and its IDI subsidiaries must meet risk-based ratios (CET1, Tier 1, Total capital) and leverage-based ratios (Tier 1 leverage and Supplementary Leverage Ratio, SLR).

- Risk-based ratio thresholds (as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021):
  - Standardized approach (BHC/IDI): CET1 11.2% / 7.0%; Tier 1 12.7% / 8.5%; Total capital 14.7% / 10.5%.

  - Buffers and surcharges: BHC ratios include minimums plus a 3.5% GSIB surcharge (Method 2), a 3.2% stress capital buffer (SCB) for Standardized ratios, and a fixed 2.5% capital conservation buffer for Advanced ratios; the countercyclical buffer is 0%. IDIs include a fixed 2.5% capital conservation buffer and are not subject to the GSIB surcharge.

- Leverage-based ratio thresholds (as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021):
  - Capital ratio requirements (BHC/IDI): Tier 1 leverage 4.0% / 4.0%; SLR 5.0% / 6.0% (comprised of a 3.0% minimum plus supplementary leverage buffers of 2.0% for BHCs and 3.0% for IDIs).

- CECL regulatory capital transition:

  - Additional details referenced in Note 27 of the 2021 Form 10-K.

nodes.title: CECL regulatory capital transition
nodes.heading: 7.21.a CECL regulatory capital transition
nodes.start_phrase: On December 31, 2021, the CECL capital transition provisions , which delayed the effects of CECL on regulatory capital for two years, expired.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 21 outlines JPMorgan Chase’s regulatory capital framework and requirements; Note 22 introduces off-balance sheet lending-related instruments, guarantees, and commitments.
- Regulators and regimes: The Federal Reserve sets capital requirements for the consolidated holding company; the OCC/FDIC set similar standards for the Firm’s insured depository institution (IDI), JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. Requirements cover risk-based (CET1, Tier 1, Total capital) and leverage-based (Tier 1 leverage, SLR) measures, with potential regulatory action for noncompliance.
- Capital thresholds: Tables present minimum and well-capitalized ratios under Basel III Standardized and Advanced approaches for both the bank holding company (BHC) and IDI as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021. BHC risk-based requirements incorporate a 3.5% GSIB surcharge (Method 2), a 3.2% stress capital buffer for Standardized, and a 2.5% capital conservation buffer for Advanced; the countercyclical buffer is 0%. IDIs have a fixed 2.5% capital conservation buffer and no GSIB surcharge. Leverage requirements include Tier 1 leverage minimums of 4% and SLR requirements of 5% for the BHC and 6% for the IDI (3% minimum plus 2%/3% buffers); there are no BHC “well-capitalized” thresholds for leverage.
- CECL transition: The two-year CECL capital transition deferral expired on December 31, 2021. Beginning January 1, 2022, the $2.9 billion CET1 benefit is being phased out 25% per year over three years; $2.2 billion remained in CET1 at June 30, 2022. A 25% phase-out also applies to related Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, and total leverage exposure elements.
- Capital status and metrics: As of both June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021, JPMorgan Chase & Co. and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. were well-capitalized and met all applicable requirements. Tables provide CET1, Tier 1, Total capital, risk-weighted assets, and resulting ratios under both Standardized and Advanced approaches, as well as leverage metrics (adjusted average assets, Tier 1 leverage ratio, total leverage exposure, SLR). Metrics reflect CECL transition effects; PPP loans receive a zero percent risk weight.
- Off-balance sheet exposures (Note 22): Describes commitments and guarantees (e.g., credit card, home equity, scored business banking) and clarifies that contractual amounts represent maximum potential credit risk but typically are not fully drawn or may expire. The Firm maintains an allowance for credit losses on lending-related commitments. Management can reduce or cancel lines (e.g., credit cards can be reduced/closed with notice or when 60+ days past due; HELOCs can be reduced/closed for property value declines or borrower credit deterioration). Tables (not reproduced here) summarize contractual amounts and carrying values as of June 30, 2022 and December 31, 2021.

nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines JPMorgan Chase’s off–balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees, and other commitments (Note 22). It explains that the contractual amounts represent the maximum potential credit exposure if customers draw on commitments or the Firm must perform under guarantees, but actual utilization is typically much lower due to refinancing, extensions, cancellations, or expirations. The Firm maintains an allowance for expected credit losses on certain wholesale and consumer lending-related commitments (referenced to Note 12) and points to Note 28 of the 2021 Form 10-K for broader policies.

Key operational points:
- Credit availability for credit card, home equity (HELOC), and certain scored business banking products reflects total available lines; the Firm does not expect simultaneous full utilization.
- The Firm can reduce or cancel credit card and certain business banking lines with notice (or without, where permitted), typically closes credit card lines at 60+ days past due, and may reduce/close HELOCs upon property value declines or borrower credit deterioration.
- Predominantly all consumer and wholesale commitments are U.S.-based.

Summary of contractual amounts and carrying values (in millions) at June 30, 2022 vs. December 31, 2021:

nodes.title: Litigation
nodes.heading: 7.24 Note 24 – Litigation
nodes.start_phrase: As of June 30, 2022, the Firm and its subsidiaries and affiliates are defendants or respondents in numerous legal proceedings, including private, civil litigations, government investigations or regulatory enforcement matters.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of litigation contingencies as of June 30, 2022: the Firm, its subsidiaries, and affiliates are involved in numerous legal proceedings worldwide, including private civil actions (individual and class), government investigations, and regulatory enforcement matters across all lines of business, with a wide range of claims (tort, contract, antitrust, securities, consumer protection), some involving novel legal theories.
- Loss exposure: estimated aggregate range of reasonably possible losses in excess of existing reserves is $0 to approximately $1.2 billion at June 30, 2022. For certain matters an estimate is not feasible. The estimate involves significant judgment due to:
  - Number and diversity of matters and their early procedural posture.
  - Multiple defendants with undetermined liability shares.
  - Unresolved issues (e.g., class certification, claim scope).
  - Uncertainty of outcomes and reliance on assumptions about court rulings and counterparty/regulatory behavior that may prove incorrect.
  - Actual outcomes may differ materially; the range will change over time.
- Material proceedings summarized:
  - Amrapali (India): ED investigation into 2010 and 2012 investments by offshore funds formerly managed by JPMorgan entities in Amrapali residential projects; numerous creditor and homebuyer actions overseen by India’s Supreme Court. August 2021 ED order fining J.P. Morgan India Private Limited approximately $31.5 million (being appealed). July 2019 Supreme Court made preliminary findings of currency control and money-laundering violations by Amrapali and others (including unspecified JPMorgan entities/offshore funds) and directed further ED inquiry under PMLA and FEMA. May 2020 ED attached approximately $25 million from J.P. Morgan India Private Limited in the PMLA investigation; the Firm is cooperating.
  - Federal Republic of Nigeria litigation (UK): JPMorgan operated an escrow/depository account holding about $1.1 billion for the FGN and two oil companies; funds were paid out in 2011 and 2013 per client instructions. In 2017 the FRN sued in the English High Court for about $875 million, alleging JPMorgan should have been on notice of a fraud. After a Feb–Apr 2022 trial, the Court dismissed the case in June 2022 in JPMorgan’s favor. The FRN has sought permission to appeal as to the 2013 payment of approximately $75 million.
  - Foreign Exchange investigations and litigation: reference to previously reported settlements with authorities concerning FX sales and trading activities and related controls; notes a May 2015 plea (discussion continues beyond the excerpt).

nodes.title: Federal Republic of Nigeria Litigation
nodes.heading: 7.24.b Federal Republic of Nigeria Litigation
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. operated an escrow and depository account for the Federal Government of Nigeria (“FGN”) and two major international oil companies.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of contingencies: As of June 30, 2022, the Firm and its affiliates are involved in numerous legal proceedings across all lines of business and multiple geographies, including private civil litigations (individual and class actions), government investigations, and regulatory enforcement matters. Claims span tort, contract, antitrust, securities, and consumer protection, including some novel legal theories, and are at varying stages.

- Loss estimate: The Firm estimates the aggregate range of reasonably possible losses in excess of reserves at $0 to approximately $1.2 billion as of June 30, 2022. Not all matters can be estimated. The estimate involves significant judgment due to the number and stages of proceedings, multiple defendants with undetermined liability, unresolved issues (e.g., class certification and claim scope), and uncertainty in outcomes and assumptions. Actual losses may differ significantly, and estimates will change over time.

- Material proceedings highlighted:
  - Amrapali (India): Investigation by India’s Enforcement Directorate into 2010/2012 investments by two offshore funds formerly managed by JPMorgan Chase entities in Amrapali residential projects. Homebuyer petitions overseen by India’s Supreme Court are ongoing. In August 2021, the ED fined J.P. Morgan India Private Limited about $31.5 million; the Firm is appealing. The Supreme Court (July 2019) made preliminary findings of violations by Amrapali and others (including unspecified JPM entities/offshore funds) and ordered further ED inquiry under PMLA and FEMA. In May 2020, the ED attached approximately $25 million from J.P. Morgan India Private Limited; the Firm is cooperating.
  - Federal Republic of Nigeria litigation: JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. operated an escrow/depository account (~$1.1 billion) for Nigeria and two oil companies. Funds were paid out in 2011 and 2013 per client instructions. Nigeria sued in November 2017 in the English High Court for about $875 million, alleging the Bank should have been on notice of a client fraud. After a February–April 2022 trial, the Court ruled for JPMorgan in June 2022 and dismissed the case. Nigeria seeks permission to appeal only as to the 2013 payment of approximately $75 million.
  - Foreign Exchange investigations and litigation: References prior settlements with authorities regarding FX sales/trading activities and related controls, including a May 2015 plea by the Firm (details continue beyond the excerpt).

nodes.title: Foreign Exchange Investigations and Litigation
nodes.heading: 7.24.c Foreign Exchange Investigations and Litigation
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm previously reported settlements with certain government authorities relating to its foreign exchange (“FX”) sales and trading activities and controls related to those activities.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of legal contingencies: The Firm and affiliates face numerous private civil litigations, government investigations, and regulatory enforcement matters across all lines of business and geographies, including class actions and matters involving novel legal theories. Proceedings range from early investigation to trial/arbitration stages and include antitrust, securities, consumer protection, contract, and tort claims.

- Loss range estimate: As of June 30, 2022, the aggregate range of reasonably possible losses in excess of reserves is estimated at $0 to approximately $1.2 billion. This estimate involves significant judgment due to the number and status of cases, multiple defendants with undetermined shares, unresolved issues (e.g., class certification, claim scope), and uncertainty of outcomes. Actual losses may differ and the range will change over time.

- Amrapali (India): Ongoing Enforcement Directorate (ED) investigation into 2010 and 2012 investments by offshore funds in Amrapali Group housing projects; August 2021 ED order fining J.P. Morgan India Private Limited about $31.5 million (being appealed). The Supreme Court of India issued preliminary findings in 2019 referencing currency control and money laundering provisions, directed further ED inquiry under PMLA and FEMA; approximately $25 million attached in May 2020. The Firm is cooperating with the PMLA investigation.

- Federal Republic of Nigeria litigation: JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. operated an escrow/depository account (~$1.1 billion) tied to an oil field dispute; after payouts in 2011 and 2013, the FRN sued in the English High Court for ~$875 million alleging JPMorgan should have been on notice of client fraud. After a Feb–Apr 2022 trial, the Court ruled entirely in JPMorgan’s favor in June 2022; FRN seeks permission to appeal regarding the 2013 ~$75 million payment only.

- Foreign Exchange matters:
  - Government investigations/resolutions: Prior settlements with authorities; in May 2015 the Firm pleaded guilty to one federal antitrust count. The U.S. Department of Labor granted a five-year QPAM exemption under ERISA through January 2023; a further exemption is needed for the remainder of the 10-year disqualification period. One remaining inquiry is before the South Africa Competition Tribunal.
  - Civil litigation: U.S. class action settlement approved in 2018; some class members opted out and filed separate suits, some of which remain pending. Additional putative class actions include consumer currency purchase claims and indirect purchaser claims (the latter settled in 2020 for $10 million with multiple defendants). Related actions are also pending in the U.K., Israel, the Netherlands, Brazil, and Australia; the U.K. Competition Appeal Tribunal denied opt-out class certification.

- Record preservation inquiries: December 2021 SEC and CFTC resolutions over failures to retain certain employee communications on unapproved electronic messaging channels and related supervision lapses. Penalties: $125 million (SEC) for J.P. Morgan Securities LLC and $75 million (CFTC) collectively for J.P. Morgan Securities LLC, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., and J.P. Morgan Securities plc. Ongoing cooperation with additional authorities’ inquiries. A March 2022 shareholder derivative suit in E.D.N.Y. alleges board oversight failures regarding recordkeeping compliance; defendants have moved to dismiss.

- Interchange litigation: Merchants allege Visa/Mastercard and certain banks conspired to fix credit/debit interchange fees and enact anticompetitive rules.
  - Monetary class action: After the 2012 settlement was reversed on appeal, a revised 2018 settlement added $900 million to the ~$5.3 billion escrow; approved by the E.D.N.Y. in December 2019, with appeals pending. Based on opt-outs, $700 million has been returned to defendants from escrow.
  - Injunctive class action: Proceeding separately; partial class certification granted in September 2021.
  - Individual merchant actions with similar allegations remain pending.

nodes.title: Inquiries Concerning Preservation Requirements
nodes.heading: 7.24.d Inquiries Concerning Preservation Requirements
nodes.start_phrase: In December 2021 certain of the Firm’s subsidiaries entered into resolutions with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC”) and the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (“CFTC”) to resolve their respective civil investigations of compliance with records preservation requirements applicable to broker-dealer firms, swap dealers and futures commission merchants.
nodes.summary:
- Antitrust and ERISA QPAM status: Following a guilty plea to a federal antitrust violation, the Firm received a five-year Department of Labor exemption allowing continued reliance on the ERISA QPAM exemption through January 2023; a further exemption is needed for the remainder of the ten-year disqualification period. The only remaining FX-related governmental inquiry is a South Africa Competition Commission matter pending before the South Africa Competition Tribunal.

- FX civil litigation: Final approval in 2018 of a U.S. class action settlement alleging FX rate manipulation; some class members opted out and filed new actions, some of which remain pending. Additional putative class actions include consumer claims over inflated foreign currency purchase rates and indirect purchaser claims (the latter settled in 2020 for $10 million with 11 other defendants). Similar actions are filed outside the U.S. (U.K., Israel, Netherlands, Brazil, Australia). In the U.K., the Competition Appeal Tribunal denied opt-out class certification.

- Records preservation inquiries: In December 2021, settlements with the SEC and CFTC over failures to preserve required communications sent over unapproved electronic channels, and related supervision failures. Penalties paid: $125 million to the SEC and $75 million to the CFTC (covering J.P. Morgan Securities LLC, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., and J.P. Morgan Securities plc). The Firm continues to receive and cooperate with additional inquiries from authorities.

- Shareholder derivative action: Filed March 2022 in the Eastern District of New York against the Firm’s Board, alleging inadequate oversight of records preservation compliance; seeks damages, restitution, disgorgement, and governance reforms. Defendants have moved to dismiss.

- Interchange litigation: Merchants and retail associations allege that Visa, Mastercard, and certain banks conspired to fix credit/debit card interchange fees and impose anticompetitive rules. After a 2012 settlement was reversed on appeal in 2017, the case was split into monetary and injunctive tracks. An amended monetary settlement in 2018 added $900 million to approximately $5.3 billion in escrow; approved in 2019 with appeals pending. Based on opt-outs, $700 million was returned to defendants. The injunctive action continues, with partial class certification granted in 2021. Some individual merchant actions remain pending.

nodes.title: Interchange Litigation
nodes.heading: 7.24.e Interchange Litigation
nodes.start_phrase: Groups of merchants and retail associations filed a series of class action complaints alleging that Visa and Mastercard, as well as certain banks, conspired to set the price of credit and debit card interchange fees and enacted related rules in violation of antitrust laws.
nodes.summary:
- Antitrust/FX matters: The firm pled guilty to a single federal antitrust violation tied to FX. The U.S. Department of Labor granted a five-year QPAM exemption under ERISA through January 2023; a further exemption is needed for the remainder of the ten-year disqualification. The only remaining FX governmental inquiry is a South Africa Competition Commission case pending before the Competition Tribunal.

- FX civil litigation: A U.S. consolidated class action alleging FX rate manipulation (including FX futures/options) received final approval in 2018, though some class members opted out and filed new suits. Additional putative class actions were filed by consumers and indirect purchasers; the indirect purchaser action was settled in 2020 for $10 million with multiple defendants. Related actions are also pending in the U.K., Israel, the Netherlands, Brazil, and Australia; the U.K. tribunal denied opt-out class certification.

- Records preservation inquiries: In December 2021, subsidiaries settled SEC and CFTC investigations over failures to preserve off-channel electronic communications and related supervision lapses. Penalties totaled $125 million (SEC) and $75 million (CFTC), involving J.P. Morgan Securities LLC, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., and J.P. Morgan Securities plc. The firm continues cooperating with other authorities. A March 2022 shareholder derivative suit alleges board oversight failures regarding recordkeeping; defendants moved to dismiss.

- Interchange litigation: Merchants sued Visa, Mastercard, and certain banks (including the firm) for alleged antitrust violations related to credit/debit interchange fees and network rules. After a 2012 settlement was reversed on appeal in 2017, the case split into monetary and injunctive classes. An amended monetary settlement in 2018 added $900 million to a prior $5.3 billion escrow and was approved in 2019; appeals are pending. Due to opt-outs, $700 million was returned to defendants. The injunctive class was certified in part in 2021. Related individual merchant suits remain pending.

nodes.title: LIBOR and Other Benchmark Rate Investigations and Litigation
nodes.heading: 7.24.f LIBOR and Other Benchmark Rate Investigations and Litigation
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase has responded to inquiries from various governmental agencies and entities around the world relating primarily to the British Bankers Association’s (“BBA”) London Interbank Offered Rate (“LIBOR”) for various currencies and the European Banking Federation’s Euro Interbank Offered Rate (“EURIBOR”).
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Legal and regulatory matters involving JPMorgan Chase related to benchmark interest rates (LIBOR/EURIBOR), precious metals and U.S. Treasuries trading, and related securities and shareholder litigation.

- Benchmark rate investigations and litigation:
  - Global regulatory inquiries into BBA-administered LIBOR (multiple currencies) and EBF’s EURIBOR.
  - Ongoing Swiss Competition Commission investigation into EURIBOR; the Firm remains a subject alongside one other bank.
  - European Commission’s December 2016 antitrust decision against the Firm regarding EURIBOR; appeal pending before the European General Court.
  - Multiple individual and putative class actions tied to benchmark rates, including U.S. dollar LIBOR.
  - For BBA-era U.S. dollar LIBOR: some actions dismissed or resolved; others ongoing. SDNY certified an antitrust class covering bonds and interest rate swaps sold directly by defendants (including the Firm).
  - A consolidated putative class action concerning the IBA-administered U.S. dollar LIBOR period was dismissed.
  - Separate individual plaintiffs filed antitrust claims alleging coordination to set U.S. dollar LIBOR and to monopolize markets for LIBOR-based consumer loans and credit cards; defendants moved to dismiss. In December 2021, the court denied plaintiffs’ motions for preliminary injunctions to halt LIBOR setting and enforcement of LIBOR-based instruments.
  - Settlements of putative class actions concerning Swiss franc LIBOR, SIBOR/SOR, and Australian BBSW remain subject to court approval.

- Metals and U.S. Treasuries investigations and follow-on litigation:
  - Resolutions with DOJ, CFTC, and SEC addressing historical trading practices by former employees in precious metals and U.S. Treasuries (2008–2016).
  - Deferred Prosecution Agreement with DOJ: criminal information charging two counts of wire fraud against JPMorgan Chase & Co.; dismissal contemplated after three years upon full compliance by JPMorgan Chase & Co., JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., and J.P. Morgan Securities LLC.
  - Total monetary payments across DOJ, CFTC, and SEC resolutions approximately $920 million, including victim compensation.
  - SDNY putative class actions alleging precious metals futures/options price manipulation under the CEA (and, in some cases, unjust enrichment and New York GBL claims) were consolidated; final settlement approval granted July 2022.
  - Putative class actions alleging manipulation of U.S. Treasury futures/options under the CEA filed in N.D. Illinois and S.D.N.Y.; transferred to and consolidated in S.D.N.Y.; final settlement approval granted June 2022.
  - Related putative class actions in Canada concerning precious metals based on similar alleged conduct.

- Securities and shareholder actions:
  - Two consolidated Securities Exchange Act putative class actions (E.D.N.Y.) filed October 2020 against the Firm and individuals, alleging SEC filings were materially false or misleading for not disclosing information about the above investigations; second amended complaint (May 2021) adds allegations that certain precious metals futures orders during the class period were materially false/misleading; defendants moved to dismiss.
  - A May 2022 shareholder derivative action (N.Y. Supreme Court) alleges breach of fiduciary duty and unjust enrichment by certain current and former officers/directors, contending the Board wrongfully rejected a shareholder demand to commence litigation and seeking relief on the Firm’s behalf.

nodes.title: Metals and U.S. Treasuries Investigations and Litigation and Related Inquiries
nodes.heading: 7.24.g Metals and U.S. Treasuries Investigations and Litigation and Related Inquiries
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm previously reported that it and/ or certain of its subsidiaries had entered into resolutions with the U.S. Department of Justice (“DOJ”), the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (“CFTC”) and the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC”), which, collectively, resolved those agencies’ respective investigations relating to historical trading practices by former employees in the precious metals and U.S. treasuries markets and related conduct from 2008 to 2016.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of JPMorgan Chase’s ongoing legal and regulatory matters focused on benchmark rate investigations, market conduct in metals and U.S. Treasuries, securities lending antitrust claims, and related shareholder litigation.
- LIBOR/EURIBOR matters: global regulatory inquiries; ongoing Swiss Competition Commission EURIBOR investigation; 2016 European Commission antitrust decision against the firm under appeal; multiple U.S. civil actions over U.S. dollar LIBOR with mixed outcomes—some dismissals, some resolved, and others proceeding.
- Class action status on U.S. dollar LIBOR: antitrust class certified in SDNY for bonds and interest rate swaps sold directly by defendants; consolidated class action for the ICE-administered period dismissed; separate individual plaintiffs’ antitrust case alleging collusion in setting USD LIBOR and monopolizing LIBOR-based consumer loans/credit cards—preliminary injunction denied in Dec 2021.
- Benchmark-related settlements pending court approval for class actions tied to Swiss franc LIBOR, Singapore’s SIBOR and SOR, and Australia’s BBSW.
- Metals and U.S. Treasuries investigations: prior resolutions with DOJ, CFTC, and SEC for historical trading practices (2008–2016); Deferred Prosecution Agreement with DOJ (two wire fraud counts) to be dismissed after three years upon full compliance; combined monetary sanctions and payments of approximately $920 million, including victim compensation.
- Civil litigation tied to market conduct: consolidated precious metals and U.S. Treasuries futures/options class actions in SDNY—settlements received final court approval in mid-2022; related putative class actions filed in Canada concerning precious metals.
- Securities Exchange Act class actions (EDNY): claims that firm disclosures were misleading regarding the above investigations; amended complaint adds allegations about false orders in precious metals futures; motion to dismiss pending.
- Shareholder derivative action (May 2022, NY state court): alleges breach of fiduciary duty and unjust enrichment by certain officers/directors, challenges the board’s rejection of litigation demand, seeks damages, disgorgement, and governance reforms related to spoofing conduct and a separate 2020 OCC resolution.
- Securities Lending Antitrust Litigation (SDNY): alleges conspiracy to block anonymous exchange trading for securities lending; motion to dismiss denied; plaintiffs seek class certification, which defendants oppose.
- Broader litigation posture: the firm is involved in numerous additional matters, asserts meritorious defenses, and intends vigorous defense; reserves established for several hundred proceedings under U.S. GAAP; quarterly reassessment of reserves.
- Legal expenses: $73 million for Q2 2022 vs. $185 million for Q2 2021; $192 million for the first half of 2022 vs. $213 million for the first half of 2021.
- Risk statement: outcomes are uncertain and could exceed reserves or carry reputational impact; based on current knowledge, reserves, and estimated loss ranges, pending matters are not expected to be material to the firm’s consolidated financial condition, though individual period results could be affected.

nodes.title: Securities Lending Antitrust Litigation
nodes.heading: 7.24.h Securities Lending Antitrust Litigation
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., J.P. Morgan Securities LLC, J.P. Morgan Prime, Inc., and J.P. Morgan Strategic Securities Lending Corp. are named as defendants in a putative class action filed in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York.
nodes.summary:
- Discussion of shareholder and regulatory-related claims seeking damages, disgorgement, and corporate governance reforms tied to alleged supervisory failures over historical spoofing conduct resolved with the DOJ, CFTC, and SEC in September 2020, and fiduciary activity issues resolved with the OCC in November 2020.
- Description of the Securities Lending Antitrust Litigation in the Southern District of New York, alleging a conspiracy to block anonymous exchange trading for securities lending; JPMorgan entities are defendants, the motion to dismiss was denied, plaintiffs seek class certification, and defendants oppose.
- Statement that JPMorgan Chase and its subsidiaries are involved in numerous additional legal proceedings, with the Firm asserting meritorious defenses and intent to defend vigorously; acknowledgment that new proceedings may arise.
- Outline of litigation reserve practices under U.S. GAAP: accrual when probable and reasonably estimable, quarterly reassessment and adjustments, and reserves established for several hundred matters.
- Reported legal expenses: $73 million (Q2 2022) vs. $185 million (Q2 2021); $192 million (H1 2022) vs. $213 million (H1 2021).
- Cautionary language on uncertainties of legal outcomes, potential for losses, fines, or penalties to exceed reserves, and possible reputational consequences; while the Firm currently believes pending matters should not have a material adverse effect on consolidated financial condition, outcomes could be material to results in specific periods depending on loss size and income levels.

nodes.title: Business segments
nodes.heading: 7.25 Note 25 – Business segments
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm is managed on an LOB basis.
nodes.summary:
- Describes JPMorgan Chase’s line-of-business (LOB) management structure and reportable segments: Consumer & Community Banking, Corporate & Investment Bank, Commercial Banking, Asset & Wealth Management, plus a Corporate segment. Segments are defined by products/services or customer type and align with how the Operating Committee evaluates performance.
- Explains that segment results are presented on a managed (FTE) basis, which adjusts revenue for tax-equivalent effects on tax-advantaged investments; reconciling items remove these adjustments to arrive at U.S. GAAP results. References Note 32 of the 2021 Form 10-K for more detail.
- Outlines capital allocation: equity is assigned to each LOB; allocation assumptions/methodologies are reassessed periodically. References the 2021 Form 10-K for LOB equity details.
- Provides a summary of Q2 2022 vs Q2 2021 firmwide managed results:
  - Total net revenue roughly flat ($30.7B vs $30.5B), with higher net interest income ($15.1B vs $12.7B) offset by lower noninterest revenue ($15.6B vs $17.7B).
  - Provision for credit losses increased to an expense of $1.1B vs a $2.3B release in the prior year.
  - Noninterest expense increased ($18.7B vs $17.7B).
  - Net income declined ($8.65B vs $11.95B); firmwide ROE fell to 13% from 18%; overhead ratio rose to 61 from 58.
  - Total assets grew to $3.84T from $3.68T; average equity was ~$248B (vs ~$251B).
- LOB highlights for Q2 2022 vs Q2 2021 (managed basis):
  - Consumer & Community Banking: total net revenue $12.6B (flat); provision expense $761M vs prior-year release; net income $3.1B vs $5.6B; ROE 24% (vs 44%); assets ~$500B; overhead ratio 61 (vs 55).
  - Corporate & Investment Bank: total net revenue $11.95B (down from $13.21B); net income $3.73B (vs $5.02B); ROE 14% (vs 23%); assets ~$1.40T; overhead ratio 56 (vs 49).
  - Commercial Banking: total net revenue $2.68B (up from $2.48B); net income $994M (vs $1.42B); ROE 15% (vs 23%); assets ~$242B; overhead ratio 43 (vs 40).
  - Asset & Wealth Management: total net revenue $4.31B (up from $4.11B); net income $1.00B (vs $1.16B); ROE 23% (vs 32%); assets ~$236B; overhead ratio 68 (vs 63).
  - Corporate: net loss $174M (improved from $1.30B loss); assets ~$1.46T.
- Reconciling items eliminate FTE tax-equivalent adjustments in arriving at GAAP; reconciling net income is zero in both periods.
- Notes a change in Q1 2022 to the methodology for allocating income taxes to LOBs, with no impact on firmwide net income; prior periods revised for comparability.

nodes.title: Segment results
nodes.heading: 7.25.a Segment results
nodes.start_phrase: The following table provides a summary of the Firm’s segment results as of or for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021 , on a managed basis.
nodes.summary:
- Describes JPMorgan Chase’s business segment reporting (Note 25), stating the firm is managed by lines of business: Consumer & Community Banking (CCB), Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB), Commercial Banking (CB), Asset & Wealth Management (AWM), plus a Corporate segment. nodes.title: Capital allocation
nodes.heading: 7.25.b Capital allocation
nodes.start_phrase: The amount of capital assigned to each business segment is referred to as equity.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose: Note 25 outlines JPMorgan Chase’s business segment reporting and results.
- Segment structure: The Firm is managed on a line-of-business basis with four reportable segments—Consumer & Community Banking (CCB), Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB), Commercial Banking (CB), and Asset & Wealth Management (AWM)—plus a Corporate segment. Segments are based on products/services and customer type and align with how the Operating Committee evaluates performance.
- Managed basis reporting: Results are presented on a managed (FTE) basis that adjusts revenue for tax-exempt income to be comparable with taxable income; related tax effects are reflected in income tax expense. Reconciling items remove these adjustments to arrive at reported U.S. GAAP results.
- Capital allocation: Equity is assigned to each LOB; assumptions and methodologies are reassessed periodically and may change. References are made to the 2021 Form 10-K for further detail.
- Data provided: Detailed tables for the three and six months ended June 30, 2022 and 2021 include noninterest revenue, net interest income, total net revenue, provision for credit losses (PCL), noninterest expense, pretax income, income tax, net income, average equity, total assets, return on equity (ROE), and overhead ratios for each segment, Corporate, reconciling items, and the Firm total.
- Firmwide Q2 2022 vs Q2 2021 highlights:
  - Total net revenue roughly flat (~$30.7B vs ~$30.5B).
  - Net income declined (~$8.6B vs ~$11.9B).
  - PCL swung from a net release to a net build (~+$1.1B vs -$2.3B).
  - Noninterest expense increased; overhead ratio rose (61 vs 58).
  - ROE decreased (13% vs 18%); total assets increased (~$3.84T vs ~$3.68T).
- Segment performance Q2 2022 vs Q2 2021:
  - CCB: Net income down (~$3.1B vs ~$5.6B); ROE 24% vs 44%.
  - CIB: Net income down (~$3.7B vs ~$5.0B); ROE 14% vs 23%.
  - CB: Net income down (~$1.0B vs ~$1.4B); ROE 15% vs 23%.
  - AWM: Net income down (~$1.0B vs ~$1.2B); ROE 23% vs 32%.
  - Corporate: Loss narrowed (~-$0.17B vs ~-$1.3B).
- First half 2022 vs 2021 highlights:
  - Total net revenue slightly lower (~$61.4B vs ~$62.7B).
  - Net income decreased (~$16.9B vs ~$26.2B).
  - PCL shifted from a significant release to a build (~+$2.6B vs -$6.4B).
  - Expenses higher; overhead ratio rose (62 vs 58).
  - ROE decreased (13% vs 21%).
- Average equity context (first half basis): CCB ~$50B, CIB ~$103B (up from ~$83B prior year), CB ~$25B, AWM ~$17B; Firm total ~ $250B.
- Methodology update: In Q1 2022 the Firm changed how it allocates income taxes to LOBs (no impact to Firmwide net income); prior periods were revised accordingly.
- Cross-references: Additional detail on managed basis, segment definitions, and capital allocation is in Note 32 and related sections of the 2021 Form 10-K.

nodes.title: Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm
nodes.heading: 8 Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm
nodes.start_phrase: We have reviewed the accompanying consolidated balance sheet of JPMorgan Chase & Co. and its subsidiaries (the “Firm”) as of J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2, and the related consolidated statements of income, comprehensive income and changes in stockholders’ equity for the three-month and six-month periods ended J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2 and 2021 and the consolidated statements of cash flows for the six-month periods ended J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 2 and 2021 , including the related notes (collectively referred to as the “interim financial statements”).
nodes.summary:
- Independent review: PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP reviewed JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s consolidated interim financial statements as of and for the periods ended June 30, 2022 (three- and six-months) and 2021. Conclusion: no material modifications are needed for conformity with U.S. GAAP.
- Prior audit reference: PwC previously audited the 2021 annual financial statements, issuing an unqualified opinion (Feb. 22, 2022) and noting a 2020 change in accounting for credit losses. The Dec. 31, 2021 balance sheet information presented herein is fairly stated in relation to the audited statements.
- Basis of review: Conducted under PCAOB standards; PwC is independent. Procedures were primarily analytical and inquiry-based, substantially less in scope than an audit; no audit opinion is expressed. Report dated August 3, 2022.
- Unaudited average balance sheet, interest, and rate data:

    - Loans: $1.09T at 4.28% yield vs $1.02T at 3.98%.
    - Investment securities: $672.8B at 1.55% vs $585.1B at 1.31% (taxable-equivalent).
    - Interest-bearing deposits cost: 0.20% vs 0.03%; long-term debt cost: 2.54% vs 1.70%.
    - Net interest income (NII): $15.23B; net yield: 1.80%; interest rate spread: 1.68% (vs $12.85B, 1.62%, and 1.57%).
    - Average noninterest-bearing deposits: $741.9B vs $654.4B.
    - Stockholders’ equity: $280.8B (preferred ~$32.8B; common ~$248.0B).
  - Six months ended June 30, 2022 vs 2021:
    - Average interest-earning assets: $3.39T vs $3.15T; total assets: $3.91T vs $3.67T.
    - Loans: $1.08T at 4.16% vs $1.02T at 4.04%.
    - Investment securities: $672.0B at 1.47% vs $583.8B at 1.34%.
    - Interest-bearing deposits cost: 0.12% vs 0.03%; long-term debt cost: 2.13% vs 1.81%.
    - NII: $29.20B; net yield: 1.74%; spread: 1.64% (vs $25.85B, 1.65%, and 1.61%).
    - Stockholders’ equity: $283.4B (preferred ~$33.2B; common ~$250.2B).

nodes.title: GLOSSARY OF TERMS AND ACRONYMS
nodes.heading: 9 GLOSSARY OF TERMS AND ACRONYMS
nodes.start_phrase: 2021 Form 10-K: Annual report on Form 10-K for year ended December 31, 2021, filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: A comprehensive glossary supporting JPMorgan Chase’s 2021 Form 10-K, defining acronyms and terms used across the report.
- Financial reporting and accounting: Definitions for AFS/HTM, amortized cost, AOCI/OCI, EPS and participating securities, measurement alternative, taxable-equivalent and managed basis reporting, pre-provision profit, overhead ratio, net yield, TBVPS, ROTCE, TCE, FTE.
- Credit quality and loan metrics: Allowance for loan losses ratios, net charge-off rates, nonaccrual loans, nonperforming assets, criticized exposures, collateral-dependent loans, PCD assets, TDRs, warehouse loans, Bridge Financing Portfolio.
- Consumer and mortgage specifics: LTV/CLTV (origination, current estimated, combined), foreclosure status (active/suspended), FICO, HELOCs, MSRs, REO; mortgage product types (Prime, Alt-A, Subprime, Option ARMs).
- Capital, liquidity, and regulatory frameworks: Basel III elements (CET1, RWA, Pillars 1/3, SLR), CCAR/SCB, GSIB, TLAC, LCR/Eligible HQLA, NSFR, Eligible LTD.
- Markets, derivatives, and risk measures: VaR/regulatory VaR, CVA/DVA/FVA, CDS and credit derivatives, ETD vs OTC vs OTC cleared, embedded derivatives, structured notes, master netting, structural interest rate risk, principal transactions revenue.
- Securities and investments: ABS/MBS, U.S. government agencies vs GSEs, G7 government securities, shelf securities, seed capital, measurement terms for AFS impairment.
- Business segments, products, and client metrics: Firm and LOBs (CIB, CCB, CB, AWM), Markets and Macro businesses, Commercial Card, Merchant Services, client assets/AUC, client deposits and third-party liabilities, revenue wallet.
- Benchmarks and rates: LIBOR/IBOR and SOFR, CMT, FX and forward points.
- Entities, regulators, and geography: JPM legal entities (e.g., JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.; J.P. Morgan Securities; JPMSE; IHC), U.S. and international regulators/SROs (SEC, Federal Reserve, OCC, FDIC, CFTC, FINRA, FCA, PRA, NFA, FASB, EC/EU), and country groupings (G7).
- Expense classifications: Definitions of volume/revenue-related, investment, and structural expenses.
- Miscellaneous operational terms: AWM/CB/CCB/CIB acronyms, MSAs used in LTV estimation, PPP, SPEs/VIEs, ROU assets, RSUs/PSUs/SARs, and notation such as NM/NA and unaudited.

- AWM: Definitions of AUM, client assets, multi-asset and alternative investments; outlines business lines (Asset Management, Global Private Bank) and client segments (Private Banking, Global Institutional, Global Funds); details fund performance measures (percentage of AUM in 4- or 5-star ratings; percentage in 1st/2nd quartile over one, three, and five years) with methodology notes on data sources, share-class treatment, currency redenomination, “primary share class” definition, and standard past-performance disclaimers.
